abstract: A novel network type is introduced which uses unit-length 2-vectors for local variables. As an example of its applications, associative memory nets are defined and their performance analyzed. Real systems corresponding to such 'phasor' models can be e.g. (neuro)biological networks of limit-cycle oscillators or optical resonators that have a hologram in their feedback path.
originalAbstract: A novel network type is introduced which uses unit-length 2-vectors for local variables. As an example of its applications, associative memory nets are defined and their performance analyzed. Real systems corresponding to such 'phasor' models can be e.g. (neuro)biological networks of limit-cycle oscillators or optical resonators that have a hologram in their feedback path.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a network whose local state is a two-dimensional vector with fixed unit length. Because the length cannot change, variation in a unit's state is expressed through its direction. This gives the network a phase-like representation, reflected in the name phasor neural network.

The authors use associative memory as an application of this representation. They define memory networks within the phasor framework and analyze their performance. The application connects the proposed local variables to a concrete computational task: storing information in a network that can subsequently retrieve associated information.

The paper also identifies physical systems corresponding to the model, including biological networks of limit-cycle oscillators and optical resonators with a hologram in the feedback path. These examples connect the mathematical representation with systems whose behavior can be described through oscillation and phase. The contribution is a neural-network formulation centered on fixed-length vector states, together with an associative-memory application and possible physical realizations of the same modeling idea.
summary.tldr: Phasor networks use unit-length two-dimensional states, with associative-memory applications and possible oscillator-based physical realizations.

title: Phasor Neural Networks

abstract: Learning procedures that measure how random perturbations of unit ac(cid:173) tivities correlate with changes in reinforcement are inefficient but simple to implement in hardware. Procedures like back-propagation (Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, 1986) which compute how changes in activities af(cid:173) fect the output error are much more efficient, but require more complex hardware. GEMINI is a hybrid procedure for multilayer networks, which shares many of the implementation advantages of correlational reinforce(cid:173) ment procedures but is more efficient. GEMINI injects noise only at the first hidden layer and measures the resultant effect on the output error. A linear network associated with each hidden layer iteratively inverts the matrix which relates the noise to the error change, thereby obtaining the error-derivatives. No back-propagation is involved, thus allowing un(cid:173) known non-linearities in the system. Two simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of GEMINI.

paragraphs: GEMINI addresses a tradeoff between learning efficiency and hardware simplicity. Learning from correlations between random activity changes and reinforcement is straightforward to implement but inefficient. Back-propagation obtains more useful error information efficiently, while requiring more complex hardware. The proposed method combines aspects of these approaches for multilayer networks.

GEMINI injects noise only into the first hidden layer and observes how the output error changes. Each hidden layer has an associated linear network that iteratively inverts a matrix relating the noise to the error change. This process produces error derivatives, supplying information about how activity changes affect the error without propagating derivatives backward through the main network.

Because the method avoids back-propagation, it permits unknown nonlinearities within the system. This connects its learning mechanism to the implementation problem that motivates the paper. The abstract reports greater efficiency than correlational reinforcement procedures while retaining many of their implementation advantages. Two simulations demonstrate the method's effectiveness, supporting the proposed combination of perturbation-based measurement and matrix-based derivative estimation.
summary.tldr: GEMINI estimates error derivatives through injected noise and iterative matrix inversion, enabling learning without back-propagation through unknown nonlinearities.

title: GEMINI: Gradient Estimation Through Matrix Inversion After Noise Injection

paragraphs: The paper investigates learning a decoder for complex binary error-correcting codes from examples. Each training example supplies a received word together with its decoded result, allowing a connectionist system to learn the required mapping. The goal is an approach that can develop decoders while keeping their construction simple and their resulting architecture compact.

The authors describe two solutions. The Cascaded Networks Decoder addresses the problem at the system level. The ECC-Enhanced Decoder instead simplifies the mapping that the learning system must solve. This distinction matters because the difficulty of learning a decoder depends partly on how the decoding problem is presented to the network.

Both designs satisfy the authors' requirements for simplicity and compactness, but only the ECC-Enhanced Decoder satisfies their additional requirement of generality. The result therefore separates two kinds of success: building a manageable decoder and providing a method applicable across complex binary codes. The abstract identifies the enhanced formulation as the design that meets both aims.
summary.tldr: Two learned decoder designs achieve simplicity and compactness, but only the ECC-Enhanced Decoder meets the authors' generality requirement.

title: Adaptive Development of Connectionist Decoders for Complex Error-Correcting Codes

abstract: Human VlSlon systems integrate information nonlocally, across long spatial ranges. For example, a moving stimulus appears smeared when viewed briefly (30 ms), yet sharp when viewed for a longer exposure (100 ms) (Burr, 1980). This suggests that visual systems combine information along a trajectory that matches the motion of the stimulus. Our self-organizing neural network model shows how developmental exposure to moving stimuli can direct the formation of horizontal trajectory-specific motion integration pathways that unsmear representations of moving stimuli. These results account for Burr's data and can potentially also model ot.her phenomena, such as visual inertia.

paragraphs: The paper addresses why a moving stimulus can appear smeared during a brief exposure yet look sharp when viewed for longer. The supplied observation contrasts exposures of 30 and 100 milliseconds. It suggests that visual processing combines information across space along a path that follows the stimulus's motion.

The authors propose a self-organizing neural network in which exposure to moving stimuli shapes the development of horizontal connections. These connections form pathways specialized for particular motion trajectories. By integrating activity along those trajectories, the model can produce sharper representations of moving stimuli, linking the development of connectivity to a specific perceptual function.

The reported results account for the exposure-dependent sharpening in Burr's observations. They also suggest a possible application to visual inertia, which is presented as a potential extension. The core contribution is a developmental explanation: experience with motion can organize long-range pathways that subsequently combine visual information in a way that reduces motion smear.
summary.tldr: A self-organizing visual network learns trajectory-specific connections that sharpen moving-stimulus representations through motion-aligned integration.

title: Unsmearing Visual Motion: Development of Long-Range Horizontal Intrinsic Connections

abstract: The wake-sleep algorithm (Hinton, Dayan, Frey and Neal 1995) is a rel(cid:173) atively efficient method of fitting a multilayer stochastic generative model to high-dimensional data. In addition to the top-down connec(cid:173) tions in the generative model, it makes use of bottom-up connections for approximating the probability distribution over the hidden units given the data, and it trains these bottom-up connections using a simple delta rule. We use a variety of synthetic and real data sets to compare the per(cid:173) formance of the wake-sleep algorithm with Monte Carlo and mean field methods for fitting the same generative model and also compare it with other models that are less powerful but easier to fit.

In addition to the top-down connec(cid:173) tions in the generative model, it makes use of bottom-up connections for approximating the probability distribution over the hidden units given the data, and it trains these bottom-up connections using a simple delta rule. We use a variety of synthetic and real data sets to compare the per(cid:173) formance of the wake-sleep algorithm with Monte Carlo and mean field methods for fitting the same generative model and also compare it with other models that are less powerful but easier to fit.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates wake-sleep as a way to fit multilayer stochastic generative models to high-dimensional data. Such a model describes observed data through hidden variables and probabilistic relationships. The question is whether an efficient training method also produces a useful estimate of the data distribution.

Wake-sleep combines top-down generative connections with bottom-up connections that approximate the distribution of hidden units given an observation. The bottom-up pathway provides an approximate account of which hidden configurations could explain the input. It is trained using a simple delta rule, making this recognition pathway part of the algorithm's computational strategy.

The authors compare wake-sleep with Monte Carlo and mean field methods for fitting the same generative model, using both synthetic and real datasets. They also compare against models that are less expressive but easier to fit. These two comparisons address different questions: how well the training algorithm uses a fixed model, and whether a more powerful model is worthwhile in practice. The supplied abstract describes this evaluation without announcing a winning method.
summary.tldr: The paper compares wake-sleep density estimation with alternative training methods and simpler, easier-to-fit models.

title: Does the Wake-sleep Algorithm Produce Good Density Estimators?

abstract: A new approach for clustering is proposed. This method is based on an analogy to a physical model; the ferromagnetic Potts model at thermal equilibrium is used as an analog computer for this hard optimization problem . We do not assume any structure of the underlying distribution of the data. Phase space of the Potts model is divided into three regions; ferromagnetic, super-paramagnetic and paramagnetic phases. The region of interest is that corresponding to the super-paramagnetic one, where domains of aligned spins appear. The range of temperatures where these structures are stable is indicated by a non-vanishing magnetic susceptibility. We use a very efficient Monte Carlo algorithm to measure the susceptibility and the spin spin correlation function. The values of the spin spin correlation function, at the super-paramagnetic phase, serve to identify the partition of the data points into clusters.

The region of interest is that corresponding to the super-paramagnetic one, where domains of aligned spins appear. The range of temperatures where these structures are stable is indicated by a non-vanishing magnetic susceptibility. paragraphs: The paper proposes a clustering method based on the ferromagnetic Potts model, a physical system whose interacting spins can form aligned groups. The authors use its equilibrium behavior as a computational analogy for dividing data into clusters. Their approach does not assume a particular structure for the probability distribution underlying the data.

The relevant physical model has ferromagnetic, super-paramagnetic, and paramagnetic regions. The method focuses on the super-paramagnetic region, where separate domains of aligned spins appear. These domains provide the organizing idea for clusters: groups emerge through collective behavior within the model. Magnetic susceptibility indicates the temperature range over which these structures remain stable.

An efficient Monte Carlo algorithm estimates both susceptibility and correlations between spins. The correlations measured in the super-paramagnetic region determine how data points are partitioned. Susceptibility thus helps identify the useful operating region, while correlation supplies the grouping information. The contribution is a clustering procedure that turns measurable properties of a simulated physical system into evidence about which data points belong together.
summary.tldr: The method identifies data clusters through stable aligned domains and spin correlations in a simulated Potts model.

title: Clustering data through an analogy to the Potts model

abstract: In this paper, we present a novel hybrid architecture for continuous speech recognition systems. It consists of a continuous HMM system extended by an arbitrary neural network that is used as a preprocessor that takes several frames of the feature vector as input to produce more discrimin(cid:173) ative feature vectors with respect to the underlying HMM system. This hybrid system is an extension of a state-of-the-art continuous HMM sys(cid:173) tem, and in fact, it is the first hybrid system that really is capable of outper(cid:173) forming these standard systems with respect to the recognition accuracy. Experimental results show an relative error reduction of about 10% that we achieved on a remarkably good recognition system based on continu(cid:173) ous HMMs for the Resource Management 1 OOO-word continuous speech recognition task.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we present a novel hybrid architecture for continuous speech recognition systems. It consists of a continuous HMM system extended by an arbitrary neural network that is used as a preprocessor that takes several frames of the feature vector as input to produce more discrimin(cid:173) ative feature vectors with respect to the underlying HMM system. This hybrid system is an extension of a state-of-the-art continuous HMM sys(cid:173) tem, and in fact, it is the first hybrid system that really is capable of outper(cid:173) forming these standard systems with respect to the recognition accuracy. Experimental results show an relative error reduction of about 10% that we achieved on a remarkably good recognition system based on continu(cid:173) ous HMMs for the Resource Management 1 OOO-word continuous speech recognition task.

paragraphs: This paper improves continuous speech recognition by adding a learned feature-processing stage to an existing continuous hidden Markov model system. The neural network serves as a preprocessor: it transforms acoustic information into features designed to help the underlying recognizer distinguish speech patterns. The architecture therefore preserves the HMM's role while changing the information it receives.

The network takes several frames of feature vectors as input, allowing its output to depend on a short sequence rather than an isolated frame. Its purpose is to make those outputs more discriminative for the particular HMM system. The architecture permits an arbitrary neural network, making the contribution a general way to connect neural feature extraction with continuous HMM recognition.

On the Resource Management 1,000-word continuous speech task, the authors report about a 10% relative error reduction over an already strong continuous-HMM system. Relative reduction means a decrease in the existing error level, not a ten-percentage-point increase in accuracy. The finding supports improving the recognizer through task-directed preprocessing.
summary.tldr: Neural preprocessing of multiple speech frames improves a continuous-HMM recognizer, yielding about a 10% relative error reduction.

title: Hybrid NN/HMM-Based Speech Recognition with a Discriminant Neural Feature Extraction

abstract: In many classification tasks, recognition accuracy is low because input patterns are corrupted by noise or are spatially or temporally overlapping. We propose an approach to overcoming these limitations based on a model of human selective attention. The model, an early selection filter guided by top-down attentional control, entertains each candidate output class in sequence and adjusts attentional gain coefficients in order to produce a strong response for that class. The chosen class is then the one that obtains the strongest response with the least modulation of attention. We present simulation results on classification of corrupted and superimposed handwritten digit patterns, showing a significant improvement in recognition rates. The algorithm has also been applied in the domain of speech recognition, with comparable results.

We propose an approach to overcoming these limitations based on a model of human selective attention. The model, an early selection filter guided by top-down attentional control, entertains each candidate output class in sequence and adjusts attentional gain coefficients in order to produce a strong response for that class. The chosen class is then the one that obtains the strongest response with the least modulation of attention. We present simulation results on classification of corrupted and superimposed handwritten digit patterns, showing a significant improvement in recognition rates. The algorithm has also been applied in the domain of speech recognition, with comparable results.

paragraphs: Noise and overlapping patterns can make recognition difficult because the input contains signals that interfere with one another. This paper proposes a recognition method inspired by human selective attention. It combines an early filtering stage with top-down control, allowing candidate interpretations to influence how the input is emphasized.

The model considers each possible output class in turn. For each candidate, it adjusts attention gain coefficients to produce a strong response for that class. The final choice favors the class obtaining the strongest response with the least attentional modulation. This makes the amount of adjustment part of the decision, alongside the strength of the class response.

Simulations on corrupted and superimposed handwritten digits show a significant improvement in recognition rates. The algorithm is also applied to speech recognition, with comparable results reported. These findings support using controlled attention to handle interference during classification. The key idea is an active recognition process: candidate classes guide filtering, and the resulting responses help determine which interpretation best fits the input.
summary.tldr: A selective-attention model tests candidate classes by adjusting input gains, improving recognition of noisy and overlapping patterns.

title: Robust Recognition of Noisy and Superimposed Patterns via Selective Attention

abstract: For many problems which would be natural for reinforcement learning, the reward signal is not a single scalar value but has multiple scalar com(cid:173) ponents. Examples of such problems include agents with multiple goals and agents with multiple users. Creating a single reward value by com(cid:173) bining the multiple components can throwaway vital information and can lead to incorrect solutions. We describe the multiple reward source problem and discuss the problems with applying traditional reinforce(cid:173) ment learning. We then present an new algorithm for finding a solution and results on simulated environments.
originalAbstract: For many problems which would be natural for reinforcement learning, the reward signal is not a single scalar value but has multiple scalar com(cid:173) ponents. Examples of such problems include agents with multiple goals and agents with multiple users. Creating a single reward value by com(cid:173) bining the multiple components can throwaway vital information and can lead to incorrect solutions. We describe the multiple reward source problem and discuss the problems with applying traditional reinforce(cid:173) ment learning. We then present an new algorithm for finding a solution and results on simulated environments.

paragraphs: This paper examines reinforcement learning problems in which feedback has several numerical components. An agent may pursue multiple goals or serve multiple users, so its rewards naturally come from more than one source. The learning problem must therefore account for several pieces of evaluative information about the agent's behavior.

The authors argue that combining these components into a single reward can discard information that is important to the solution. Once different sources have been merged, the learner may lose distinctions that matter to the original problem. The abstract states that this can lead to incorrect solutions, making reward representation a substantive part of the learning problem.

The paper describes this multiple-reward setting, discusses difficulties with applying traditional reinforcement learning, and introduces an algorithm for finding a solution. It also presents results in simulated environments. The contribution is to treat multiple reward sources explicitly and connect that formulation to a learning method, rather than assume that producing one combined number fully preserves the task.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces an algorithm for reinforcement learning with multiple reward sources, where combining rewards can lose essential information.

title: Balancing Multiple Sources of Reward in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: High dimensional data that lies on or near a low dimensional manifold can be described by a collection of local linear models. Such a description, however, does not provide a global parameterization of the manifold—arguably an important goal of unsupervised learning. In this paper, we show how to learn a collection of local linear models that solves this more difficult problem. Our local linear models are represented by a mixture of factor analyzers, and the “global coordination” of these models is achieved by adding a regularizing term to the standard maximum likelihood objective function. The regularizer breaks a degeneracy in the mixture model’s parameter space, favoring models whose internal coordinate systems are aligned in a consistent way. As a result, the internal coordinates change smoothly and continuously as one traverses a connected path on the manifold—even when the path crosses the domains of many different local models. The regularizer takes the form of a Kullback-Leibler divergence and illustrates an unexpected application of variational methods: not to perform approximate inference in intractable probabilistic models, but to learn more useful internal representations in tractable ones.

Such a description, however, does not provide a global parameterization of the manifold—arguably an important goal of unsupervised learning. In this paper, we show how to learn a collection of local linear models that solves this more difficult problem. Our local linear models are represented by a mixture of factor analyzers, and the “global coordination” of these models is achieved by adding a regularizing term to the standard maximum likelihood objective function. The regularizer breaks a degeneracy in the mixture model’s parameter space, favoring models whose internal coordinate systems are aligned in a consistent way. As a result, the internal coordinates change smoothly and continuously as one traverses a connected path on the manifold—even when the path crosses the domains of many different local models. The regularizer takes the form of a Kullback-Leibler divergence and illustrates an unexpected application of variational methods: not to perform approximate inference in intractable probabilistic models, but to learn more useful internal representations in tractable ones.

paragraphs: High-dimensional observations can lie near a surface with far fewer underlying dimensions. A collection of local linear models can describe separate parts of that surface, but those models need not share compatible coordinates. Moving between their regions can therefore fail to provide a coherent global description of the data.

The paper represents the local models as a mixture of factor analyzers and adds a regularization term to maximum-likelihood learning. The regularizer favors consistent alignment of their internal coordinate systems. It resolves a freedom in the mixture’s parameterization that otherwise permits locally valid but mutually uncoordinated representations.

The resulting internal coordinates vary smoothly and continuously along connected paths on the manifold, including paths crossing several local models. The regularizer is expressed as a Kullback-Leibler divergence. This gives variational methods a representation-learning role: they help choose useful internal coordinates even though the probabilistic models already permit tractable inference. The contribution links local statistical descriptions to a coordinated representation of the overall manifold.
summary.tldr: A KL-divergence regularizer aligns local factor-analyzer coordinates into a smooth global representation of a data manifold.

title: Global Coordination of Local Linear Models

abstract: We give results about the learnability and required complexity of logical formulae to solve classiﬁcation problems. These results are obtained by linking propositional logic with kernel machines. In particular we show that decision trees and disjunctive normal forms (DNF) can be repre- sented by the help of a special kernel, linking regularized risk to separa- tion margin. Subsequently we derive a number of lower bounds on the required complexity of logic formulae using properties of algorithms for generation of linear estimators, such as perceptron and maximal percep- tron learning.
originalAbstract: We give results about the learnability and required complexity of logical formulae to solve classiﬁcation problems. These results are obtained by linking propositional logic with kernel machines. In particular we show that decision trees and disjunctive normal forms (DNF) can be repre- sented by the help of a special kernel, linking regularized risk to separa- tion margin. Subsequently we derive a number of lower bounds on the required complexity of logic formulae using properties of algorithms for generation of linear estimators, such as perceptron and maximal percep- tron learning.

paragraphs: This paper connects classification by logical formulas with classification by kernel machines. It asks both whether logical representations can be learned and how complex they must be to solve a classification problem. The connection creates a way to study symbolic rules through properties of a geometric learning representation.

The authors show that a special kernel can represent decision trees and disjunctive normal forms. They also link regularized risk to the separation margin, connecting an objective that accounts for prediction and regularization with the geometric separation of classes. This provides a bridge between the structure of logical classifiers and quantities studied in kernel learning.

The paper then derives several lower bounds on the complexity required of logical formulas. These bounds use properties of algorithms that generate linear estimators, including perceptron and maximal perceptron learning. Their significance is that they constrain how simple a successful logical solution can be, while the kernel representation provides the mathematical route for obtaining those constraints.
summary.tldr: A kernel representation of logical classifiers connects margins and regularized risk to lower bounds on formula complexity.

title: Kernel Machines and Boolean Functions

abstract: Decision trees are surprisingly adaptive in three important respects: They automatically (1) adapt to favorable conditions near the Bayes decision boundary; (2) focus on data distributed on lower dimensional manifolds; (3) reject irrelevant features. In this paper we examine a decision tree based on dyadic splits that adapts to each of these conditions to achieve minimax optimal rates of convergence. The proposed classifier is the first known to achieve these optimal rates while being practical and im- plementable.
originalAbstract: Decision trees are surprisingly adaptive in three important respects: They automatically (1) adapt to favorable conditions near the Bayes decision boundary; (2) focus on data distributed on lower dimensional manifolds; (3) reject irrelevant features. In this paper we examine a decision tree based on dyadic splits that adapts to each of these conditions to achieve minimax optimal rates of convergence. The proposed classifier is the first known to achieve these optimal rates while being practical and im- plementable.

paragraphs: The paper examines how decision trees can take advantage of structure that makes a classification problem easier. It considers three favorable conditions: useful behavior near the Bayes decision boundary, data concentrated on lower-dimensional manifolds, and features that are irrelevant to the prediction task. Each offers a different opportunity for adaptation.

The authors study a particular decision tree based on dyadic splits. They show that this classifier adapts to each of the three conditions and achieves minimax-optimal convergence rates. In plain language, the theoretical claim concerns how quickly learning improves as data increase, relative to the best possible worst-case rate for the corresponding setting.

The paper also emphasizes that the proposed classifier is practical and implementable, describing it as the first known method to combine these optimal rates with that property. The contribution links statistical guarantees to a concrete tree construction. The optimality claim applies to the classifier and conditions analyzed, rather than automatically extending to every decision-tree algorithm.
summary.tldr: A practical dyadic decision tree achieves minimax-optimal learning rates by adapting to favorable boundaries, low-dimensional data, and irrelevant features.

title: On the Adaptive Properties of Decision Trees

abstract: Linear text classiﬁcation algorithms work by computing an inner prod- uct between a test document vector and a parameter vector. In many such algorithms, including naive Bayes and most TFIDF variants, the parame- ters are determined by some simple, closed-form, function of training set statistics; we call this mapping mapping from statistics to parameters, the parameter function. Much research in text classiﬁcation over the last few decades has consisted of manual efforts to identify better parameter func- tions. In this paper, we propose an algorithm for automatically learning this function from related classiﬁcation problems. The parameter func- tion found by our algorithm then deﬁnes a new learning algorithm for text classiﬁcation, which we can apply to novel classiﬁcation tasks. We ﬁnd that our learned classiﬁer outperforms existing methods on a variety of multiclass text classiﬁcation tasks. arg maxk2f1;:::;KgPn

paragraphs: Many linear text classifiers score a document by taking an inner product between its document vector and a parameter vector. In methods such as naive Bayes and many TFIDF variants, a simple function converts training-set statistics into those parameters. The paper calls this conversion the parameter function and makes it the object of learning.

The authors propose learning the parameter function automatically from related classification problems. Once learned, the function defines a text-classification learning algorithm that can be applied to new tasks. The transferred object is therefore a rule for turning a task's training statistics into classifier parameters.

This approach replaces a manually designed part of the learning algorithm with one learned across related problems. The authors find that their resulting classifier outperforms existing methods on a variety of multiclass text-classification tasks. The findings support transfer at the level of the parameter-construction rule: experience across tasks can inform how a classifier is built for a new task, rather than only supplying parameters for one fixed classification problem.
summary.tldr: The paper learns a reusable mapping from training statistics to classifier parameters and reports improved performance across multiclass text tasks.

title: Transfer learning for text classification

abstract: We utilize the ensemble of trees framework, a tractable mixture over super- exponential number of tree-structured distributions [1], to develop a new model for multivariate density estimation. The model is based on a construction of tree- structured copulas – multivariate distributions with uniform on [0, 1] marginals. By averaging over all possible tree structures, the new model can approximate distributions with complex variable dependencies. We propose an EM algorithm to estimate the parameters for these tree-averaged models for both the real-valued and the categorical case. Based on the tree-averaged framework, we propose a new model for joint precipitation amounts data on networks of rain stations.
originalAbstract: We utilize the ensemble of trees framework, a tractable mixture over super- exponential number of tree-structured distributions [1], to develop a new model for multivariate density estimation. The model is based on a construction of tree- structured copulas – multivariate distributions with uniform on [0, 1] marginals. By averaging over all possible tree structures, the new model can approximate distributions with complex variable dependencies. We propose an EM algorithm to estimate the parameters for these tree-averaged models for both the real-valued and the categorical case. Based on the tree-averaged framework, we propose a new model for joint precipitation amounts data on networks of rain stations.

paragraphs: Estimating a multivariate distribution requires describing both individual variables and their dependencies. This paper develops a model that averages over tree-structured distributions. A single tree offers a restricted pattern of relationships, but combining many trees allows the model to approximate more complex dependencies while using a framework in which the mixture remains tractable.

The construction uses tree-structured copulas: joint distributions whose individual variables each have a uniform distribution between zero and one. This provides a way to express dependence through the joint distribution. The model averages over every possible tree structure, drawing on an ensemble framework that handles a super-exponential number of trees without making the mixture computationally intractable.

The authors propose an expectation-maximization algorithm to estimate parameters for both real-valued and categorical tree-averaged models. They also use the framework to propose a model of joint rainfall amounts across a network of weather stations. That application gives a concrete setting where dependencies among multiple measurement locations are central to the modeling problem.
summary.tldr: Tractable averaging over tree-structured copulas provides a multivariate model for complex dependencies, with EM learning and a rainfall application.

title: Learning with Tree-Averaged Densities and Distributions

abstract: This paper discusses non-parametric regression between Riemannian manifolds. This learning problem arises frequently in many application areas ranging from signal processing, computer vision, over robotics to computer graphics. We present a new algorithmic scheme for the solution of this general learning problem based on regularized empirical risk minimization. The regularization functional takes into account the geometry of input and output manifold, and we show that it implements a prior which is particularly natural. Moreover, we demonstrate that our algorithm performs well in a difficult surface registration problem.

The abstract identifies applications across signal processing, computer vision, robotics, and computer graphics, motivating a general method that incorporates the geometry on both sides.

The authors propose an algorithmic scheme based on regularized empirical risk minimization. This combines fitting the observed data with a regularization term that expresses preferences about the learned relationship. Crucially, the regularizer takes account of both the input manifold and the output manifold. The paper shows that this construction implements a prior the authors characterize as particularly natural.

The approach is demonstrated on a difficult surface-registration problem, where the authors report good performance. That application gives a concrete setting in which a relationship must be learned between geometric objects. The contribution is a general regression formulation whose fitting criterion explicitly includes manifold geometry, together with evidence that the resulting algorithm can work well on a demanding registration task.
summary.tldr: A regularized regression framework incorporates input and output manifold geometry and performs well on a difficult surface-registration task.

title: Non-parametric Regression Between Manifolds

abstract: In this paper we introduce Context-Sensitive Decision Forests - A new perspective to exploit contextual information in the popular decision forest framework for the object detection problem. They are tree-structured classifiers with the ability to access intermediate prediction (here: classification and regression) information during training and inference time. This intermediate prediction is available to each sample, which allows us to develop context-based decision criteria, used for refining the prediction process. In addition, we introduce a novel split criterion which in combination with a priority based way of constructing the trees, allows more accurate regression mode selection and hence improves the current context information. In our experiments, we demonstrate improved results for the task of pedestrian detection on the challenging TUD data set when compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: The paper introduces decision forests that use intermediate predictions as contextual information during object detection. Each sample can access classification and regression information produced within the prediction process. This capability is available during both training and inference, allowing later decisions to take account of predictions already being formed.

The authors use this information to define context-dependent decision criteria that refine the prediction process. They also propose a new splitting criterion and a priority-based procedure for constructing trees. Together, these changes allow more accurate selection of regression modes, which improves the context available to the forest. Intermediate predictions consequently become information that the model can use in further decisions.

Experiments on pedestrian detection using the TUD dataset show improved results relative to the compared state-of-the-art methods. The evidence supports the proposed use of evolving prediction information in that detection setting. The broader methodological contribution is a decision-forest framework in which context participates directly in the tree-based prediction process.
summary.tldr: Context-sensitive decision forests reuse intermediate predictions to refine object detection, improving reported pedestrian-detection results.

title: Context-Sensitive Decision Forests for Object Detection

abstract: Analytic shrinkage is a statistical technique that offers a fast alternative to cross-validation for the regularization of covariance matrices and has appealing consistency properties. We show that the proof of consistency implies bounds on the growth rates of eigenvalues and their dispersion, which are often violated in data. We prove consistency under assumptions which do not restrict the covariance structure and therefore better match real world data. In addition, we propose an extension of analytic shrinkage --orthogonal complement shrinkage-- which adapts to the covariance structure. Finally we demonstrate the superior performance of our novel approach on data from the domains of finance, spoken letter and optical character recognition, and neuroscience.

paragraphs: Estimating a covariance matrix involves learning how variables vary together. The paper revisits the theoretical consistency of this approach, examining what its supporting proof actually requires of the covariance matrix.

The authors show that the existing consistency argument implies restrictions on how eigenvalues grow and how dispersed they can be. These restrictions are often violated in data. They then prove consistency under assumptions that do not constrain the covariance structure. This broadens the structural scope of the guarantee while retaining an assumption-based theoretical result.

The paper also introduces orthogonal complement shrinkage, an extension designed to adapt to covariance structure. Evaluations cover finance, spoken-letter recognition, optical character recognition, and neuroscience, with superior performance reported for the new approach. The work therefore contributes both a revised foundation for analytic shrinkage and an adaptive method whose benefits are demonstrated across several kinds of data.
summary.tldr: The paper broadens consistency guarantees for analytic covariance shrinkage and introduces a structure-adaptive extension with improved empirical performance.

title: Generalizing Analytic Shrinkage for Arbitrary Covariance Structures

abstract: To extract motion information, the brain needs to compensate for time delays that are ubiquitous in neural signal transmission and processing. Here we propose a simple yet effective mechanism to implement anticipative tracking in neural systems. The proposed mechanism utilizes the property of spike-frequency adaptation (SFA), a feature widely observed in neuronal responses. We employ continuous attractor neural networks (CANNs) as the model to describe the tracking behaviors in neural systems. Incorporating SFA, a CANN exhibits intrinsic mobility, manifested by the ability of the CANN to hold self-sustained travelling waves. In tracking a moving stimulus, the interplay between the external drive and the intrinsic mobility of the network determines the tracking performance. Interestingly, we find that the regime of anticipation effectively coincides with the regime where the intrinsic speed of the travelling wave exceeds that of the external drive. Depending on the SFA amplitudes, the network can achieve either perfect tracking, with zero-lag to the input, or perfect anticipative tracking, with a constant leading time to the input. Our model successfully reproduces experimentally observed anticipative tracking behaviors, and sheds light on our understanding of how the brain processes motion information in a timely manner.

summary.tldr: Spike-frequency adaptation gives a neural tracking model intrinsic motion that can produce zero-lag or anticipatory tracking under suitable conditions.

title: Spike Frequency Adaptation Implements Anticipative Tracking in Continuous Attractor Neural Networks

abstract: Self-paced learning (SPL) is a recently proposed learning regime inspired by the learning process of humans and animals that gradually incorporates easy to more complex samples into training. Existing methods are limited in that they ignore an important aspect in learning: diversity. To incorporate this information, we propose an approach called self-paced learning with diversity (SPLD) which formalizes the preference for both easy and diverse samples into a general regularizer. This regularization term is independent of the learning objective, and thus can be easily generalized into various learning tasks. Albeit non-convex, the optimization of the variables included in this SPLD regularization term for sample selection can be globally solved in linearithmic time. We demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the conventional SPL on three real-world datasets. Specifically, SPLD achieves the best MAP so far reported in literature on the Hollywood2 and Olympic Sports datasets.

paragraphs: Self-paced learning gradually introduces training examples from easier to more complex ones. This paper argues that difficulty alone leaves out an important consideration: diversity among the selected examples. The proposed method, self-paced learning with diversity, explicitly favors examples that are both easy and diverse as training proceeds.

The authors express these preferences through a general regularization term. Because that term is independent of the learning objective, the approach can be adapted to different learning tasks. Although the sample-selection optimization is nonconvex, the variables in this regularizer can be optimized globally in linearithmic time. That guarantee concerns the selection subproblem, rather than global optimization of every model trained with it.

Experiments on three real-world datasets show significant improvements over conventional self-paced learning. On Hollywood2 and Olympic Sports, the method achieves the highest mean average precision reported in the literature considered by the paper. The findings support treating diversity as an explicit part of a training curriculum, alongside example difficulty, with both an efficient selection procedure and empirical evidence in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Adding diversity to self-paced sample selection improves reported results while allowing globally optimal, efficient optimization of the selection regularizer.

title: Self-Paced Learning with Diversity

abstract: Multilayer Neural Networks (MNNs) are commonly trained using gradient descent-based methods, such as BackPropagation (BP). Inference in probabilistic graphical models is often done using variational Bayes methods, such as Expectation Propagation (EP). We show how an EP based approach can also be used to train deterministic MNNs. Specifically, we approximate the posterior of the weights given the data using a “mean-field” factorized distribution, in an online setting. Using online EP and the central limit theorem we find an analytical approximation to the Bayes update of this posterior, as well as the resulting Bayes estimates of the weights and outputs. Despite a different origin, the resulting algorithm, Expectation BackPropagation (EBP), is very similar to BP in form and efficiency. However, it has several additional advantages: (1) Training is parameter-free, given initial conditions (prior) and the MNN architecture. This is useful for large-scale problems, where parameter tuning is a major challenge. (2) The weights can be restricted to have discrete values. This is especially useful for implementing trained MNNs in precision limited hardware chips, thus improving their speed and energy efficiency by several orders of magnitude. We test the EBP algorithm numerically in eight binary text classification tasks. In all tasks, EBP outperforms: (1) standard BP with the optimal constant learning rate (2) previously reported state of the art. Interestingly, EBP-trained MNNs with binary weights usually perform better than MNNs with continuous (real) weights - if we average the MNN output using the inferred posterior.

paragraphs: The paper develops a Bayesian approach to training deterministic multilayer neural networks. It approximates the posterior distribution of weights with a factorized, mean-field distribution in an online setting. Using expectation propagation and the central limit theorem, the authors derive analytical approximations to posterior updates and to estimates of network weights and outputs.

The resulting expectation backpropagation algorithm resembles ordinary backpropagation in form and efficiency. Its training is parameter-free once the prior and network architecture are specified. It also permits discrete weights, which the authors identify as useful for precision-limited hardware with potential speed and energy-efficiency advantages. The prior and architecture remain part of the setup.

On eight binary text classification tasks, expectation backpropagation outperforms standard backpropagation with the optimal constant learning rate and previously reported state-of-the-art results. Networks with binary weights usually perform better than those with continuous weights when outputs are averaged using the inferred posterior. That qualification matters: the reported binary-weight advantage concerns posterior-averaged predictions, rather than an unconditional advantage of binary weights.
summary.tldr: Expectation backpropagation derives efficient Bayesian training updates for continuous or discrete network weights, given a prior and architecture.

title: Expectation Backpropagation: Parameter-Free Training of Multilayer Neural Networks with Continuous or Discrete Weights

abstract: The Frank-Wolfe (FW) optimization algorithm has lately re-gained popularity thanks in particular to its ability to nicely handle the structured constraints appearing in machine learning applications. However, its convergence rate is known to be slow (sublinear) when the solution lies at the boundary. A simple less-known fix is to add the possibility to take away steps' during optimization, an operation that importantly does not require a feasibility oracle. In this paper, we highlight and clarify several variants of the Frank-Wolfe optimization algorithm that has been successfully applied in practice: FW with away steps, pairwise FW, fully-corrective FW and Wolfe's minimum norm point algorithm, and prove for the first time that they all enjoy global linear convergence under a weaker condition than strong convexity. The constant in the convergence rate has an elegant interpretation as the product of the (classical) condition number of the function with a novel geometric quantity that plays the role of the condition number' of the constraint set. We provide pointers to where these algorithms have made a difference in practice, in particular with the flow polytope, the marginal polytope and the base polytope for submodular optimization.

paragraphs: Frank-Wolfe optimization is attractive for machine-learning problems with structured constraints, but its convergence can be slow when the solution lies on the boundary. The paper examines variants that improve this behavior, including the use of away steps. Such steps add flexibility during optimization without requiring a feasibility oracle.

The authors clarify four algorithms: Frank-Wolfe with away steps, pairwise Frank-Wolfe, fully corrective Frank-Wolfe, and Wolfe’s minimum norm point algorithm. They prove global linear convergence for all four under a condition weaker than strong convexity. Linear convergence describes a geometric reduction in error, providing a stronger rate than the sublinear behavior highlighted for ordinary Frank-Wolfe.

The rate constant combines the objective’s condition number with a new geometric quantity describing the constraint set. This interpretation connects convergence to both the function being optimized and the feasible region’s shape. The paper also points to practical uses involving flow, marginal, and submodular base polytopes, linking its theoretical analysis to structured optimization applications.
summary.tldr: Four Frank-Wolfe variants receive global linear convergence guarantees under a condition weaker than strong convexity.

title: On the Global Linear Convergence of Frank-Wolfe Optimization Variants

abstract: We present a framework for efficient inference in structured image models that explicitly reason about objects. We achieve this by performing probabilistic inference using a recurrent neural network that attends to scene elements and processes them one at a time. Crucially, the model itself learns to choose the appropriate number of inference steps. We use this scheme to learn to perform inference in partially specified 2D models (variable-sized variational auto-encoders) and fully specified 3D models (probabilistic renderers). We show that such models learn to identify multiple objects - counting, locating and classifying the elements of a scene - without any supervision, e.g., decomposing 3D images with various numbers of objects in a single forward pass of a neural network at unprecedented speed. We further show that the networks produce accurate inferences when compared to supervised counterparts, and that their structure leads to improved generalization.

paragraphs: Understanding a scene can involve identifying its individual objects, including how many there are, where they appear, and what they are. This paper presents an inference framework for image models that explicitly represent objects. A recurrent neural network attends to scene elements and processes them sequentially, making probabilistic inferences about the scene.

A central feature is that the model learns how many inference steps to take. This lets the inference process accommodate scenes containing different numbers of objects. The authors apply the framework both to partially specified two-dimensional models, expressed as variable-sized variational autoencoders, and to fully specified three-dimensional models based on probabilistic renderers.

The reported models learn to count, locate, and classify multiple objects without supervision. The paper demonstrates decomposition of three-dimensional images in a single neural-network forward pass at very high speed. It also reports accurate inference relative to supervised counterparts and improved generalization arising from the network structure. These findings connect explicit object reasoning with efficient learned inference.
summary.tldr: A recurrent attention model learns to infer objects and choose its own number of processing steps, enabling fast unsupervised scene understanding.

title: Attend, Infer, Repeat: Fast Scene Understanding with Generative Models

abstract: With the newly proposed privacy definition of Rényi Differential Privacy (RDP) in (Mironov, 2017), we re-examine the inherent privacy of releasing a single sample from a posterior distribution. We exploit the impact of the prior distribution in mitigating the influence of individual data points. In particular, we focus on sampling from an exponential family and specific generalized linear models, such as logistic regression. We propose novel RDP mechanisms as well as offering a new RDP analysis for an existing method in order to add value to the RDP framework. Each method is capable of achieving arbitrary RDP privacy guarantees, and we offer experimental results of their efficacy.

We propose novel RDP mechanisms as well as offering a new RDP analysis for an existing method in order to add value to the RDP framework. paragraphs: Releasing a sample from a Bayesian posterior produces a randomized output influenced by the underlying data. This paper studies the privacy of releasing one such sample using Rényi differential privacy, or RDP. The analysis asks how posterior sampling can limit the effect that an individual data point has on the released result.

A central ingredient is the prior distribution. The authors exploit its ability to moderate the influence of individual observations, making the prior part of the privacy mechanism. Their focus is sampling in exponential-family settings and specific generalized linear models, including logistic regression. This gives the work a concrete statistical scope.

The paper introduces new RDP mechanisms and supplies an RDP analysis of an existing method. Each method can achieve arbitrary RDP privacy guarantees, and experiments provide evidence of efficacy. The contribution combines mechanism design with privacy accounting, showing how posterior sampling and prior choice can be used within the RDP framework for the model families considered.
summary.tldr: The paper develops and analyzes Rényi-private posterior-sampling mechanisms that use priors to limit individual observations' influence.

title: Renyi Differential Privacy Mechanisms for Posterior Sampling

abstract: We study the question of fair clustering under the {\em disparate impact} doctrine, where each protected class must have approximately equal representation in every cluster. We formulate the fair clustering problem under both the k-center and the k-median objectives, and show that even with two protected classes the problem is challenging, as the optimum solution can violate common conventions---for instance a point may no longer be assigned to its nearest cluster center! En route we introduce the concept of fairlets, which are minimal sets that satisfy fair representation while approximately preserving the clustering objective. We show that any fair clustering problem can be decomposed into first finding good fairlets, and then using existing machinery for traditional clustering algorithms. While finding good fairlets can be NP-hard, we proceed to obtain efficient approximation algorithms based on minimum cost flow. We empirically demonstrate the \emph{price of fairness} by quantifying the value of fair clustering on real-world datasets with sensitive attributes.

paragraphs: This paper studies clustering with a representation requirement: every cluster should contain approximately equal representation from each protected class. It formulates this requirement for both k-center and k-median objectives. Even with only two protected classes, fairness can change familiar clustering behavior, including making the optimal assignment place a point somewhere other than its nearest center.

The main device is a fairlet, a minimal group that satisfies the representation requirement while approximately preserving the clustering objective. The authors show how fair clustering can be split into finding suitable fairlets and then applying existing clustering algorithms. This decomposition gives ordinary clustering machinery a way to operate on groups that already satisfy the fairness requirement.

Finding good fairlets can itself be NP-hard. The paper nevertheless develops efficient approximation algorithms using minimum-cost flow. Experiments on real datasets with sensitive attributes quantify the price of fairness. This makes the tradeoff concrete: enforcing representation changes the clustering objective, and the method provides a structured way to obtain and assess fair solutions.
summary.tldr: Fairlets turn representation-constrained clustering into a fair grouping step followed by conventional clustering.

title: Fair Clustering Through Fairlets

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a robust algorithm, \textsl{TranSync}, for the 1D translation synchronization problem, in which the aim is to recover the global coordinates of a set of nodes from noisy measurements of relative coordinates along an observation graph. The basic idea of TranSync is to apply truncated least squares, where the solution at each step is used to gradually prune out noisy measurements. We analyze TranSync under both deterministic and randomized noisy models, demonstrating its robustness and stability. Experimental results on synthetic and real datasets show that TranSync is superior to state-of-the-art convex formulations in terms of both efficiency and accuracy.

The basic idea of TranSync is to apply truncated least squares, where the solution at each step is used to gradually prune out noisy measurements. We analyze TranSync under both deterministic and randomized noisy models, demonstrating its robustness and stability. Experimental results on synthetic and real datasets show that TranSync is superior to state-of-the-art convex formulations in terms of both efficiency and accuracy.

paragraphs: Translation synchronization reconstructs global coordinates from measurements of relative coordinates. This paper considers the one-dimensional case, where measurements are available along the edges of an observation graph and contain noise. The task is to combine those local relationships into a coherent set of positions despite unreliable measurements.

The proposed algorithm, TranSync, uses truncated least squares. At each step, the current coordinate estimate helps identify measurements to prune, gradually removing noisy information from the calculation. Estimation and pruning therefore work together: a solution informs which observations remain, and the retained observations support the next solution. This iterative procedure is the central mechanism for robustness.

The authors analyze robustness and stability under both deterministic and randomized noise models. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show better efficiency and accuracy than state-of-the-art convex formulations. The contribution combines a concrete strategy for progressively rejecting noisy measurements with theoretical analysis and empirical comparisons, supporting truncated least squares as an effective approach to the stated one-dimensional synchronization problem.
summary.tldr: TranSync reconstructs one-dimensional coordinates by iteratively pruning noisy relative measurements with truncated least squares.

title: Translation Synchronization via Truncated Least Squares

abstract: In this paper, we study the problems of principle Generalized Eigenvector computation and Canonical Correlation Analysis in the stochastic setting. We propose a simple and efficient algorithm for these problems. We prove the global convergence of our algorithm, borrowing ideas from the theory of fast-mixing Markov chains and two-Time-Scale Stochastic Approximation, showing that it achieves the optimal rate of convergence. In the process, we develop tools for understanding stochastic processes with Markovian noise which might be of independent interest.

We propose a simple and efficient algorithm for these problems. We prove the global convergence of our algorithm, borrowing ideas from the theory of fast-mixing Markov chains and two-Time-Scale Stochastic Approximation, showing that it achieves the optimal rate of convergence. In the process, we develop tools for understanding stochastic processes with Markovian noise which might be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Gen-Oja addresses principal generalized eigenvector computation and canonical correlation analysis in a stochastic setting. The paper proposes a simple, efficient algorithm for these problems, with streaming computation as its focus. Its central contribution is not only an update procedure but also a theoretical account of how that procedure converges.

The authors prove global convergence and show that the algorithm achieves an optimal convergence rate. Their analysis draws on fast-mixing Markov chains and stochastic approximation with two time scales. Bringing these ideas together provides a way to reason about the evolving stochastic process behind the computation and to establish how quickly the algorithm approaches its target.

In developing the proof, the paper also produces tools for studying stochastic processes with Markovian noise. Such noise has dependence across successive steps, making its behavior relevant to the analysis rather than something that can simply be treated as independent variation. The authors suggest that these tools may be useful beyond the two problems studied, giving the work a possible methodological contribution alongside its algorithmic guarantees.
summary.tldr: Gen-Oja provides a simple stochastic algorithm for generalized eigenvectors and canonical correlation analysis with global convergence at an optimal rate.

title: Gen-Oja: Simple & Efficient Algorithm for Streaming Generalized Eigenvector Computation

abstract: Expectation-Maximization (EM) is a popular tool for learning latent variable models, but the vanilla batch EM does not scale to large data sets because the whole data set is needed at every E-step. Stochastic Expectation Maximization (sEM) reduces the cost of E-step by stochastic approximation. However, sEM has a slower asymptotic convergence rate than batch EM, and requires a decreasing sequence of step sizes, which is difficult to tune. In this paper, we propose a variance reduced stochastic EM (sEM-vr) algorithm inspired by variance reduced stochastic gradient descent algorithms. We show that sEM-vr has the same exponential asymptotic convergence rate as batch EM. Moreover, sEM-vr only requires a constant step size to achieve this rate, which alleviates the burden of parameter tuning. We compare sEM-vr with batch EM, sEM and other algorithms on Gaussian mixture models and probabilistic latent semantic analysis, and sEM-vr converges significantly faster than these baselines.

Stochastic Expectation Maximization (sEM) reduces the cost of E-step by stochastic approximation. However, sEM has a slower asymptotic convergence rate than batch EM, and requires a decreasing sequence of step sizes, which is difficult to tune. In this paper, we propose a variance reduced stochastic EM (sEM-vr) algorithm inspired by variance reduced stochastic gradient descent algorithms. We show that sEM-vr has the same exponential asymptotic convergence rate as batch EM. Moreover, sEM-vr only requires a constant step size to achieve this rate, which alleviates the burden of parameter tuning. We compare sEM-vr with batch EM, sEM and other algorithms on Gaussian mixture models and probabilistic latent semantic analysis, and sEM-vr converges significantly faster than these baselines.

paragraphs: Expectation-Maximization learns models with latent variables, but standard batch EM needs the entire dataset at every expectation step. Stochastic EM reduces that cost through stochastic approximation. Its tradeoffs include slower asymptotic convergence and a decreasing step-size schedule that can be difficult to tune, creating a tension between cheaper updates and the progress those updates achieve.

The paper introduces variance-reduced stochastic EM, inspired by variance-reduction methods for stochastic gradient descent. The authors show that it attains the same exponential asymptotic convergence rate as batch EM. It achieves that rate with a constant step size, reducing the need to design a sequence of progressively smaller steps.

Experiments compare the method with batch EM, ordinary stochastic EM, and other algorithms on Gaussian mixture models and probabilistic latent semantic analysis. The proposed method converges significantly faster in those comparisons. The contribution thus combines a convergence-rate result with a simpler step-size requirement and empirical evidence of faster learning on two latent-variable modeling tasks.
summary.tldr: Variance-reduced stochastic EM matches batch EM's exponential asymptotic convergence rate with a constant step size and converges faster in reported experiments.

title: Stochastic Expectation Maximization with Variance Reduction

abstract: Monte Carlo sampling in high-dimensional, low-sample settings is important in many machine learning tasks. We improve current methods for sampling in Euclidean spaces by avoiding independence, and instead consider ways to couple samples. We show fundamental connections to optimal transport theory, leading to novel sampling algorithms, and providing new theoretical grounding for existing strategies. We compare our new strategies against prior methods for improving sample efficiency, including QMC, by studying discrepancy. We explore our findings empirically, and observe benefits of our sampling schemes for reinforcement learning and generative modelling.

We explore our findings empirically, and observe benefits of our sampling schemes for reinforcement learning and generative modelling.

This paper investigates sampling in Euclidean spaces under those conditions. Its central move is to coordinate samples through dependence rather than requiring them to be independent.

The authors establish connections between this coupling of samples and optimal transport theory. Those connections lead to new sampling algorithms and provide theoretical explanations for existing strategies. The approach makes the relationship among samples part of the design problem, offering a geometric way to reason about how a limited collection of samples is arranged.

The paper compares the proposed strategies with earlier sample-efficiency methods, including quasi-Monte Carlo, through the study of discrepancy. It also explores their behavior empirically and observes benefits in reinforcement learning and generative modeling. These findings support coupled sampling as a useful strategy in the investigated settings, with both a theoretical foundation and evidence from applications.
summary.tldr: Geometrically coupling samples through optimal-transport ideas improves sampling strategies and shows empirical benefits in learning applications.

title: Geometrically Coupled Monte Carlo Sampling

abstract: The inherent noise of neural systems makes it difficult to construct models which accurately capture experimental measurements of their activity. While much research has been done on how to efficiently model neural activity with descriptive models such as linear-nonlinear-models (LN), Bayesian inference for mechanistic models has received considerably less attention. One reason for this is that these models typically lead to intractable likelihoods and thus make parameter inference difficult. Here, we develop an approximate Bayesian inference scheme for a fully stochastic, biophysically inspired model of glutamate release at the ribbon synapse, a highly specialized synapse found in different sensory systems. The model translates known structural features of the ribbon synapse into a set of stochastically coupled equations. We approximate the posterior distributions by updating a parametric prior distribution via Bayesian updating rules and show that model parameters can be efficiently estimated for synthetic and experimental data from in vivo two-photon experiments in the zebrafish retina. Also, we find that the model captures complex properties of the synaptic release such as the temporal precision and outperforms a standard GLM. Our framework provides a viable path forward for linking mechanistic models of neural activity to measured data.

Mechanistic models can describe those processes, but their likelihoods are often too difficult to evaluate for straightforward parameter inference. This paper addresses that obstacle for glutamate release at ribbon synapses, specialized synapses found in sensory systems.

The authors translate known structural features of the synapse into coupled stochastic equations. They then develop an approximate Bayesian procedure that updates a parametric prior to approximate posterior distributions over model parameters. The aim is to infer the parameters of a biologically motivated, fully stochastic model while retaining a representation of uncertainty about those parameters.

The method efficiently estimates parameters from both synthetic data and in vivo two-photon measurements in the zebrafish retina. The authors report that the model captures complex release behavior, including temporal precision, and outperforms a standard generalized linear model. These results provide a concrete demonstration that approximate inference can make a mechanistic account of synaptic activity usable with experimental measurements.
summary.tldr: Approximate Bayesian inference makes a stochastic, biologically motivated model of ribbon-synapse release tractable for synthetic and retinal data.

title: Approximate Bayesian Inference for a Mechanistic Model of Vesicle Release at a Ribbon Synapse

abstract: Imitation Learning (IL) has been successfully applied to complex sequential decision-making problems where standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms fail. A number of recent methods extend IL to few-shot learning scenarios, where a meta-trained policy learns to quickly master new tasks using limited demonstrations. However, although Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) often outperforms Behavioral Cloning (BC) in terms of imitation quality, most of these approaches build on BC due to its simple optimization objective. In this work, we propose SMILe, a scalable framework for Meta Inverse Reinforcement Learning (Meta-IRL) based on maximum entropy IRL, which can learn high-quality policies from few demonstrations. We examine the efficacy of our method on a variety of high-dimensional simulated continuous control tasks and observe that SMILe significantly outperforms Meta-BC. Furthermore, we observe that SMILe performs comparably or outperforms Meta-DAgger, while being applicable in the state-only setting and not requiring online experts. To our knowledge, our approach is the first efficient method for Meta-IRL that scales to the function approximator setting. For datasets and reproducing results please refer to https://github.com/KamyarGh/rl swiss/blob/master/reproducing/smile paper.md .

Many approaches use behavioral cloning because its optimization objective is simple, even though inverse reinforcement learning often produces better imitation. This paper introduces SMILe to make meta inverse reinforcement learning practical at a larger scale.

SMILe builds on maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning and uses context-conditional policies. Its purpose is to learn high-quality behavior from limited demonstrations while scaling to the function approximator setting. The authors evaluate it on a variety of simulated continuous control tasks with high-dimensional inputs or control problems.

In those evaluations, SMILe significantly outperforms Meta-BC and performs comparably to or better than Meta-DAgger. It can also operate with state-only demonstrations and does not require an online expert, making the information requirements an important part of the comparison. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first efficient Meta-IRL method to scale to function approximators. The findings support inverse reinforcement learning as a workable basis for rapid imitation across tasks.
summary.tldr: SMILe scales meta inverse reinforcement learning to learn from few demonstrations, outperforming Meta-BC and matching or exceeding Meta-DAgger in simulated control.

title: SMILe: Scalable Meta Inverse Reinforcement Learning through Context-Conditional Policies

abstract: The nonparametric learning of positive-valued functions appears widely in machine learning, especially in the context of estimating intensity functions of point processes. Yet, existing approaches either require computing expensive projections or semidefinite relaxations, or lack convexity and theoretical guarantees after introducing nonlinear link functions. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm, pseudo mirror descent, that performs efficient estimation of positive functions within a Hilbert space without expensive projections. The algorithm guarantees positivity by performing mirror descent with an appropriately selected Bregman divergence, and a pseudo-gradient is adopted to speed up the gradient evaluation procedure in practice. We analyze both asymptotic and nonasymptotic convergence of the algorithm. Through simulations, we show that pseudo mirror descent outperforms the state-of-the-art benchmarks for learning intensities of Poisson and multivariate Hawkes processes, in terms of both computational efficiency and accuracy.
