paragraphs: Some learning problems require an estimated function to remain positive, including the intensity functions used to describe point processes. Enforcing positivity can complicate optimization. The paper describes existing approaches that require costly projections or semidefinite relaxations, or that introduce nonlinear link functions at the expense of convexity and theoretical guarantees.

Pseudo mirror descent estimates positive functions in a Hilbert space without expensive projection steps. It uses mirror descent with a carefully chosen Bregman divergence to guarantee positivity. A pseudo-gradient accelerates gradient evaluation in practice. The approach therefore addresses the constraint through the optimization geometry while separately reducing the work required to calculate updates.

The authors analyze convergence both asymptotically and with nonasymptotic results, covering limiting behavior and behavior before that limit. Simulations estimate intensities for Poisson and multivariate Hawkes processes. In those experiments, the method outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks in computational efficiency and accuracy. The findings support an approach that combines guaranteed positivity, convergence analysis, and practical speed for the intensity-learning tasks examined.
summary.tldr: Pseudo mirror descent guarantees positive function estimates without costly projections and improves simulated point-process intensity learning.

title: Learning Positive Functions with Pseudo Mirror Descent

abstract: This paper is concerned with multi-view reinforcement learning (MVRL), which allows for decision making when agents share common dynamics but adhere to different observation models. We define the MVRL framework by extending partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) to support more than one observation model and propose two solution methods through observation augmentation and cross-view policy transfer. We empirically evaluate our method and demonstrate its effectiveness in a variety of environments. Specifically, we show reductions in sample complexities and computational time for acquiring policies that handle multi-view environments.
originalAbstract: This paper is concerned with multi-view reinforcement learning (MVRL), which allows for decision making when agents share common dynamics but adhere to different observation models. We define the MVRL framework by extending partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) to support more than one observation model and propose two solution methods through observation augmentation and cross-view policy transfer. We empirically evaluate our method and demonstrate its effectiveness in a variety of environments. Specifically, we show reductions in sample complexities and computational time for acquiring policies that handle multi-view environments.

paragraphs: Different agents can interact with the same underlying dynamics while receiving different observations. Multi-view reinforcement learning formalizes decision making in this setting. The shared part is how the environment evolves; the differing part is how that environment is observed. This distinction creates an opportunity to connect learning across views.

The paper extends partially observable Markov decision processes so that a single framework supports multiple observation models. It then proposes two solution methods: observation augmentation and cross-view policy transfer. These methods provide routes for using observations or learned decision policies across the multiple views covered by the framework.

Experiments in a variety of environments demonstrate reduced sample requirements and computation time when acquiring policies that handle multiple views. The findings suggest that accounting explicitly for shared dynamics can make learning more efficient in the tested settings. The contribution combines a formal description of the problem with practical methods and empirical evidence for their effectiveness.
summary.tldr: A multi-view reinforcement-learning framework shares learning across observation models to reduce policy-learning samples and computation in experiments.

title: Multi-View Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Unsupervised text attribute transfer automatically transforms a text to alter a specific attribute (e.g. sentiment) without using any parallel data, while simultaneously preserving its attribute-independent content. The dominant approaches are trying to model the content-independent attribute separately, e.g., learning different attributes' representations or using multiple attribute-specific decoders. However, it may lead to inflexibility from the perspective of controlling the degree of transfer or transferring over multiple aspects at the same time. To address the above problems, we propose a more flexible unsupervised text attribute transfer framework which replaces the process of modeling attribute with minimal editing of latent representations based on an attribute classifier. Specifically, we first propose a Transformer-based autoencoder to learn an entangled latent representation for a discrete text, then we transform the attribute transfer task to an optimization problem and propose the Fast-Gradient-Iterative-Modification algorithm to edit the latent representation until conforming to the target attribute. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves very competitive performance on three public data sets. Furthermore, we also show that our model can not only control the degree of transfer freely but also allow to transfer over multiple aspects at the same time.

paragraphs: Text attribute transfer changes a property such as sentiment while aiming to preserve the content independent of that property. The unsupervised setting lacks paired examples of the same content expressed with different attributes. The paper addresses the difficulty of controlling how much an attribute changes, or changing several attributes together, in approaches that model attributes separately.

The method begins with a Transformer-based autoencoder that learns a latent representation in which content and attributes remain entangled. An attribute classifier then guides small edits to that representation. The authors formulate transfer as an optimization problem and introduce Fast-Gradient-Iterative-Modification, which repeatedly modifies the representation until it conforms to the desired attribute.

This shifts the mechanism of control toward editing a shared representation rather than relying on separate attribute-specific representations or decoders. Experiments on three public datasets show very competitive performance. The authors also demonstrate control over the degree of transfer and the ability to modify multiple aspects simultaneously, supporting the framework’s intended flexibility across different requested transformations.
summary.tldr: Classifier-guided edits to entangled text representations enable attribute transfer with controllable strength and simultaneous changes to multiple aspects.

title: Controllable Unsupervised Text Attribute Transfer via Editing Entangled Latent Representation

abstract: Although deep convolutional neural networks achieve state-of-the-art performance across nearly all image classification tasks, their decisions are difficult to interpret. One approach that offers some level of interpretability by design is \textit{hard attention}, which uses only relevant portions of the image. However, training hard attention models with only class label supervision is challenging, and hard attention has proved difficult to scale to complex datasets. Here, we propose a novel hard attention model, which we term Saccader. Key to Saccader is a pretraining step that requires only class labels and provides initial attention locations for policy gradient optimization. Our best models narrow the gap to common ImageNet baselines, achieving $75\%$ top-1 and $91\%$ top-5 while attending to less than one-third of the image.

paragraphs: Hard-attention image classifiers make decisions using selected portions of an image. Those selections offer some interpretability because they expose the regions used by the model. However, learning where to look from class labels alone is challenging, and such models have been difficult to scale to complex image-classification datasets.

The paper introduces Saccader, a hard-attention model whose central ingredient is a pretraining stage requiring only class labels. This stage supplies initial attention locations for subsequent policy-gradient optimization. It gives the attention-learning process a starting point obtained from the same type of supervision used for classification.

The best reported models achieve 75% top-1 and 91% top-5 accuracy on ImageNet while attending to less than one-third of the image. These results narrow the gap to common ImageNet baselines. The contribution shows that class-label-based pretraining can support effective hard attention at this scale, while preserving the model's use of selected image regions as part of its decision process.
summary.tldr: Saccader uses class-label-only pretraining to improve hard attention, reaching 75% ImageNet top-1 accuracy while attending to under one-third of each image.

title: Saccader: Improving Accuracy of Hard Attention Models for Vision

abstract: Nearest neighbor is a popular class of classification methods with many desirable properties. For a large data set which cannot be loaded into the memory of a single machine due to computation, communication, privacy, or ownership limitations, we consider the divide and conquer scheme: the entire data set is divided into small subsamples, on which nearest neighbor predictions are made, and then a final decision is reached by aggregating the predictions on subsamples by majority voting. We name this method the big Nearest Neighbor (bigNN) classifier, and provide its rates of convergence under minimal assumptions, in terms of both the excess risk and the classification instability, which are proven to be the same rates as the oracle nearest neighbor classifier and cannot be improved. To significantly reduce the prediction time that is required for achieving the optimal rate, we also consider the pre-training acceleration technique applied to the bigNN method, with proven convergence rate. We find that in the distributed setting, the optimal choice of the neighbor k should scale with both the total sample size and the number of partitions, and there is a theoretical upper limit for the latter. Numerical studies have verified the theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification becomes harder to organize when a dataset cannot reside on one machine because of computational, communication, privacy, or ownership constraints. The paper studies a divide-and-conquer approach called bigNN. Each smaller data partition produces a nearest-neighbor prediction, and majority voting combines those predictions into a final classification.

The authors establish convergence rates for both excess risk and classification instability under minimal assumptions. These rates match those of an oracle nearest-neighbor classifier and are shown to be unimprovable in the analyzed setting. They also study a pre-training acceleration technique that substantially reduces the prediction time needed to achieve the optimal rate, with a convergence guarantee of its own.

The analysis identifies a coordination requirement across partitions: the best choice of neighbor count depends on both the total sample size and the number of partitions. It also establishes a theoretical upper limit on partition count. Numerical studies verify the theoretical findings, supporting distributed classification while showing that partitioning and local neighbor selection must be chosen together.
summary.tldr: Distributed nearest-neighbor voting achieves optimal convergence rates under the analyzed assumptions, with theory guiding partition counts, neighbor selection, and prediction acceleration.

title: Rates of Convergence for Large-scale Nearest Neighbor Classification

abstract: The squared Wasserstein distance is a natural quantity to compare probability distributions in a non-parametric setting. This quantity is usually estimated with the plug-in estimator, defined via a discrete optimal transport problem which can be solved to $\epsilon$-accuracy by adding an entropic regularization of order $\epsilon$ and using for instance Sinkhorn's algorithm. In this work, we propose instead to estimate it with the Sinkhorn divergence, which is also built on entropic regularization but includes debiasing terms. We show that, for smooth densities, this estimator has a comparable sample complexity but allows higher regularization levels, of order $\epsilon^{1/2}$, which leads to improved computational complexity bounds and a strong speedup in practice. Our theoretical analysis covers the case of both randomly sampled densities and deterministic discretizations on uniform grids. We also propose and analyze an estimator based on Richardson extrapolation of the Sinkhorn divergence which enjoys improved statistical and computational efficiency guarantees, under a condition on the regularity of the approximation error, which is in particular satisfied for Gaussian densities. We finally demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed estimators with numerical experiments.

paragraphs: The squared Wasserstein distance compares probability distributions through an optimal transport problem. Estimating it commonly involves a discrete approximation, with entropic regularization making computation more manageable. This paper proposes using the Sinkhorn divergence, which adds debiasing terms, to improve the computational cost of estimating the same underlying quantity.

For smooth densities, the authors show comparable sample complexity while permitting stronger regularization. To achieve accuracy epsilon, the regularization can scale with the square root of epsilon rather than epsilon. This yields better computational complexity bounds and substantial practical speedups. The analysis covers both distributions represented by random samples and deterministic discretizations on uniform grids.

The paper also studies an estimator using Richardson extrapolation of the Sinkhorn divergence to improve statistical and computational efficiency further. Those additional guarantees require a regularity condition on the approximation error, which holds for Gaussian densities. Numerical experiments demonstrate the estimators' efficiency. The central result connects debiasing to greater freedom to regularize, with explicit smoothness and regularity conditions supporting the theoretical improvements.
summary.tldr: For smooth densities, debiased Sinkhorn estimators permit stronger regularization and faster squared Wasserstein distance estimation.

title: Faster Wasserstein Distance Estimation with the Sinkhorn Divergence

abstract: Consider learning a policy purely on the basis of demonstrated behavior---that is, with no access to reinforcement signals, no knowledge of transition dynamics, and no further interaction with the environment. This *strictly batch imitation learning* problem arises wherever live experimentation is costly, such as in healthcare. One solution is simply to retrofit existing algorithms for apprenticeship learning to work in the offline setting. But such an approach leans heavily on off-policy evaluation or offline model estimation, and can be indirect and inefficient. We argue that a good solution should be able to explicitly parameterize a policy (i.e. respecting action conditionals), implicitly learn from rollout dynamics (i.e. leveraging state marginals), and---crucially---operate in an entirely offline fashion. To address this challenge, we propose a novel technique by *energy-based distribution matching* (EDM): By identifying parameterizations of the (discriminative) model of a policy with the (generative) energy function for state distributions, EDM yields a simple but effective solution that equivalently minimizes a divergence between the occupancy measure for the demonstrator and a model thereof for the imitator. Through experiments with application to control and healthcare settings, we illustrate consistent performance gains over existing algorithms for strictly batch imitation learning.

paragraphs: Strictly batch imitation learning means learning behavior entirely from demonstrations, without rewards, known transition dynamics, or further interaction with the environment. This setting matters where live experimentation is costly, including healthcare. The paper seeks a direct approach that learns both action choices and information about the states encountered in demonstrated behavior.

Energy-based distribution matching, or EDM, links the parameterization of a policy model with an energy function describing state distributions. This couples a model of actions conditioned on states with a model of which states occur. The construction is equivalent to minimizing a divergence between the demonstrator's occupancy measure and a corresponding model for the imitator.

The coupling allows the method to use state-distribution information while keeping an explicit policy and operating entirely offline. It addresses the authors' concern that adapting apprenticeship-learning algorithms can depend indirectly on off-policy evaluation or estimated dynamics. Experiments in control and healthcare settings show consistent gains over existing strictly batch imitation algorithms, supporting the usefulness of this joint treatment of actions and visited states.
summary.tldr: EDM links policy learning with energy-based state modeling to improve imitation learning using only a fixed batch of demonstrations.

title: Strictly Batch Imitation Learning by Energy-based Distribution Matching

abstract: We study reinforcement learning in continuous state and action spaces endowed with a metric. We provide a refined analysis of the algorithm of Sinclair, Banerjee, and Yu (2019) and show that its regret scales with the zooming dimension of the instance. This parameter, which originates in the bandit literature, captures the size of the subsets of near optimal actions and is always smaller than the covering dimension used in previous analyses. As such, our results are the first provably adaptive guarantees for reinforcement learning in metric spaces.
originalAbstract: We study reinforcement learning in continuous state and action spaces endowed with a metric. We provide a refined analysis of the algorithm of Sinclair, Banerjee, and Yu (2019) and show that its regret scales with the zooming dimension of the instance. This parameter, which originates in the bandit literature, captures the size of the subsets of near optimal actions and is always smaller than the covering dimension used in previous analyses. As such, our results are the first provably adaptive guarantees for reinforcement learning in metric spaces.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with continuous states and actions needs a way to account for how large and complicated those spaces are. This paper considers spaces equipped with a metric, which provides a notion of distance. It revisits an existing algorithm and sharpens the analysis of its regret, the performance loss associated with learning rather than already acting optimally.

The refined guarantee depends on the instance's zooming dimension. This quantity captures the size of the sets of nearly optimal actions, so it focuses on the portions of the problem that contain promising decisions. Earlier analyses used covering dimension, a broader measure of the space's complexity; the abstract states that zooming dimension is always smaller.

The significance is that the guarantee reflects the structure of the particular learning problem instead of relying only on the full space's dimension. The contribution is a refined analysis of an existing algorithm. The authors identify it as the first provably adaptive guarantee for reinforcement learning in metric spaces.
summary.tldr: A refined regret analysis makes continuous-space reinforcement-learning guarantees depend on the complexity of nearly optimal actions.

title: Provably adaptive reinforcement learning in metric spaces

abstract: In this work we propose a graph-based learning framework to train models with provable robustness to adversarial perturbations. In contrast to regularization-based approaches, we formulate the adversarially robust learning problem as one of loss minimization with a Lipschitz constraint, and show that the saddle point of the associated Lagrangian is characterized by a Poisson equation with weighted Laplace operator. Further, the weighting for the Laplace operator is given by the Lagrange multiplier for the Lipschitz constraint, which modulates the sensitivity of the minimizer to perturbations. We then design a provably robust training scheme using graph-based discretization of the input space and a primal-dual algorithm to converge to the Lagrangian's saddle point. Our analysis establishes a novel connection between elliptic operators with constraint-enforced weighting and adversarial learning. We also study the complementary problem of improving the robustness of minimizers with a margin on their loss, formulated as a loss-constrained minimization problem of the Lipschitz constant. We propose a technique to obtain robustified minimizers, and evaluate fundamental Lipschitz lower bounds by approaching Lipschitz constant minimization via a sequence of gradient $p$-norm minimization problems. Ultimately, our results show that, for a desired nominal performance, there exists a fundamental lower bound on the sensitivity to adversarial perturbations that depends only on the loss function and the data distribution, and that improvements in robustness beyond this bound can only be made at the expense of nominal performance. Our training schemes provably achieve these bounds both under constraints on performance and~robustness.
originalAbstract: In this work we propose a graph-based learning framework to train models with provable robustness to adversarial perturbations. In contrast to regularization-based approaches, we formulate the adversarially robust learning problem as one of loss minimization with a Lipschitz constraint, and show that the saddle point of the associated Lagrangian is characterized by a Poisson equation with weighted Laplace operator. Further, the weighting for the Laplace operator is given by the Lagrange multiplier for the Lipschitz constraint, which modulates the sensitivity of the minimizer to perturbations. We then design a provably robust training scheme using graph-based discretization of the input space and a primal-dual algorithm to converge to the Lagrangian's saddle point. Our analysis establishes a novel connection between elliptic operators with constraint-enforced weighting and adversarial learning. We also study the complementary problem of improving the robustness of minimizers with a margin on their loss, formulated as a loss-constrained minimization problem of the Lipschitz constant. We propose a technique to obtain robustified minimizers, and evaluate fundamental Lipschitz lower bounds by approaching Lipschitz constant minimization via a sequence of gradient $p$-norm minimization problems. Ultimately, our results show that, for a desired nominal performance, there exists a fundamental lower bound on the sensitivity to adversarial perturbations that depends only on the loss function and the data distribution, and that improvements in robustness beyond this bound can only be made at the expense of nominal performance. Our training schemes provably achieve these bounds both under constraints on performance and~robustness.

paragraphs: This paper trains models under an explicit constraint on how sensitive their outputs can be to changes in the input. That sensitivity is measured by a Lipschitz constant. The authors formulate robust learning as minimizing loss subject to this constraint, making the desired robustness part of the optimization problem itself.

Their analysis connects the solution to a Poisson equation involving a weighted Laplace operator. The weights come from the constraint's Lagrange multiplier and regulate sensitivity to perturbations. A graph discretization of the input space and a primal-dual algorithm turn this connection into a training procedure with provable convergence to the associated saddle point.

The paper also reverses the question: how small can sensitivity become while maintaining a specified level of loss? It derives a fundamental lower bound determined by the loss function and data distribution. Within this framework, improving robustness beyond that bound requires sacrificing nominal performance. The proposed training schemes provably reach the bounds under either performance or robustness constraints, characterizing an achievable trade-off rather than promising unrestricted robustness.
summary.tldr: Graph-based constrained training achieves provable robustness bounds and characterizes the sensitivity that must remain at a desired performance level.

title: Lipschitz Bounds and Provably Robust Training by Laplacian Smoothing

abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) are popular probabilistic models of diversity. In this paper, we investigate DPPs from a new perspective: property testing of distributions. Given sample access to an unknown distribution $q$ over the subsets of a ground set, we aim to distinguish whether $q$ is a DPP distribution or $\epsilon$-far from all DPP distributions in $\ell_1$-distance. In this work, we propose the first algorithm for testing DPPs. Furthermore, we establish a matching lower bound on the sample complexity of DPP testing. This lower bound also extends to showing a new hardness result for the problem of testing the more general class of log-submodular distributions.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes are probability models used to represent diversity among selected items. This paper asks whether samples from an unknown distribution over subsets are compatible with that model family. The task is property testing: deciding whether the distribution has the DPP property using sample access.

The testing problem separates two cases. The unknown distribution is either a DPP or at least ε away from every DPP in ℓ1 distance. This explicit separation defines what the algorithm must distinguish. The authors provide the first algorithm for DPP testing and establish a matching lower bound on its sample complexity.

The matching lower bound shows that the required sample count reflects an intrinsic difficulty of the testing problem, at the level captured by the result. The lower-bound argument also yields a new hardness result for testing the broader family of log-submodular distributions. The contribution therefore identifies both an achievable testing procedure and a fundamental statistical obstacle, with implications beyond DPPs.
summary.tldr: The first DPP property-testing algorithm comes with a matching sample-complexity lower bound and a related hardness result for log-submodular distributions.

title: Testing Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: Deep learning classifiers are susceptible to well-crafted, imperceptible variations of their inputs, known as adversarial attacks. In this regard, the study of powerful attack models sheds light on the sources of vulnerability in these classifiers, hopefully leading to more robust ones. In this paper, we introduce AdvFlow: a novel black-box adversarial attack method on image classifiers that exploits the power of normalizing flows to model the density of adversarial examples around a given target image. We see that the proposed method generates adversaries that closely follow the clean data distribution, a property which makes their detection less likely. Also, our experimental results show competitive performance of the proposed approach with some of the existing attack methods on defended classifiers.

Also, our experimental results show competitive performance of the proposed approach with some of the existing attack methods on defended classifiers.

paragraphs: An image classifier can change its prediction when its input receives a carefully constructed modification that a person barely notices. Studying these adversarial examples helps expose vulnerabilities in learned classifiers. This paper introduces AdvFlow, a black-box attack method designed to produce such examples while making them resemble ordinary image data.

The approach uses normalizing flows to model the density of adversarial examples around a particular target image. This makes the distribution of generated examples central to the attack: the method aims to produce misleading inputs that also follow the distribution of clean data. The authors observe this resemblance and connect it to a lower likelihood of detection.

Experiments report competitive performance against some existing attack methods on defended classifiers. That finding supports AdvFlow as a useful attack approach in the evaluated settings, while its distributional behavior highlights an additional concern for defenses. An adversarial input may be difficult to identify not only because its visual changes are subtle, but also because it resembles the data a classifier normally encounters.
summary.tldr: AdvFlow uses normalizing flows to generate black-box adversarial images that resemble clean data and perform competitively against some attacks on defended classifiers.

title: AdvFlow: Inconspicuous Black-box Adversarial Attacks using Normalizing Flows

abstract: Most popular optimizers for deep learning can be broadly categorized as adaptive methods (e.g.~Adam) and accelerated schemes (e.g.~stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with momentum). For many models such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), adaptive methods typically converge faster but generalize worse compared to SGD; for complex settings such as generative adversarial networks (GANs), adaptive methods are typically the default because of their stability. We propose AdaBelief to simultaneously achieve three goals: fast convergence as in adaptive methods, good generalization as in SGD, and training stability. The intuition for AdaBelief is to adapt the stepsize according to the "belief" in the current gradient direction. Viewing the exponential moving average (EMA) of the noisy gradient as the prediction of the gradient at the next time step, if the observed gradient greatly deviates from the prediction, we distrust the current observation and take a small step; if the observed gradient is close to the prediction, we trust it and take a large step. We validate AdaBelief in extensive experiments, showing that it outperforms other methods with fast convergence and high accuracy on image classification and language modeling. Specifically, on ImageNet, AdaBelief achieves comparable accuracy to SGD. Furthermore, in the training of a GAN on Cifar10, AdaBelief demonstrates high stability and improves the quality of generated samples compared to a well-tuned Adam optimizer. Code is available athttps://github.com/juntang-zhuang/Adabelief-Optimizer

paragraphs: AdaBelief addresses a familiar tension in neural network training: adaptive optimizers often learn quickly, while momentum-based stochastic gradient descent can generalize better. Some settings, including generative adversarial networks, also place a premium on training stability. The paper proposes an optimizer intended to combine these strengths by changing how it decides whether to trust a gradient.

Its reference point is an exponential moving average of recent gradients, interpreted as a prediction of the next gradient. When the observed gradient differs substantially from that prediction, AdaBelief reduces the step size. When observation and prediction agree, it permits a larger step. The central idea is that agreement with recent behavior provides a useful signal for choosing the size of an update.

The reported experiments show fast convergence and high accuracy on image classification and language modeling. On ImageNet, accuracy is comparable to SGD. In a Cifar10 GAN experiment, AdaBelief also provides stable training and better generated samples than a well-tuned Adam optimizer. These findings support the proposed combination of speed, generalization, and stability in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: AdaBelief adjusts update sizes according to how closely observed gradients match their predictions, with reported benefits for convergence, accuracy, and stability.

title: AdaBelief Optimizer: Adapting Stepsizes by the Belief in Observed Gradients

abstract: Individual's opinions are fundamentally shaped and evolved by their interactions with other people, and social phenomena such as disagreement and polarization are now tightly woven into daily life. The quantification and optimization of these concepts have been the subject of much recent research behind a wealth of high-impact data mining applications. In particular, researchers have addressed the question of how such concepts can be optimized by influencing the opinion of a small number of individuals or by designing the network from scratch.Here, rather than a “design-from-scratch” approach or altering the initial opinion, we study the optimization problem of recommending $k$ new links to minimize the sum of polarization and disagreement in a social network with $n$ nodes and $m$ edges. We show that our objective function of this combinatorial optimization problem is not submodular, although it is monotone. We propose a simple greedy algorithm with a constant-factor approximation that solves the problem in cubic running time, and we provide theoretical analysis of the approximation guarantee for the algorithm. To overcome the computation challenge for large networks, we also provide a fast algorithm with computation complexity $\Otil (mk\eps^{-2})$ for any $\eps>0$, where the $\Otil (\cdot)$ notation suppresses the ${\rm poly} (\log n)$ factors. Extensive experiments on real datasets demonstrate both the efficiency and effectiveness of our algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how adding connections to an existing social network can reduce a combined measure of polarization and disagreement. The decision is to recommend a fixed number of new links. Existing opinions and the starting network provide the setting, so the optimization concerns which additional relationships would most improve the stated objective.

The authors show that the objective is monotone but not submodular. These properties distinguish predictable improvement from the stronger diminishing-returns structure often useful in network optimization. They develop a simple greedy algorithm with a constant-factor approximation guarantee and cubic running time, providing a theoretical bound on its solution quality.

To handle larger networks, they also propose a faster algorithm whose stated complexity scales with the existing edge count, the number of recommended links, and an inverse-squared accuracy parameter, apart from logarithmic factors in network size. Experiments on real datasets demonstrate efficiency and effectiveness. The contribution combines a formal link-selection objective with algorithms intended to make that objective computationally manageable.
summary.tldr: The paper develops theoretically supported algorithms for selecting new social links to reduce a combined polarization-and-disagreement objective.

title: Minimizing Polarization and Disagreement in Social Networks via Link Recommendation

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are powerful black-box predictors that have achieved impressive performance on a wide variety of tasks. However, their accuracy comes at the cost of intelligibility: it is usually unclear how they make their decisions. This hinders their applicability to high stakes decision-making domains such as healthcare. We propose Neural Additive Models (NAMs) which combine some of the expressivity of DNNs with the inherent intelligibility of generalized additive models. NAMs learn a linear combination of neural networks that each attend to a single input feature. These networks are trained jointly and can learn arbitrarily complex relationships between their input feature and the output. Our experiments on regression and classification datasets show that NAMs are more accurate than widely used intelligible models such as logistic regression and shallow decision trees. They perform similarly to existing state-of-the-art generalized additive models in accuracy, but are more flexible because they are based on neural nets instead of boosted trees. To demonstrate this, we show how NAMs can be used for multitask learning on synthetic data and on the COMPAS recidivism data due to their composability, and demonstrate that the differentiability of NAMs allows them to train more complex interpretable models for COVID-19.

paragraphs: Neural Additive Models aim to combine flexible prediction with understandable decisions. Each component neural network receives just one input feature, and the model combines these components linearly. This additive structure makes each feature's contribution accessible, while the individual networks can learn complex relationships between their feature and the output.

The components are trained jointly, allowing the model to fit its collection of feature contributions together. Across regression and classification datasets, the authors report higher accuracy than widely used interpretable methods such as logistic regression and shallow decision trees. Accuracy is similar to existing state-of-the-art generalized additive models, with additional flexibility from using neural networks instead of boosted trees.

The paper demonstrates that flexibility in two ways. Composable components support multitask learning on synthetic data and COMPAS recidivism data. Differentiability also supports training more complex interpretable models for COVID-19. These examples show how the architecture retains an intelligible additive foundation while connecting to capabilities available in neural-network modeling.
summary.tldr: Neural Additive Models combine single-feature neural networks to deliver interpretable predictions with accuracy comparable to leading generalized additive models.

title: Neural Additive Models: Interpretable Machine Learning with Neural Nets

abstract: Richly segmented 3D scene reconstructions are an integral basis for many high-level scene understanding tasks, such as for robotics, motion planning, or augmented reality. Existing works in 3D perception from a single RGB image tend to focus on geometric reconstruction only, or geometric reconstruction with semantic segmentation or instance segmentation.Inspired by 2D panoptic segmentation, we propose to unify the tasks of geometric reconstruction, 3D semantic segmentation, and 3D instance segmentation into the task of panoptic 3D scene reconstruction -- from a single RGB image, predicting the complete geometric reconstruction of the scene in the camera frustum of the image, along with semantic and instance segmentations.We propose a new approach for holistic 3D scene understanding from a single RGB image which learns to lift and propagate 2D features from an input image to a 3D volumetric scene representation.Our panoptic 3D reconstruction metric evaluates both geometric reconstruction quality as well as panoptic segmentation.Our experiments demonstrate that our approach for panoptic 3D scene reconstruction outperforms alternative approaches for this task.

paragraphs: A useful three-dimensional scene description needs more than geometry: it should also identify semantic categories and distinguish individual object instances. This paper unifies those requirements into panoptic 3D scene reconstruction from one RGB image. The target is a complete reconstruction within the camera's viewing volume, together with semantic and instance segmentations.

The proposed approach learns to lift two-dimensional image features into a three-dimensional volumetric representation and propagate them through that representation. This connects information extracted from the input image to a scene description that includes shape, category, and instance identity. Treating these outputs together supports a richer form of scene understanding than geometric reconstruction alone.

The authors also introduce an evaluation metric that considers reconstruction quality and panoptic segmentation jointly. Their experiments show better performance than alternative approaches on this combined task. The contribution therefore includes a unified task, a learned reconstruction approach, and an evaluation method aligned with the richer output. Such representations are motivated by applications including robotics, motion planning, and augmented reality.
summary.tldr: The method reconstructs 3D geometry, semantic categories, and object instances jointly from a single RGB image.

title: Panoptic 3D Scene Reconstruction From a Single RGB Image

abstract: Neural networks and Gaussian processes are complementary in their strengths and weaknesses. Having a better understanding of their relationship comes with the promise to make each method benefit from the strengths of the other. In this work, we establish an equivalence between the forward passes of neural networks and (deep) sparse Gaussian process models. The theory we develop is based on interpreting activation functions as interdomain inducing features through a rigorous analysis of the interplay between activation functions and kernels. This results in models that can either be seen as neural networks with improved uncertainty prediction or deep Gaussian processes with increased prediction accuracy. These claims are supported by experimental results on regression and classification datasets.

The theory we develop is based on interpreting activation functions as interdomain inducing features through a rigorous analysis of the interplay between activation functions and kernels. paragraphs: The paper develops a mathematical connection between neural networks and Gaussian process models, motivated by their complementary strengths and weaknesses. Its central result establishes an equivalence between neural-network forward passes and forward passes in sparse Gaussian process models, including deep versions. This connects the computations used to make predictions in the two model families.

The theory interprets neural-network activation functions as interdomain inducing features. The authors obtain this interpretation by analyzing how activation functions interact with kernels. That relationship supplies the mathematical basis for constructing models that admit both a neural-network interpretation and a sparse Gaussian process interpretation, linking architectural choices to probabilistic modeling.

The resulting models can be viewed as neural networks with better uncertainty prediction or as deep Gaussian processes with better predictive accuracy. Experiments on regression and classification datasets support those improvements. The contribution therefore combines a theoretical correspondence with models intended to bring useful properties of each approach into the other, with empirical support on the studied prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: A forward-pass equivalence connects neural networks to sparse deep Gaussian processes and supports models with improved uncertainty or accuracy.

title: Deep Neural Networks as Point Estimates for Deep Gaussian Processes

abstract: We propose a novel training method that integrates rules into deep learning, in a way the strengths of the rules are controllable at inference. Deep Neural Networks with Controllable Rule Representations (DeepCTRL) incorporates a rule encoder into the model coupled with a rule-based objective, enabling a shared representation for decision making. DeepCTRL is agnostic to data type and model architecture. It can be applied to any kind of rule defined for inputs and outputs. The key aspect of DeepCTRL is that it does not require retraining to adapt the rule strength -- at inference, the user can adjust it based on the desired operation point on accuracy vs. rule verification ratio. In real-world domains where incorporating rules is critical -- such as Physics, Retail and Healthcare -- we show the effectiveness of DeepCTRL in teaching rules for deep learning. DeepCTRL improves the trust and reliability of the trained models by significantly increasing their rule verification ratio, while also providing accuracy gains at downstream tasks. Additionally, DeepCTRL enables novel use cases such as hypothesis testing of the rules on data samples, and unsupervised adaptation based on shared rules between datasets.

paragraphs: Rules can encode useful constraints or domain knowledge, but a fixed training objective leaves little flexibility afterward. DeepCTRL incorporates a rule encoder and rule-based objective into a neural network so that rule influence can be adjusted when the trained model is used.

The method creates a shared representation for decision-making and supports rules defined over inputs and outputs. At inference, a user chooses an operating point between predictive accuracy and the fraction of outputs that verify the rule, without retraining the network.

Demonstrations in physics, retail, and healthcare show increased rule-verification ratios and accuracy gains on downstream tasks. The authors also explore rule hypothesis testing and unsupervised adaptation through shared rules. The abstract does not claim every rule is valid or every prediction satisfies it; controllable rule strength exposes a tradeoff whose usefulness depends on the selected rules and application.
summary.tldr: DeepCTRL lets users adjust learned rule strength during inference without retraining.

title: Controlling Neural Networks with Rule Representations

abstract: In reinforcement learning, pre-trained low-level skills have the potential to greatly facilitate exploration. However, prior knowledge of the downstream task is required to strike the right balance between generality (fine-grained control) and specificity (faster learning) in skill design. In previous work on continuous control, the sensitivity of methods to this trade-off has not been addressed explicitly, as locomotion provides a suitable prior for navigation tasks, which have been of foremost interest. In this work, we analyze this trade-off for low-level policy pre-training with a new benchmark suite of diverse, sparse-reward tasks for bipedal robots. We alleviate the need for prior knowledge by proposing a hierarchical skill learning framework that acquires skills of varying complexity in an unsupervised manner. For utilization on downstream tasks, we present a three-layered hierarchical learning algorithm to automatically trade off between general and specific skills as required by the respective task. In our experiments, we show that our approach performs this trade-off effectively and achieves better results than current state-of-the-art methods for end-to-end hierarchical reinforcement learning and unsupervised skill discovery.

paragraphs: Pretrained skills can help a reinforcement-learning agent explore, but their level of specialization matters. General skills preserve fine control, while specific skills can accelerate learning when they fit the task. Choosing that balance beforehand is difficult without knowing what the agent will eventually need to do.

The paper studies this tension using a new collection of diverse bipedal-robot tasks with sparse rewards. It proposes an unsupervised framework that learns skills at different levels of complexity. A three-layer hierarchical learning algorithm then uses those skills on downstream tasks, automatically adjusting the balance between general and specialized behavior.

Learning several levels of skills alleviates the need to choose a single level using prior task knowledge. This broadens the investigation beyond navigation settings, where locomotion already supplies a useful prior. In the reported experiments, the hierarchy handles the trade-off effectively and outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods for end-to-end hierarchical reinforcement learning and unsupervised skill discovery. The findings support varying skill complexity as a practical resource for exploration across the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised skill hierarchy helps robots balance fine control and specialized behavior when exploring diverse sparse-reward tasks.

title: Hierarchical Skills for Efficient Exploration

abstract: The development of data-dependent heuristics and representations for biological sequences that reflect their evolutionary distance is critical for large-scale biological research. However, popular machine learning approaches, based on continuous Euclidean spaces, have struggled with the discrete combinatorial formulation of the edit distance that models evolution and the hierarchical relationship that characterises real-world datasets. We present Neural Distance Embeddings (NeuroSEED), a general framework to embed sequences in geometric vector spaces, and illustrate the effectiveness of the hyperbolic space that captures the hierarchical structure and provides an average 38% reduction in embedding RMSE against the best competing geometry. The capacity of the framework and the significance of these improvements are then demonstrated devising supervised and unsupervised NeuroSEED approaches to multiple core tasks in bioinformatics. Benchmarked with common baselines, the proposed approaches display significant accuracy and/or runtime improvements on real-world datasets. As an example for hierarchical clustering, the proposed pretrained and from-scratch methods match the quality of competing baselines with 30x and 15x runtime reduction, respectively.

paragraphs: Biological sequence analysis needs representations that reflect evolutionary distance. This is challenging because edit distance has a discrete, combinatorial structure, while real datasets also contain hierarchical relationships. The paper introduces Neural Distance Embeddings, or NeuroSEED, as a general framework for mapping sequences into geometric vector spaces.

A central result concerns the choice of geometry. Hyperbolic space captures hierarchical structure and yields an average 38% reduction in embedding root mean squared error compared with the best competing geometry. This result concerns how accurately the embedding represents the target distances, making geometry an important part of the representation rather than merely its storage format.

The authors then develop supervised and unsupervised NeuroSEED approaches for several core bioinformatics tasks. On real-world datasets, they report significant improvements in accuracy, runtime, or both against common baselines. For hierarchical clustering, pretrained and from-scratch methods match competing clustering quality while reducing runtime by factors of 30 and 15 respectively. These results connect improved distance representation with practical downstream computational gains.
summary.tldr: NeuroSEED embeds biological sequences into geometric spaces, with hyperbolic embeddings improving distance accuracy and enabling faster bioinformatics workflows.

title: Neural Distance Embeddings for Biological Sequences

abstract: There are so many models in the literature that it is difficult for practitioners to decide which combinations are likely to be effective for a new task. This paper attempts to address this question by capturing relationships among checkpoints published on the web. We model the space of tasks as a Gaussian process. The covariance can be estimated from checkpoints and unlabeled probing data. With the Gaussian process, we can identify representative checkpoints by a maximum mutual information criterion. This objective is submodular. A greedy method identifies representatives that are likely to "cover'' the task space. These representatives generalize to new tasks with superior performance. Empirical evidence is provided for applications from both computational linguistics as well as computer vision.
originalAbstract: There are so many models in the literature that it is difficult for practitioners to decide which combinations are likely to be effective for a new task. This paper attempts to address this question by capturing relationships among checkpoints published on the web. We model the space of tasks as a Gaussian process. The covariance can be estimated from checkpoints and unlabeled probing data. With the Gaussian process, we can identify representative checkpoints by a maximum mutual information criterion. This objective is submodular. A greedy method identifies representatives that are likely to "cover'' the task space. These representatives generalize to new tasks with superior performance. Empirical evidence is provided for applications from both computational linguistics as well as computer vision.

paragraphs: A large collection of published model checkpoints gives practitioners many possible starting points for a new task. The challenge is choosing useful representatives from that collection. This paper approaches selection by estimating relationships among checkpoints, aiming to identify a set that spans the task space and can transfer effectively to tasks not yet encountered.

The authors model the space of tasks with a Gaussian process. Its covariance, which expresses relationships within that space, can be estimated using checkpoints and unlabeled probing data. They then choose representative checkpoints using a maximum mutual information objective, so selection is guided by how much information the chosen set provides under the model.

The selection objective is submodular, and the paper uses a greedy method to find representatives likely to cover the task space. Empirical evidence from computational linguistics and computer vision shows superior performance when these representatives generalize to new tasks. The approach turns checkpoint selection into a structured coverage problem, using estimated relationships to organize available models instead of assessing each checkpoint solely in isolation.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-process model of checkpoint relationships guides the selection of representative models that transfer well to unseen tasks.

title: Exploiting a Zoo of Checkpoints for Unseen Tasks

abstract: Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) has emerged to learn generalizable representations from contrastive views. However, it is still in its infancy with two concerns: 1) changing the graph structure through data augmentation to generate contrastive views may mislead the message passing scheme, as such graph changing action deprives the intrinsic graph structural information, especially the directional structure in directed graphs; 2) since GCL usually uses predefined contrastive views with hand-picking parameters, it does not take full advantage of the contrastive information provided by data augmentation, resulting in incomplete structure information for models learning. In this paper, we design a directed graph data augmentation method called Laplacian perturbation and theoretically analyze how it provides contrastive information without changing the directed graph structure. Moreover, we present a directed graph contrastive learning framework, which dynamically learns from all possible contrastive views generated by Laplacian perturbation. Then we train it using multi-task curriculum learning to progressively learn from multiple easy-to-difficult contrastive views. We empirically show that our model can retain more structural features of directed graphs than other GCL models because of its ability to provide complete contrastive information. Experiments on various benchmarks reveal our dominance over the state-of-the-art approaches.

Another concern is that manually selected views and parameters expose the model to only part of the contrastive information an augmentation method could provide.

This paper introduces Laplacian perturbation, an augmentation method for directed graphs. The authors theoretically analyze how it supplies contrastive information while preserving the directed graph structure. Their learning framework dynamically learns from the possible views generated by this method, rather than relying on a predefined selection. A multi-task curriculum organizes learning progressively from easier to harder contrastive views.

The central aim is to vary the learning signal while retaining the directional relationships that make the original graph informative. Empirically, the model preserves more structural features than the compared graph contrastive learning models. Benchmark experiments also report better performance than state-of-the-art approaches, supporting the combination of structure-preserving augmentation and progressive learning across views.
summary.tldr: Laplacian perturbation creates contrastive views that preserve directed graph structure, while curriculum learning progressively uses those views to improve representations.

title: Directed Graph Contrastive Learning

abstract: The Probabilistic Watershed is a semi-supervised learning algorithm applied on undirected graphs. Given a set of labeled nodes (seeds), it defines a Gibbs probability distribution over all possible spanning forests disconnecting the seeds. It calculates, for every node, the probability of sampling a forest connecting a certain seed with the considered node. We propose the "Directed Probabilistic Watershed", an extension of the Probabilistic Watershed algorithm to directed graphs. Building on the Probabilistic Watershed, we apply the Matrix Tree Theorem for directed graphs and define a Gibbs probability distribution over all incoming directed forests rooted at the seeds. Similar to the undirected case, this turns out to be equivalent to the Directed Random Walker. Furthermore, we show that in the limit case in which the Gibbs distribution has infinitely low temperature, the labeling of the Directed Probabilistic Watershed is equal to the one induced by the incoming directed forest of minimum cost. Finally, for illustration, we compare the empirical performance of the proposed method with other semi-supervised segmentation methods for directed graphs.

paragraphs: Probabilistic Watershed assigns labels on a graph using a small set of labeled nodes called seeds. Its original form works with undirected graphs and assigns probabilities according to how nodes connect to seeds across possible spanning forests.

This paper extends the construction to directed graphs, where edge direction matters. The method places a Gibbs probability distribution over incoming directed forests rooted at the seeds. Using the directed Matrix Tree Theorem, it builds a probabilistic labeling procedure that respects those directed connections.

The authors show that this construction is equivalent to the Directed Random Walker. They also characterize a limiting case: as the Gibbs temperature approaches zero, its labeling matches that induced by the minimum-cost incoming directed forest. This links the probabilistic formulation to a cost-minimizing forest construction.

The paper illustrates the method through empirical comparisons with other semi-supervised segmentation approaches for directed graphs. Its stated theoretical contribution is the connection among directed forest probabilities, random walks, and minimum-cost labeling, providing several complementary views of the same labeling problem.
summary.tldr: Directed Probabilistic Watershed extends seed-based graph labeling to directed edges and connects it to random walks and minimum-cost forests.

title: Directed Probabilistic Watershed

abstract: In recent years, the ML community has seen surges of interest in both adversarially robust learning and implicit layers, but connections between these two areas have seldom been explored. In this work, we combine innovations from these areas to tackle the problem of N-k security-constrained optimal power flow (SCOPF). N-k SCOPF is a core problem for the operation of electrical grids, and aims to schedule power generation in a manner that is robust to potentially $k$ simultaneous equipment outages. Inspired by methods in adversarially robust training, we frame N-k SCOPF as a minimax optimization problem -- viewing power generation settings as adjustable parameters and equipment outages as (adversarial) attacks -- and solve this problem via gradient-based techniques. The loss function of this minimax problem involves resolving implicit equations representing grid physics and operational decisions, which we differentiate through via the implicit function theorem. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework in solving N-3 SCOPF, which has traditionally been considered as prohibitively expensive to solve given that the problem size depends combinatorially on the number of potential outages.

paragraphs: Electrical-grid operators need generation schedules that remain workable when equipment fails. The N-k security-constrained optimal power flow problem asks for schedules robust to potentially k simultaneous outages. Considering combinations of failures becomes expensive because the number of possible outage sets grows combinatorially with the equipment that could fail.

The paper treats this planning problem as a minimax optimization inspired by adversarially robust learning. Generation settings are the adjustable choices, while equipment outages play the role of adversarial attacks. Gradient-based methods seek schedules that withstand the challenging outage configurations considered by the optimization. This connects a physical planning problem to methods developed for learning under adversarial disturbances.

Computing the objective requires solving implicit equations for grid physics and operational decisions. The authors use the implicit function theorem to differentiate through those equations, enabling gradient-based optimization of the overall problem. They demonstrate the framework on N-3 planning, a setting traditionally regarded as prohibitively expensive. The stated result shows the usefulness of combining adversarial optimization with differentiation through physical-system equations.
summary.tldr: The paper combines adversarial optimization and implicit differentiation to schedule power generation against simultaneous equipment outages.

title: Adversarially robust learning for security-constrained optimal power flow

abstract: Labeling articulated objects in unconstrained settings has a wide variety of applications including entertainment, neuroscience, psychology, ethology, and many fields of medicine. Large offline labeled datasets do not exist for all but the most common articulated object categories (e.g., humans). Hand labeling these landmarks within a video sequence is a laborious task. Learned landmark detectors can help, but can be error-prone when trained from only a few examples. Multi-camera systems that train fine-grained detectors have shown significant promise in detecting such errors, allowing for self-supervised solutions that only need a small percentage of the video sequence to be hand-labeled. The approach, however, is based on calibrated cameras and rigid geometry, making it expensive, difficult to manage, and impractical in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we address these bottlenecks by combining a non-rigid 3D neural prior with deep flow to obtain high-fidelity landmark estimates from videos with only two or three uncalibrated, handheld cameras. With just a few annotations (representing $1-2\%$ of the frames), we are able to produce 2D results comparable to state-of-the-art fully supervised methods, along with 3D reconstructions that are impossible with other existing approaches. Our Multi-view Bootstrapping in the Wild (MBW) approach demonstrates impressive results on standard human datasets, as well as tigers, cheetahs, fish, colobus monkeys, chimpanzees, and flamingos from videos captured casually in a zoo. We release the codebase for MBW as well as this challenging zoo dataset consisting of image frames of tail-end distribution categories with their corresponding 2D and 3D labels generated from minimal human intervention.

title: MBW: Multi-view Bootstrapping in the Wild

abstract: Our environment is filled with rich and dynamic acoustic information. When we walk into a cathedral, the reverberations as much as appearance inform us of the sanctuary's wide open space. Similarly, as an object moves around us, we expect the sound emitted to also exhibit this movement. While recent advances in learned implicit functions have led to increasingly higher quality representations of the visual world, there have not been commensurate advances in learning spatial auditory representations. To address this gap, we introduce Neural Acoustic Fields (NAFs), an implicit representation that captures how sounds propagate in a physical scene. By modeling acoustic propagation in a scene as a linear time-invariant system, NAFs learn to continuously map all emitter and listener location pairs to a neural impulse response function that can then be applied to arbitrary sounds. We demonstrate NAFs on both synthetic and real data, and show that the continuous nature of NAFs enables us to render spatial acoustics for a listener at arbitrary locations. We further show that the representation learned by NAFs can help improve visual learning with sparse views. Finally we show that a representation informative of scene structure emerges during the learning of NAFs.

paragraphs: The sound heard in a scene depends on both where it originates and where the listener stands. Neural Acoustic Fields represent this spatial relationship with a learned implicit function. The aim is to capture how a physical scene transforms sound, providing an auditory representation alongside the learned representations developed for visual scenes.

The method models acoustic propagation as a linear time-invariant system. Given an emitter location and a listener location, the network produces an impulse response describing the scene's acoustic effect for that pair. That response can then be applied to arbitrary sounds, separating the spatial propagation model from the particular sound being played.

Experiments on synthetic and real data show that the continuous representation can render acoustics for listeners at arbitrary locations. The authors also find that the learned representation can improve visual learning when only sparse views are available. Information about scene structure emerges during acoustic learning, suggesting that modeling how sound travels captures spatial properties useful beyond producing the sound itself.
summary.tldr: Neural Acoustic Fields learn location-dependent sound propagation and produce representations that can also aid visual learning from sparse views.

title: Learning Neural Acoustic Fields

abstract: In the past few years, transformers have achieved promising performance on various computer vision tasks. Unfortunately, the immense inference overhead of most existing vision transformers withholds them from being deployed on edge devices such as cell phones and smart watches. Knowledge distillation is a widely used paradigm for compressing cumbersome architectures into compact students via transferring information. However, most of them are designed for convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which do not fully investigate the character of vision transformers. In this paper, we fully utilize the patch-level information and propose a fine-grained manifold distillation method for transformer-based networks. Specifically, we train a tiny student model to match a pre-trained teacher model in the patch-level manifold space. Then, we decouple the manifold matching loss into three terms with careful design to further reduce the computational costs for the patch relationship. Equipped with the proposed method, a DeiT-Tiny model containing 5M parameters achieves 76.5\% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k, which is +2.0\% higher than previous distillation approaches. Transfer learning results on other classification benchmarks and downstream vision tasks also demonstrate the superiority of our method over the state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: Large vision transformers can be expensive to run on devices such as phones and watches. Knowledge distillation addresses this by training a compact student using information from a larger teacher. This paper argues that approaches designed around convolutional networks do not fully exploit a distinctive source of information in transformers: their image patches.

The proposed method trains a tiny student to match a pretrained teacher in a patch-level manifold space. The transfer therefore uses structure in patch representations and their relationships. To reduce the cost of computing those relationships, the authors split the manifold-matching objective into three carefully designed terms.

With this method, a DeiT-Tiny model containing five million parameters reaches 76.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k, reported as a 2.0% improvement over previous distillation approaches. Transfer experiments on other classification benchmarks and downstream vision tasks also favor the method over the compared approaches. The findings support patch-level representation structure as a useful teaching signal for compact vision transformers.
summary.tldr: Matching a teacher's patch-level representation structure improves compact vision transformers, with DeiT-Tiny reaching 76.5% ImageNet-1k top-1 accuracy.

title: Learning Efficient Vision Transformers via Fine-Grained Manifold Distillation

abstract: Gaussian processes scale prohibitively with the size of the dataset. In response, many approximation methods have been developed, which inevitably introduce approximation error. This additional source of uncertainty, due to limited computation, is entirely ignored when using the approximate posterior. Therefore in practice, GP models are often as much about the approximation method as they are about the data. Here, we develop a new class of methods that provides consistent estimation of the combined uncertainty arising from both the finite number of data observed and the finite amount of computation expended. The most common GP approximations map to an instance in this class, such as methods based on the Cholesky factorization, conjugate gradients, and inducing points. For any method in this class, we prove (i) convergence of its posterior mean in the associated RKHS, (ii) decomposability of its combined posterior covariance into mathematical and computational covariances, and (iii) that the combined variance is a tight worst-case bound for the squared error between the method's posterior mean and the latent function. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the consequences of ignoring computational uncertainty and show how implicitly modeling it improves generalization performance on benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Gaussian process inference becomes expensive as datasets grow, making approximations common. Those approximations introduce error in addition to the uncertainty caused by limited observations. This paper argues that using an approximate posterior without accounting for computational uncertainty leaves out a consequential part of what the model does not know.

The authors develop a class of methods that consistently estimates uncertainty from both finite data and finite computation. Common approaches based on Cholesky factorization, conjugate gradients, and inducing points can be represented within this class. The framework therefore connects several existing approximation strategies to a shared treatment of the uncertainty their computation introduces.

For methods in the class, the paper proves posterior-mean convergence in the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space and separates the combined covariance into mathematical and computational components. It also shows that the combined variance gives a tight worst-case bound on squared error between the estimated mean and latent function. Benchmark experiments demonstrate consequences of ignoring computational uncertainty and show improved generalization when it is implicitly modeled.
summary.tldr: A unified Gaussian process framework accounts for uncertainty from both limited data and approximate computation, with error guarantees and empirical generalization gains.

title: Posterior and Computational Uncertainty in Gaussian Processes

abstract: Unsupervised learning of latent variable models (LVMs) is widely used to represent data in machine learning. When such model reflects the ground truth factors and the mechanisms mapping them to observations, there is reason to expect that such models allow generalisation in downstream tasks. It is however well known that such identifiability guaranties are typically not achievable without putting constraints on the model class. This is notably the case for nonlinear Independent Component Analysis, in which the LVM maps statistically independent variables to observations via a deterministic nonlinear function. Several families of spurious solutions fitting perfectly the data, but that do not correspond to the ground truth factors can be constructed in generic settings. However, recent work suggests that constraining the function class of such models may promote identifiability. Specifically, function classes with constraints on their partial derivatives, gathered in the Jacobian matrix, have been proposed, such as orthogonal coordinate transformations (OCT), which impose orthogonality of the Jacobian columns. In the present work, we prove that a subclass of these transformations, conformal maps, is identifiable and provide novel theoretical results suggesting that OCTs have properties that prevent families of spurious solutions to spoil identifiability in a generic setting.

paragraphs: A latent-variable model can fit observed data without recovering the underlying factors that generated it. This is a central difficulty in nonlinear independent component analysis, where statistically independent hidden variables are transformed into observations by a deterministic nonlinear function. In unrestricted settings, multiple spurious explanations can match the data perfectly.

The paper studies whether restricting the mixing function can resolve this ambiguity. It focuses on constraints on the Jacobian, the matrix describing how each output changes with each input. Orthogonal coordinate transformations require the columns of this matrix to be mutually orthogonal. The authors examine these transformations and a more restricted subclass called conformal maps.

The strongest stated result is an identifiability proof for conformal maps. Additional theoretical results suggest that the broader orthogonal class has properties that prevent certain families of spurious solutions from undermining identifiability in generic settings. The distinction matters: the paper proves identifiability for the subclass while providing supporting theoretical evidence for the broader class. Its contribution clarifies how structural restrictions can help recover meaningful latent factors.
summary.tldr: The paper proves identifiability for conformal mixing functions and provides theoretical evidence that broader orthogonal transformations resist spurious nonlinear ICA solutions.

title: Function Classes for Identifiable Nonlinear Independent Component Analysis

abstract: The "Patient Instruction" (PI), which contains critical instructional information provided both to carers and to the patient at the time of discharge, is essential for the patient to manage their condition outside hospital. An accurate and easy-to-follow PI can improve the self-management of patients which can in turn reduce hospital readmission rates. However, writing an appropriate PI can be extremely time consuming for physicians, and is subject to being incomplete or error-prone for (potentially overworked) physicians. Therefore, we propose a new task that can provide an objective means of avoiding incompleteness, while reducing clinical workload: the automatic generation of the PI, which is imagined as being a document that the clinician can review, modify, and approve as necessary (rather than taking the human "out of the loop"). We build a benchmark clinical dataset and propose the Re$^3$Writer, which imitates the working patterns of physicians to first retrieve related working experience from historical PIs written by physicians, then reason related medical knowledge. Finally, it refines the retrieved working experience and reasoned medical knowledge to extract useful information, which is used to generate the PI for previously-unseen patient according to their health records during hospitalization. Our experiments show that, using our method, the performance of 6 different models can be substantially boosted across all metrics, with up to 20%, 11%, and 19% relative improvements in BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, and METEOR, respectively. Meanwhile, we show results from human evaluations to measure the effectiveness in terms of its usefulness for clinical practice. The code is available at https://github.com/AI-in-Health/Patient-Instructions.

paragraphs: Discharge instructions help patients and carers manage conditions outside hospital, but preparing complete and accurate instructions takes clinicians time. This paper introduces automatic patient-instruction generation as a task and builds a clinical benchmark dataset. The intended output is a draft that a clinician can review, modify, and approve, keeping clinical judgment within the workflow.

It retrieves relevant experience from historical instructions, reasons about related medical knowledge, and refines those sources to extract useful information. The paper also reports human evaluations assessing usefulness for clinical practice. These findings support the generation framework's measured quality and evaluated usefulness; the work positions the system as assistance for clinician-reviewed discharge documentation.
summary.tldr: Re³Writer combines historical instruction retrieval, medical reasoning, and refinement to improve patient-instruction drafts intended for clinician review.

title: Retrieve, Reason, and Refine: Generating Accurate and Faithful Patient Instructions

abstract: Established methods for unsupervised representation learning such as variational autoencoders produce none or poorly calibrated uncertainty estimates making it difficult to evaluate if learned representations are stable and reliable. In this work, we present a Bayesian autoencoder for unsupervised representation learning, which is trained using a novel variational lower-bound of the autoencoder evidence. This is maximized using Monte Carlo EM with a variational distribution that takes the shape of a Laplace approximation. We develop a new Hessian approximation that scales linearly with data size allowing us to model high-dimensional data. Empirically, we show that our Laplacian autoencoder estimates well-calibrated uncertainties in both latent and output space. We demonstrate that this results in improved performance across a multitude of downstream tasks.
