This is maximized using Monte Carlo EM with a variational distribution that takes the shape of a Laplace approximation. We develop a new Hessian approximation that scales linearly with data size allowing us to model high-dimensional data. Empirically, we show that our Laplacian autoencoder estimates well-calibrated uncertainties in both latent and output space. We demonstrate that this results in improved performance across a multitude of downstream tasks.

paragraphs: An unsupervised representation can be useful while still leaving uncertainty about how stable or reliable it is. This paper addresses the absence or poor calibration of uncertainty estimates in established representation-learning methods. It introduces a Bayesian autoencoder that learns representations together with uncertainty in both the latent representation and the output.

Training maximizes a new variational lower bound on the autoencoder evidence using Monte Carlo expectation-maximization. The variational distribution has the form of a Laplace approximation. To make this approach workable for high-dimensional data, the authors develop a Hessian approximation whose scaling is linear in data size, addressing a computational obstacle in the uncertainty calculation.

Empirically, the Laplacian autoencoder produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates in latent and output spaces. The authors also demonstrate improved performance across multiple downstream tasks. The findings connect the reliability of uncertainty estimates to practical representation quality: accounting for uncertainty is useful both for assessing learned features and for the later tasks that consume them.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian autoencoder uses Laplace-shaped uncertainty approximations to improve uncertainty calibration and downstream performance.

title: Laplacian Autoencoders for Learning Stochastic Representations

abstract: Deep active learning aims to reduce the annotation cost for the training of deep models, which is notoriously data-hungry. Until recently, deep active learning methods were ineffectual in the low-budget regime, where only a small number of examples are annotated. The situation has been alleviated by recent advances in representation and self-supervised learning, which impart the geometry of the data representation with rich information about the points. Taking advantage of this progress, we study the problem of subset selection for annotation through a “covering” lens, proposing ProbCover – a new active learning algorithm for the low budget regime, which seeks to maximize Probability Coverage. We then describe a dual way to view the proposed formulation, from which one can derive strategies suitable for the high budget regime of active learning, related to existing methods like Coreset. We conclude with extensive experiments, evaluating ProbCover in the low-budget regime. We show that our principled active learning strategy improves the state-of-the-art in the low-budget regime in several image recognition benchmarks. This method is especially beneficial in the semi-supervised setting, allowing state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods to match the performance of fully supervised methods, while using much fewer labels nonetheless. Code is available at https://github.com/avihu111/TypiClust.

The paper builds on improved representations from representation learning and self-supervised learning, whose geometry contains useful information about relationships among examples.

It seeks a subset that maximizes Probability Coverage, using the representation space to guide the choice of examples. The authors also give a dual interpretation of this formulation that leads toward strategies for larger annotation budgets and connects to existing approaches such as Coreset.

The gains are especially useful when combined with semi-supervised learning, which also uses unlabeled examples. In the reported experiments, this combination allows leading semi-supervised methods to match fully supervised performance while requiring substantially fewer labels.
summary.tldr: ProbCover selects examples for labeling by maximizing coverage in representation space, improving active learning when annotation budgets are small.

title: Active Learning Through a Covering Lens

abstract: To unveil how the brain learns, ongoing work seeks biologically-plausible approximations of gradient descent algorithms for training recurrent neural networks (RNNs). Yet, beyond task accuracy, it is unclear if such learning rules converge to solutions that exhibit different levels of generalization than their non-biologically-plausible counterparts. Leveraging results from deep learning theory based on loss landscape curvature, we ask: how do biologically-plausible gradient approximations affect generalization? We first demonstrate that state-of-the-art biologically-plausible learning rules for training RNNs exhibit worse and more variable generalization performance compared to their machine learning counterparts that follow the true gradient more closely. Next, we verify that such generalization performance is correlated significantly with loss landscape curvature, and we show that biologically-plausible learning rules tend to approach high-curvature regions in synaptic weight space. Using tools from dynamical systems, we derive theoretical arguments and present a theorem explaining this phenomenon. This predicts our numerical results, and explains why biologically-plausible rules lead to worse and more variable generalization properties. Finally, we suggest potential remedies that could be used by the brain to mitigate this effect. To our knowledge, our analysis is the first to identify the reason for this generalization gap between artificial and biologically-plausible learning rules, which can help guide future investigations into how the brain learns solutions that generalize.

The authors find that the biologically plausible rules studied generalize worse and less consistently than machine learning rules that follow the true gradient more closely. They connect this difference to the curvature of the loss landscape, which describes how sharply loss changes around a set of weights. Generalization is significantly correlated with curvature, and the biologically plausible rules tend toward regions of higher curvature.

The theory predicts the numerical findings and provides an explanation for the observed generalization gap. The authors also suggest possible remedies the brain could use. Those remedies are proposed possibilities, while the main contribution is an account of how approximate learning dynamics affect generalization.
summary.tldr: The paper links poorer generalization in biologically plausible recurrent-network learning rules to their tendency to reach high-curvature regions of the loss landscape.

title: Beyond accuracy: generalization properties of bio-plausible temporal credit assignment rules

abstract: In today’s data-rich environment, context-based dynamic pricing has gained much attention. To model the demand as a function of price and context, the existing literature either adopts a parametric model or a non-parametric model. The former is easier to implement but may suffer from model mis-specification, whereas the latter is more robust but does not leverage many structural properties of the underlying problem. This paper combines these two approaches by studying the context-based dynamic pricing with online learning, where the unknown expected demand admits a semi-parametric partially linear structure. Specifically, we consider two demand models, whose expected demand at price $p$ and context $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is given by $bp+g(x)$ and $ f(p)+ a^\top x$ respectively. We assume that $g(x)$ is $\beta$-H{\"o}lder continuous in the first model, and $f(p)$ is $k$th-order smooth with an additional parameter $\delta$ in the second model. For both models, we design an efficient online learning algorithm with provable regret upper bounds, and establish matching lower bounds. This enables us to characterize the statistical complexity for the two learning models, whose optimal regret rates are $\widetilde \Theta(\sqrt T \vee T^{\frac{d}{d+2\beta}})$ and $\widetilde \Theta(\sqrt T \vee (\delta T^{k+1})^{\frac{1}{2k+1}})$ respectively. The numerical results demonstrate that our learning algorithms are more effective than benchmark algorithms, and also reveal the effects of parameters $d$, $\beta$ and $\delta$ on the algorithm's empirical regret, which are consistent with our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn prices online when demand depends on both price and contextual information. Fully parametric models can be convenient but misspecify demand, while fully non-parametric approaches may overlook useful structure. The authors examine partially linear models that combine a structured component with a more flexible unknown function.

They consider two forms of expected demand. One adds a linear price effect to a nonlinear context effect; the other adds a nonlinear price effect to a linear context effect. The first assumes a specified degree of Hölder continuity for the context function. The second assumes smoothness of a specified order for the price function, together with an additional parameter delta. These assumptions determine the learning difficulty analyzed in the paper.

For both settings, the authors provide efficient online algorithms and matching regret bounds up to logarithmic factors. These characterize how unavoidable performance loss depends on the time horizon and model parameters. Numerical results show improvements over benchmark algorithms and parameter effects consistent with the theory, supporting the value of combining flexible demand modeling with exploitable linear structure.
summary.tldr: Partially linear demand models enable online pricing algorithms with regret guarantees that match lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

title: Context-Based Dynamic Pricing with Partially Linear Demand Model

abstract: There has been a rapidly growing interest in Automatic Symptom Detection (ASD) and Automatic Diagnosis (AD) systems in the machine learning research literature, aiming to assist doctors in telemedicine services. These systems are designed to interact with patients, collect evidence about their symptoms and relevant antecedents, and possibly make predictions about the underlying diseases. Doctors would review the interactions, including the evidence and the predictions, collect if necessary additional information from patients, before deciding on next steps. Despite recent progress in this area, an important piece of doctors' interactions with patients is missing in the design of these systems, namely the differential diagnosis. Its absence is largely due to the lack of datasets that include such information for models to train on. In this work, we present a large-scale synthetic dataset of roughly 1.3 million patients that includes a differential diagnosis, along with the ground truth pathology, symptoms and antecedents for each patient. Unlike existing datasets which only contain binary symptoms and antecedents, this dataset also contains categorical and multi-choice symptoms and antecedents useful for efficient data collection. Moreover, some symptoms are organized in a hierarchy, making it possible to design systems able to interact with patients in a logical way. As a proof-of-concept, we extend two existing AD and ASD systems to incorporate the differential diagnosis, and provide empirical evidence that using differentials as training signals is essential for the efficiency of such systems or for helping doctors better understand the reasoning of those systems.

paragraphs: Systems for automatic symptom detection and diagnosis can gather patient information and suggest possible diseases for doctors to review. The paper identifies a missing component in their training data: differential diagnosis, the consideration of alternative diagnoses alongside the underlying condition. Without this information, systems lack a training signal for an important part of clinical reasoning.

DDXPlus supplies roughly 1.3 million synthetic patient records. Each includes a differential diagnosis, the ground truth pathology, symptoms, and relevant antecedents. Its information goes beyond yes-or-no attributes to include categorical and multiple-choice responses. Some symptoms also have a hierarchy, creating opportunities for systems to organize their questions in a logical sequence.

As a proof of concept, the authors extend two existing diagnosis and symptom detection systems to use differential diagnoses. Their experiments provide evidence that these training signals are essential for system efficiency or for helping doctors understand system reasoning. The contribution is a synthetic research dataset and an initial demonstration of its value within systems intended to support clinician review.
summary.tldr: DDXPlus adds differential diagnoses and richer symptom information to roughly 1.3 million synthetic patient records for studying automatic diagnosis systems.

title: DDXPlus: A New Dataset For Automatic Medical Diagnosis

abstract: Considering two decision-making tasks $A$ and $B$, each of which wishes to compute an effective decision $Y$ for a given query $X$, can we solve task $B$ by using query-decision pairs $(X, Y)$ of $A$ without knowing the latent decision-making model? Such problems, called inverse decision-making with task migrations, are of interest in that the complex and stochastic nature of real-world applications often prevents the agent from completely knowing the underlying system. In this paper, we introduce such a new problem with formal formulations and present a generic framework for addressing decision-making tasks in social contagion management. On the theory side, we present a generalization analysis for justifying the learning performance of our framework. In empirical studies, we perform a sanity check and compare the presented method with other possible learning-based and graph-based methods. We have acquired promising experimental results, confirming for the first time that it is possible to solve one decision-making task by using the solutions associated with another one.

paragraphs: When an underlying system is complex or only partly known, examples of good decisions may be more accessible than its full model. This paper formalizes inverse decision-making with task migration: using query-decision pairs from task A to solve a different task B.

The authors develop a general framework for social-contagion management, where decisions depend on a latent stochastic process. A generalization analysis supports the learning approach, asking when experience from one type of decision can inform another without first observing the complete decision-making system.

Empirical studies include a sanity check and comparisons with learning-based and graph-based alternatives. The reported results are promising and support the feasibility of cross-task decision transfer in the studied setting. The abstract does not provide metrics or exact migration assumptions, so it does not establish that arbitrary pairs of decision problems can be solved from one another’s examples.
summary.tldr: Social-Inverse learns to solve a social-contagion task from decisions made for another task.

title: Social-Inverse: Inverse Decision-making of Social Contagion Management with Task Migrations

abstract: Machine learning on blockchain graphs is an emerging field with many applications such as ransomware payment tracking, price manipulation analysis, and money laundering detection. However, analyzing blockchain data requires domain expertise and computational resources, which pose a significant barrier and hinder advancement in this field. We introduce Chartalist, the first comprehensive platform to methodically access and use machine learning across a large selection of blockchains to address this challenge. Chartalist contains ML-ready datasets from unspent transaction output (UTXO) (e.g., Bitcoin) and account-based blockchains (e.g., Ethereum). We envision that Chartalist can facilitate data modeling, analysis, and representation of blockchain data and attract a wider community of scientists to analyze blockchains. Chartalist is an open-science initiative at https://github.com/cakcora/Chartalist.

paragraphs: Blockchain graphs offer data for studying activities such as ransomware payments, price manipulation, and money laundering. However, turning blockchain records into material suitable for machine learning requires specialist knowledge and computational resources. The paper addresses this preparation barrier, which can prevent researchers from working on these problems even when the underlying records are available.

Chartalist provides a platform and machine-learning-ready datasets spanning a broad selection of blockchains. Its coverage includes both unspent transaction output systems, such as Bitcoin, and account-based systems, such as Ethereum. Supporting both categories gives researchers access to data across distinct blockchain structures within a common initiative for systematic machine learning work.

The central contribution is research infrastructure: organized datasets intended to support modeling, analysis, and representation of blockchain data. The authors present Chartalist as an open-science effort and hope it will broaden participation in blockchain research. The abstract positions tracking and detection tasks as potential applications; its stated contribution is making the data more accessible, rather than demonstrating a particular detection system's effectiveness.
summary.tldr: Chartalist supplies machine-learning-ready graph datasets across different blockchain types to lower barriers to research.

title: Chartalist: Labeled Graph Datasets for UTXO and Account-based Blockchains

abstract: Pruning is one of the predominant approaches for compressing deep neural networks (DNNs). Lately, coresets (provable data summarizations) were leveraged for pruning DNNs, adding the advantage of theoretical guarantees on the trade-off between the compression rate and the approximation error. However, coresets in this domain were either data dependant or generated under restrictive assumptions on both the model's weights and inputs. In real-world scenarios, such assumptions are rarely satisfied, limiting the applicability of coresets. To this end, we suggest a novel and robust framework for computing such coresets under mild assumptions on the model's weights and without any assumption on the training data. The idea is to compute the importance of each neuron in each layer with respect to the output of the following layer. This is achieved by an elegant combination of L\"{o}wner ellipsoid and Caratheodory theorem.Our method is simultaneously data-independent, applicable to various networks and datasets (due to the simplified assumptions), and theoretically supported. Experimental results show that our method outperforms existing coreset based neural pruning approaches across a wide range of networks and datasets. For example, our method achieved a $62\%$ compression rate on ResNet50 on ImageNet with $1.09\%$ drop in accuracy.

paragraphs: Pruning compresses a neural network by removing parts of it. Coreset approaches add theoretical control over how compression trades off against approximation error, but earlier methods depend on data or restrictive assumptions about weights and inputs. This paper develops a framework that requires only mild weight assumptions and makes no assumptions about the training data.

The method evaluates each neuron according to its importance for the output of the following layer. It combines Löwner ellipsoids and Carathéodory’s theorem to construct the relevant summaries. This geometric approach makes the pruning procedure data-independent while retaining theoretical support, broadening its applicability beyond the more restrictive coreset settings described by the authors.

Experiments report improvements over existing coreset-based pruning methods across varied networks and datasets. One example achieves a 62% compression rate for ResNet50 on ImageNet with a reported 1.09% drop in accuracy. The contribution is therefore a less restrictive framework with practical evidence behind it, while the remaining mild assumptions on weights still qualify its theoretical scope.
summary.tldr: A geometric coreset framework enables data-independent neural pruning with theoretical support under mild weight assumptions.

title: Pruning Neural Networks via Coresets and Convex Geometry: Towards No Assumptions

abstract: Score distillation sampling (SDS) has shown great promise in text-to-3D generation by distilling pretrained large-scale text-to-image diffusion models, but suffers from over-saturation, over-smoothing, and low-diversity problems. In this work, we propose to model the 3D parameter as a random variable instead of a constant as in SDS and present *variational score distillation* (VSD), a principled particle-based variational framework to explain and address the aforementioned issues in text-to-3D generation. We show that SDS is a special case of VSD and leads to poor samples with both small and large CFG weights. In comparison, VSD works well with various CFG weights as ancestral sampling from diffusion models and simultaneously improves the diversity and sample quality with a common CFG weight (i.e., 7.5). We further present various improvements in the design space for text-to-3D such as distillation time schedule and density initialization, which are orthogonal to the distillation algorithm yet not well explored. Our overall approach, dubbed *ProlificDreamer*, can generate high rendering resolution (i.e., 512$\times$512) and high-fidelity NeRF with rich structure and complex effects (e.g., smoke and drops). Further, initialized from NeRF, meshes fine-tuned by VSD are meticulously detailed and photo-realistic.

paragraphs: Text-to-3D methods can extract guidance from pretrained text-to-image diffusion models through score distillation sampling, or SDS. The paper identifies excessive saturation, excessive smoothing, and limited diversity as problems with this approach. It proposes variational score distillation, VSD, which models the 3D parameters as a random variable instead of a fixed quantity.

VSD uses a particle-based variational framework, with SDS appearing as a special case. The authors show poor SDS samples at both small and large classifier-free guidance weights, while VSD works well across different weights. At the common weight of 7.5, VSD improves both diversity and sample quality, addressing two aspects of generation together.

The complete ProlificDreamer system also changes the distillation schedule and density initialization, design choices separate from the distillation algorithm. It generates NeRF scenes rendered at 512 by 512 resolution with rich structure and effects such as smoke and drops. Meshes initialized from those NeRFs and refined using VSD are reported to have detailed, photorealistic appearance.
summary.tldr: ProlificDreamer uses variational score distillation and additional design improvements to produce higher-quality, more diverse text-guided 3D content.

title: ProlificDreamer: High-Fidelity and Diverse Text-to-3D Generation with Variational Score Distillation

abstract: Recently, Montasser at al. (2019) showed that finite VC dimension is not sufficient for proper adversarially robust PAC learning. In light of this hardness, there is a growing effort to study what type of relaxations to the adversarially robust PAC learning setup can enable proper learnability. In this work, we initiate the study of proper learning under relaxations of the worst-case robust loss. We give a family of robust loss relaxations under which VC classes are properly PAC learnable with sample complexity close to what one would require in the standard PAC learning setup. On the other hand, we show that for an existing and natural relaxation of the worst-case robust loss, finite VC dimension is not sufficient for proper learning. Lastly, we give new generalization guarantees for the adversarially robust empirical risk minimizer.

paragraphs: A proper learning algorithm must return a predictor from the hypothesis class it is learning. For adversarial robustness, finite VC dimension alone does not ensure that such learning is possible under the usual probabilistic guarantees. This paper investigates whether relaxing the worst-case robust loss can restore proper learnability.

The authors identify a family of relaxed robust losses for which VC classes are properly PAC learnable. The required sample complexity is close to that of standard PAC learning. This establishes that some changes to the robustness objective can make proper learning feasible without a large increase in the amount of training data required.

The paper also proves a negative result: an existing, natural relaxation still cannot guarantee proper learning from finite VC dimension alone. The choice of relaxation therefore matters; weakening worst-case robustness does not automatically remove the difficulty. Finally, the authors provide new generalization guarantees for adversarially robust empirical risk minimization. Together, these results clarify which forms of relaxed robustness support learning and which retain a fundamental obstacle.
summary.tldr: Some relaxations of worst-case robust loss restore proper PAC learnability for VC classes, while another natural relaxation does not.

title: On Proper Learnability between Average- and Worst-case Robustness

abstract: We describe a new setting for learning a deep graph generative model (GGM) from aggregate graph statistics, rather than from the graph adjacency matrix. Matching the statistics of observed training graphs is the main approach for learning traditional GGMs (e.g, BTER, Chung-Lu, and Erdos-Renyi models). Privacy researchers have proposed learning from graph statistics as a way to protect privacy. We develop an architecture for training a deep GGM to match statistics while preserving local differential privacy guarantees. Empirical evaluation on 8 datasets indicates that our deep GGM model generates more realistic graphs than the traditional GGMs when both are learned from graph statistics only. We also benchmark our deep GGM trained on statistics only, against state-of-the-art deep GGM models that are trained on the entire adjacency matrix. The results show that graph statistics are often sufficient to build a competitive deep GGM that generates realistic graphs while protecting local privacy.

We also benchmark our deep GGM trained on statistics only, against state-of-the-art deep GGM models that are trained on the entire adjacency matrix. The results show that graph statistics are often sufficient to build a competitive deep GGM that generates realistic graphs while protecting local privacy.

paragraphs: Graph generators are often trained using the full adjacency matrix, which specifies the connections in each training graph. This paper studies training a deep generator from aggregate graph statistics instead. Traditional graph generators already use statistical matching, and learning from summaries has also been proposed as a way to protect privacy.

The authors develop an architecture that trains a deep graph generator to match statistics while preserving local differential privacy guarantees. This changes the information supplied during learning: the model learns from aggregate properties rather than the entire connection structure. The aim is to retain realistic graph generation while working within that privacy-preserving setting.

Across eight datasets, the deep model generates more realistic graphs than the traditional generators compared under the same statistics-only training condition. The authors also compare it with leading deep generators trained on full adjacency matrices. Their findings indicate that statistics are often enough to produce a competitive deep generator. That qualified result supports useful graph generation with local privacy, without claiming that summaries always replace full graph information.
summary.tldr: A deep graph generator trained on aggregate statistics produces competitive graphs while preserving local differential privacy guarantees.

title: Neural Graph Generation from Graph Statistics

abstract: We propose weakly coupled deep Q-networks (WCDQN), a novel deep reinforcement learning algorithm that enhances performance in a class of structured problems called weakly coupled Markov decision processes (WCMDP). WCMDPs consist of multiple independent subproblems connected by an action space constraint, which is a structural property that frequently emerges in practice. Despite this appealing structure, WCMDPs quickly become intractable as the number of subproblems grows. WCDQN employs a single network to train multiple DQN ``subagents,'' one for each subproblem, and then combine their solutions to establish an upper bound on the optimal action value. This guides the main DQN agent towards optimality. We show that the tabular version, weakly coupled Q-learning (WCQL), converges almost surely to the optimal action value. Numerical experiments show faster convergence compared to DQN and related techniques in settings with as many as 10 subproblems, $3^{10}$ total actions, and a continuous state space.

The paper therefore pairs a tabular convergence guarantee with empirical evidence for the neural approach.
summary.tldr: WCDQN combines subproblem learners into an action-value upper bound that accelerates learning in weakly coupled decision problems.

title: Weakly Coupled Deep Q-Networks

abstract: We present RoboHive, a comprehensive software platform and ecosystem for research in the field of Robot Learning and Embodied Artificial Intelligence. Our platform encompasses a diverse range of pre-existing and novel environments, including dexterous manipulation with the Shadow Hand, whole-arm manipulation tasks with Franka and Fetch robots, quadruped locomotion, among others. Included environments are organized within and cover multiple domains such as hand manipulation, locomotion, multi-task, multi-agent, muscles, etc. In comparison to prior works, RoboHive offers a streamlined and unified task interface taking dependency on only a minimal set of well-maintained packages, features tasks with high physics fidelity and rich visual diversity, and supports common hardware drivers for real-world deployment. The unified interface of RoboHive offers a convenient and accessible abstraction for algorithmic research in imitation, reinforcement, multi-task, and hierarchical learning. Furthermore, RoboHive includes expert demonstrations and baseline results for most environments, providing a standard for benchmarking and comparisons. Details: https://sites.google.com/view/robohive

It brings together existing and new environments covering tasks such as dexterous hand manipulation, whole-arm manipulation, and quadruped locomotion. Its domains also include multi-task, multi-agent, and muscle-based environments, providing a broad collection for studying different learning problems.

The platform organizes these environments behind a unified task interface with a minimal set of maintained dependencies. It includes tasks with high physics fidelity and visual diversity, and supports common hardware drivers for deployment on real robots. The shared interface is intended to make algorithmic research convenient across imitation, reinforcement, multi-task, and hierarchical learning.

Expert demonstrations and baseline results are provided for most environments, giving researchers reference material for benchmarking and comparison. The contribution is the combination of varied tasks, a consistent interface, and supporting evaluation resources. These elements give researchers a common platform for developing and comparing methods across several areas of robot learning.
summary.tldr: RoboHive unifies diverse robot learning environments, hardware support, demonstrations, and baseline results behind a common interface.

title: RoboHive: A Unified Framework for Robot Learning

abstract: Equivariant networks are specifically designed to ensure consistent behavior with respect to a set of input transformations, leading to higher sample efficiency and more accurate and robust predictions. However, redesigning each component of prevalent deep neural network architectures to achieve chosen equivariance is a difficult problem and can result in a computationally expensive network during both training and inference. A recently proposed alternative towards equivariance that removes the architectural constraints is to use a simple canonicalization network that transforms the input to a canonical form before feeding it to an unconstrained prediction network. We show here that this approach can effectively be used to make a large pretrained network equivariant. However, we observe that the produced canonical orientations can be misaligned with those of the training distribution, hindering performance. Using dataset-dependent priors to inform the canonicalization function, we are able to make large pretrained models equivariant while maintaining their performance. This significantly improves the robustness of these models to deterministic transformations of the data, such as rotations. We believe this equivariant adaptation of large pretrained models can help their domain-specific applications with known symmetry priors.

paragraphs: Equivariance means that a model responds consistently to a specified transformation of its input. Building that behavior into every component of a large network can be difficult and computationally expensive. This paper studies adapting an existing pretrained model through a smaller canonicalization network that first places inputs into a standard form.

The authors find that canonicalization can make large pretrained networks equivariant, but its chosen orientations may differ from those encountered during pretraining. That mismatch can hurt predictions even when transformation consistency is achieved. They address it by using dataset-dependent prior information to guide the canonicalization function toward forms compatible with the model’s training distribution.

The resulting adaptation maintains model performance while substantially improving robustness to deterministic transformations such as rotations. The finding makes the relationship between canonicalization and pretraining central: choosing a consistent orientation also needs to respect what the predictor has learned. The authors suggest that this approach could support applications where relevant symmetries are known, rather than claiming benefits for every possible input transformation.
summary.tldr: Dataset-informed canonicalization makes large pretrained models equivariant while preserving performance and improving robustness to transformations.

title: Equivariant Adaptation of Large Pretrained Models

abstract: Aligning the world model with the environment for the agent’s specific task is crucial in model-based reinforcement learning. While value-equivalent models may achieve better task awareness than maximum-likelihood models, they sacrifice a large amount of semantic information and face implementation issues. To combine the benefits of both types of models, we propose Task-aware Environment Modeling Pipeline with bi-level Optimization (TEMPO), a bi-level model learning framework that introduces an additional level of optimization on top of a maximum-likelihood model by incorporating a meta weighter network that weights each training sample. The meta weighter in the upper level learns to generate novel sample weights by minimizing a proposed task-aware model loss. The model in the lower level focuses on important samples while maintaining rich semantic information in state representations. We evaluate TEMPO on a variety of continuous and discrete control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite and Atari video games. Our results demonstrate that TEMPO achieves state-of-the-art performance regarding asymptotic performance, training stability, and convergence speed.

paragraphs: A world model helps a reinforcement-learning agent represent its environment, but accurate environment modeling does not automatically emphasize what matters for the agent’s task. Models focused on value can offer greater task awareness while sacrificing semantic information and presenting implementation difficulties. TEMPO aims to combine task relevance with the richer representations of maximum-likelihood models.

The framework adds a second optimization level that learns how much weight to assign each training sample. At the upper level, a meta weighter network minimizes a task-aware model loss. At the lower level, the world model learns from the weighted samples, concentrating on important examples while maintaining semantic information in its state representations.

The authors evaluate TEMPO on continuous and discrete control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite and Atari games. They report state-of-the-art results in eventual performance, training stability, and convergence speed. The contribution is a way to align model training with the task through learned sample importance, while keeping the underlying environment-modeling objective as part of the learning process.
summary.tldr: TEMPO learns task-aware sample weights through two-level optimization to improve world-model learning and control performance.

title: Task-aware world model learning with meta weighting via bi-level optimization

abstract: Object pose estimation plays a vital role in embodied AI and computer vision, enabling intelligent agents to comprehend and interact with their surroundings. Despite the practicality of category-level pose estimation, current approaches encounter challenges with partially observed point clouds, known as the multihypothesis issue. In this study, we propose a novel solution by reframing categorylevel object pose estimation as conditional generative modeling, departing from traditional point-to-point regression. Leveraging score-based diffusion models, we estimate object poses by sampling candidates from the diffusion model and aggregating them through a two-step process: filtering out outliers via likelihood estimation and subsequently mean-pooling the remaining candidates. To avoid the costly integration process when estimating the likelihood, we introduce an alternative method that distils an energy-based model from the original score-based model, enabling end-to-end likelihood estimation. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the REAL275 dataset, surpassing 50% and 60% on strict 5 ◦ 2cm and 5 ◦ 5cm metrics, respectively. Furthermore, our method demonstrates strong generalization to novel categories without the need for fine-tuning and can readily adapt to object pose tracking tasks, yielding comparable results to the current state-of-the-art baselines. Our checkpoints and demonstrations can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/genpose.

paragraphs: A partially observed point cloud can support several plausible interpretations of an object's pose. This paper addresses that ambiguity by treating category-level pose estimation as conditional generation. A score-based diffusion model samples candidate poses, allowing the method to represent multiple hypotheses before producing its final estimate.

The candidates are combined in two stages. First, likelihood estimates identify and remove outliers. Then the remaining candidates are averaged. Because likelihood estimation through the original diffusion model involves costly integration, the authors distill an energy-based model from it to provide end-to-end likelihood estimation. This connects the generation and selection of pose hypotheses within the overall approach.

On REAL275, the method reports state-of-the-art performance, exceeding 50% on the strict 5-degree, 2-centimeter metric and 60% on the 5-degree, 5-centimeter metric. It also shows strong generalization to new categories without fine-tuning. Adaptation to pose tracking produces results comparable to state-of-the-art baselines. These findings support generating and filtering multiple poses as a useful response to ambiguity in incomplete observations.
summary.tldr: A diffusion-based pose estimator samples multiple hypotheses, filters them by likelihood, and averages the survivors to handle incomplete object observations.

title: Generative Category-level Object Pose Estimation via Diffusion Models

abstract: In modern machine learning, inner product attention computation is a fundamental task for training large language models such as Transformer, GPT-1, BERT, GPT-2, GPT-3 and ChatGPT. Formally, in this problem, one is given as input three matrices $Q, K, V \in [-B,B]^{n \times d}$, and the goal is to construct the matrix $\mathrm{Att}(Q,K,V) := \mathrm{diag}(A {\bf 1}_n)^{-1} A V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, where $A = \exp(QK^\top/d)$ is the `attention matrix', and $\exp$ is applied entry-wise. Straightforward methods for this problem explicitly compute the $n \times n$ attention matrix $A$, and hence require time $\Omega(n^2)$ even when $d = n^{o(1)}$ is small. In this paper, we investigate whether faster algorithms are possible by \emph{implicitly} making use of the matrix $A$. We present two results, showing that there is a sharp transition at $B = \Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$.$\bullet$ If $d = O(\log n)$ and $B = o(\sqrt{\log n})$, there is an $n^{1+o(1)}$ time algorithm to approximate $\mathrm{Att}(Q,K,V)$ up to $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ additive error.$\bullet$ If $d = O(\log n)$ and $B = \Theta (\sqrt{\log n})$, assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis from fine-grained complexity theory, it is impossible to approximate $\mathrm{Att}(Q,K,V)$ up to $1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$ additive error in truly subquadratic time $n^{2 - \Omega(1)}$.This gives a theoretical explanation for the phenomenon observed in practice that attention computation is much more efficient when the input matrices have smaller entries.

paragraphs: Standard attention computation forms a matrix containing pairwise interactions among n inputs, which creates a quadratic-time burden even when their dimension is small. This paper asks whether algorithms can approximate the output faster by using that matrix implicitly. Its main result ties the answer to B, the maximum absolute entry in the query, key, and value matrices.

When the dimension is O(log n) and B grows more slowly than the square root of log n, the authors give an almost-linear-time approximation algorithm. It achieves inverse-polynomial additive error. Thus, under these dimension and magnitude conditions, obtaining an accurate attention output does not require explicitly constructing every entry of the full attention matrix.

At entry bounds on the order of the square root of log n, the paper establishes a contrasting hardness result. Assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, an approximation with the stated error cannot be computed in truly subquadratic time. The conditional lower bound and constructive upper bound reveal a sharp transition, providing a theoretical explanation for why smaller input entries can make attention computation more efficient.
summary.tldr: For logarithmic-dimensional attention, the paper identifies an entry-size threshold separating almost-linear approximation from conditional subquadratic hardness.

title: Fast Attention Requires Bounded Entries

abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated highly-expressive generative capabilities in vision and NLP. Recent studies in reinforcement learning (RL) have shown that diffusion models are also powerful in modeling complex policies or trajectories in offline datasets. However, these works have been limited to single-task settings where a generalist agent capable of addressing multi-task predicaments is absent. In this paper, we aim to investigate the effectiveness of a single diffusion model in modeling large-scale multi-task offline data, which can be challenging due to diverse and multimodal data distribution. Specifically, we propose Multi-Task Diffusion Model (\textsc{MTDiff}), a diffusion-based method that incorporates Transformer backbones and prompt learning for generative planning and data synthesis in multi-task offline settings. \textsc{MTDiff} leverages vast amounts of knowledge available in multi-task data and performs implicit knowledge sharing among tasks. For generative planning, we find \textsc{MTDiff} outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms across 50 tasks on Meta-World and 8 maps on Maze2D. For data synthesis, \textsc{MTDiff} generates high-quality data for testing tasks given a single demonstration as a prompt, which enhances the low-quality datasets for even unseen tasks.

paragraphs: A model trained on many reinforcement learning tasks must accommodate varied behaviors and multiple plausible ways of acting. MTDiff studies whether one diffusion model can handle that diversity in existing offline datasets. Its goal is to use shared experience across tasks for both planning and generating additional training data.

The method combines a Transformer backbone with prompt learning inside a diffusion-based system. This gives the model a way to use task information while learning from the broader collection of trajectories. The authors describe knowledge sharing across tasks as implicit: the shared model learns from the combined data rather than treating each task as a separate modeling problem.

For planning, MTDiff outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms across 50 Meta-World tasks and eight Maze2D maps in the reported experiments. For data synthesis, a single demonstration can prompt generation for a testing task. The generated data improves low-quality datasets, including those for unseen tasks, showing that the same modeling approach can support both action planning and dataset enhancement.
summary.tldr: MTDiff uses one prompted diffusion model to plan across tasks and generate data that improves offline reinforcement learning datasets.

title: Diffusion Model is an Effective Planner and Data Synthesizer for Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We establish precise structural and risk equivalences between subsampling and ridge regularization for ensemble ridge estimators. Specifically, we prove that linear and quadratic functionals of subsample ridge estimators, when fitted with different ridge regularization levels $\lambda$ and subsample aspect ratios $\psi$, are asymptotically equivalent along specific paths in the $(\lambda,\psi)$-plane (where $\psi$ is the ratio of the feature dimension to the subsample size). Our results only require bounded moment assumptions on feature and response distributions and allow for arbitrary joint distributions. Furthermore, we provide a data-dependent method to determine the equivalent paths of $(\lambda,\psi)$. An indirect implication of our equivalences is that optimally tuned ridge regression exhibits a monotonic prediction risk in the data aspect ratio. This resolves a recent open problem raised by Nakkiran et al. for general data distributions under proportional asymptotics, assuming a mild regularity condition that maintains regression hardness through linearized signal-to-noise ratios.

paragraphs: This paper establishes precise connections between changing the amount of training data and changing ridge regularization in ensemble ridge estimators. It studies combinations of regularization strength and subsample aspect ratio, where the latter is feature dimension divided by subsample size. Along particular paths through these combinations, certain properties of the resulting estimators become equivalent asymptotically.

The equivalences cover linear and quadratic functionals, yielding both structural and prediction-risk relationships. They require bounded moment assumptions on feature and response distributions while allowing arbitrary joint distributions. The authors also provide a data-dependent procedure for identifying the equivalent paths, connecting the mathematical relationships to information available from a dataset.

A consequence concerns optimally tuned ridge regression: its prediction risk is monotonic in the data aspect ratio under proportional asymptotics. This resolves the stated open problem for general data distributions subject to a mild regularity condition that maintains regression difficulty through linearized signal-to-noise ratios. The equivalences are asymptotic and path-specific, rather than claims that arbitrary finite-data subsampling and regularization choices are interchangeable.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies asymptotic paths along which subsampling and ridge regularization have equivalent structural and risk properties.

title: Generalized equivalences between subsampling and ridge regularization

abstract: Autonomous agents operating in real-world scenarios frequently encounter uncertainty and make decisions based on incomplete information. Planning under uncertainty can be mathematically formalized using partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). However, finding an optimal plan for POMDPs can be computationally expensive and is feasible only for small tasks. In recent years, approximate algorithms, such as tree search and sample-based methodologies, have emerged as state-of-the-art POMDP solvers for larger problems. Despite their effectiveness, these algorithms offer only probabilistic and often asymptotic guarantees toward the optimal solution due to their dependence on sampling. To address these limitations, we derive a deterministic relationship between a simplified solution that iseasier to obtain and the theoretically optimal one. First, we derive bounds for selecting a subset of the observations to branch from while computing a complete belief at each posterior node. Then, since a complete belief update may be computationally demanding, we extend the bounds to support reduction of both the state and the observation spaces. We demonstrate how our guarantees can be integrated with existing state-of-the-art solvers that sample a subset of states and observations. As a result, the returned solution holds deterministic bounds relative to the optimal policy. Lastly, we substantiate our findings with supporting experimental results.

paragraphs: Partially observable Markov decision processes describe planning when an agent cannot directly observe the full state of its environment. Exact optimal planning is expensive, so larger problems often rely on approximate search and sampling. This paper addresses the strength of the resulting guarantees, which are commonly probabilistic and may only apply as computation grows indefinitely.

The authors derive a deterministic relationship between an easier, simplified planning problem and the optimal solution. They first bound the effect of branching on only a subset of possible observations while still computing a complete belief at each resulting node. Its significance is that computational shortcuts can be accompanied by explicit bounds on the solution they return.
summary.tldr: The paper derives deterministic bounds for simplified POMDP planning and shows how to attach them to existing sampling-based solvers.

title: Online POMDP Planning with Anytime Deterministic Guarantees

abstract: Policy Optimization (PO) methods are among the most popular Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms in practice. Recently, Sherman et al. [2023a] proposed a PO-based algorithm with rate-optimal regret guarantees under the linear Markov Decision Process (MDP) model. However, their algorithm relies on a costly pure exploration warm-up phase that is hard to implement in practice. This paper eliminates this undesired warm-up phase, replacing it with a simple and efficient contraction mechanism. Our PO algorithm achieves rate-optimal regret with improved dependence on the other parameters of the problem (horizon and function approximation dimension) in two fundamental settings: adversarial losses with full-information feedback and stochastic losses with bandit feedback.

paragraphs: This paper develops a policy-optimization algorithm for reinforcement learning under a linear Markov decision process model. It addresses a drawback of an earlier method with rate-optimal regret guarantees: the need for a costly initial phase devoted purely to exploration. The authors describe that phase as difficult to implement in practice.

Their algorithm replaces the exploration warmup with a simple, efficient contraction mechanism. The theoretical goal is to retain rate-optimal regret while improving how the guarantee depends on other problem parameters. Regret tracks the performance shortfall accumulated during learning, so controlling it concerns the cost of learning as well as eventual policy quality.

The resulting guarantees have improved dependence on the decision horizon and the dimension used for function approximation. They apply in two settings: adversarial losses with full-information feedback and stochastic losses with bandit feedback. The contribution is therefore a warmup-free procedure with stronger parameter dependence in these specified linear-MDP settings, preserving the central regret-rate guarantee of the earlier approach.
summary.tldr: A contraction mechanism removes pure-exploration warmup while retaining rate-optimal regret with improved parameter dependence in two linear-MDP settings.

title: Warm-up Free Policy Optimization: Improved Regret in Linear Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Exploring the integration of if-then logic rules within neural network architectures presents an intriguing area. This integration seamlessly transforms the rule learning task into neural network training using backpropagation and stochastic gradient descent. From a well-trained sparse and shallow neural network, one can interpret each layer and neuron through the language of logic rules, and a global explanatory rule set can be directly extracted. However, ensuring interpretability may impose constraints on the flexibility, depth, and width of neural networks. In this paper, we propose HyperLogic: a novel framework leveraging hypernetworks to generate weights of the main network. HyperLogic can unveil multiple diverse rule sets, each capable of capturing heterogeneous patterns in data. This provides a simple yet effective method to increase model flexibility and preserve interpretability. We theoretically analyzed the benefits of the HyperLogic by examining the approximation error and generalization capabilities under two types of regularization terms: sparsity and diversity regularizations. Experiments on real data demonstrate that our method can learn more diverse, accurate, and concise rules.

paragraphs: HyperLogic addresses a tension in learning interpretable if-then rules with neural networks. However, keeping the network easy to interpret can restrict its depth, width, and flexibility, limiting the patterns it can express.

The proposed framework uses a hypernetwork to generate the weights of the main network. This allows HyperLogic to produce multiple diverse rule sets, each capturing different patterns in the data. The approach expands the range of rules the system can learn while preserving the ability to express its learned behavior through interpretable logical rules.

summary.tldr: HyperLogic uses hypernetworks to generate diverse interpretable rule sets, improving rule accuracy and conciseness in real-data experiments.

title: HyperLogic: Enhancing Diversity and Accuracy in Rule Learning with HyperNets

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in many real-world applications. Nonetheless, LLMs are often criticized for their tendency to produce hallucinations, wherein the models fabricate incorrect statements on tasks beyond their knowledge and perception. To alleviate this issue, graph retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) has been extensively explored which leverages the factual knowledge in knowledge graphs (KGs) to ground the LLM's responses in established facts and principles. However, most state-of-the-art LLMs are closed-source, making it challenging to develop a prompting framework that can efficiently and effectively integrate KGs into LLMs with hard prompts only. Generally, existing KG-enhanced LLMs usually suffer from three critical issues, including huge search space, high API costs, and laborious prompt engineering, that impede their widespread application in practice. To this end, we introduce a novel **Know**ledge **Gr**aph based **P**romp**T**ing framework, namely **KnowGPT**, to enhance LLMs with domain knowledge. KnowGPT contains a knowledge extraction module to extract the most informative knowledge from KGs, and a context-aware prompt construction module to automatically convert extracted knowledge into effective prompts. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that KnowGPT significantly outperforms all competitors. Notably, KnowGPT achieves a 92.6% accuracy on OpenbookQA leaderboard, comparable to human-level performance.

The authors report that KnowGPT significantly outperforms its competitors on three benchmarks. Its reported OpenbookQA leaderboard accuracy is 92.6%, described as comparable to human-level performance on that benchmark. These results support the effectiveness of the framework for the evaluated tasks; the human comparison is specific to the reported benchmark performance.
summary.tldr: KnowGPT automatically extracts knowledge-graph information and builds context-aware prompts, achieving strong results across three benchmarks.

title: KnowGPT: Knowledge Graph based Prompting for Large Language Models

abstract: Diffusion models are capable of generating photo-realistic images that combine elements which do not appear together in natural images, demonstrating their ability to compositionally generalize. Nonetheless, the precise mechanism of compositionality and how it is acquired through training remains elusive. Here, we consider a highly reduced setting to examine whether diffusion models learn semantically meaningful and fully factorized representations of composable features. We performed extensive controlled experiments on conditional DDPMs trained to generate various forms of 2D Gaussian data. We demonstrate that the models learn factorized, semi-continuous manifold representations that are orthogonal in underlying continuous latent features of independent variations but are not aligned for different values of the same feature. With such representations, models demonstrate superior compositionality but have limited ability to interpolate over unseen values of a given feature. Our experimental results further demonstrate that diffusion models can attain compositionality with a small amount of compositional examples, suggesting a novel way to train DDPMs. Finally, we connect manifold formation in diffusion models to percolation theory in physics, thereby offering insights into the sudden onset of factorized representation learning. Our thorough toy experiments thus contribute a deeper understanding of how diffusion models capture compositional structure in data, paving the way for future research aimed at enhancing factorization and compositional generalization in generative models for real-world applications.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how diffusion models learn to combine features in new ways. This reduced setting lets them examine the organization of learned representations and its relationship to compositional behavior.

The models learn partially continuous, factorized representations. Independent underlying variations occupy orthogonal directions, but representations for different values of the same feature do not align. This distinction explains the observed combination of strong compositionality and limited interpolation: recombining features and generating unseen values within a feature are different capabilities.

The experiments also show that a small amount of compositional training examples can be enough for the models to acquire compositionality. The authors connect the formation of representation manifolds to percolation theory, offering an account of its sudden emergence. These findings provide insight from a deliberately simplified setting and suggest directions for training diffusion models, while extensions to real-world generation remain a motivation for future research.
summary.tldr: Controlled Gaussian-data experiments reveal how diffusion models can learn compositional representations while still struggling to interpolate unseen feature values.

title: How Diffusion Models Learn to Factorize and Compose

abstract: Deep neural networks provide Reinforcement Learning (RL) powerful function approximators to address large-scale decision-making problems. However, these approximators introduce challenges due to the non-stationary nature of RL training. One source of the challenges in RL is that output predictions can churn, leading to uncontrolled changes after each batch update for states not included in the batch. Although such a churn phenomenon exists in each step of network training, it remains under-explored on how churn occurs and impacts RL. In this work, we start by characterizing churn in a view of Generalized Policy Iteration with function approximation, and we discover a chain effect of churn that leads to a cycle where the churns in value estimation and policy improvement compound and bias the learning dynamics throughout the iteration. Further, we concretize the study and focus on the learning issues caused by the chain effect in different settings, including greedy action deviation in value-based methods, trust region violation in proximal policy optimization, and dual bias of policy value in actor-critic methods. We then propose a method to reduce the chain effect across different settings, called Churn Approximated ReductIoN (CHAIN), which can be easily plugged into most existing DRL algorithms. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in both reducing churn and improving learning performance across online and offline, value-based and policy-based RL settings.

paragraphs: A neural network update can change predictions for states that were absent from the training batch. This paper calls those uncontrolled changes churn and studies their consequences in reinforcement learning. The concern is especially relevant because value estimates and policies influence each other throughout training, so a change can propagate beyond its immediate source.

The authors analyze churn through generalized policy iteration with function approximation. They identify a chain effect in which changes to value estimation and policy improvement compound and bias subsequent learning. They examine concrete manifestations: altered greedy actions in value-based methods, trust-region violations in proximal policy optimization, and coupled policy-value bias in actor-critic methods.

Their proposed method, CHAIN, reduces this chain effect and can be incorporated into most existing deep reinforcement-learning algorithms. Experiments show reduced churn and improved learning across online and offline settings, including both value-based and policy-based approaches. The findings make uncontrolled changes outside an update batch a concrete target for improving training, rather than treating each update's effects as confined to the states it directly uses.
summary.tldr: CHAIN improves reinforcement learning by reducing compounding unintended changes between value estimates and policies.

title: Improving Deep Reinforcement Learning by Reducing the Chain Effect of Value and Policy Churn

abstract: Anomaly detection is widely used for identifying critical errors and suspicious behaviors, but current methods lack interpretability.We leverage common properties of existing methods and recent advances in generative models to introduce counterfactual explanations for anomaly detection.Given an input, we generate its counterfactual as a diffusion-based repair that shows what a non-anomalous version $\textit{should have looked like}$.A key advantage of this approach is that it enables a domain-independent formal specification of explainability desiderata, offering a unified framework for generating and evaluating explanations.We demonstrate the effectiveness of our anomaly explainability framework, AR-Pro, on vision (MVTec, VisA) and time-series (SWaT, WADI, HAI) anomaly datasets. The code used for the experiments is accessible at: https://github.com/xjiae/arpro.

paragraphs: An anomaly detector can flag an unusual input without making clear what is wrong with it. AR-Pro addresses this interpretability problem by generating a repaired version of the input. The repair serves as a counterfactual explanation: it presents a non-anomalous alternative that can be compared with the original to understand the detector's judgment.

The method uses a diffusion-based generative process to produce these repairs. Its contribution also concerns how explanations should be specified and assessed. Drawing on properties shared by existing anomaly detection methods, the authors formulate desirable explanation properties in a way that does not depend on a particular application domain.

This gives AR-Pro a common framework for both generating explanations and evaluating them. The authors demonstrate its effectiveness on image anomaly datasets MVTec and VisA and time-series datasets SWaT, WADI, and HAI. These results support the use of repair-based explanations across both kinds of data, with formal properties providing a shared language for assessing the explanations.
summary.tldr: AR-Pro explains anomalies through diffusion-generated repairs and a domain-independent framework for specifying and evaluating explanation properties.

title: AR-Pro: Counterfactual Explanations for Anomaly Repair with Formal Properties

abstract: Developing meaningful and efficient representations that separate the fundamental structure of the data generation mechanism is crucial in representation learning. However, Disentangled Representation Learning has not fully shown its potential on real images, because of correlated generative factors, their resolution and limited access to ground truth labels. Specifically on the latter, we investigate the possibility of leveraging synthetic data to learn general-purpose disentangled representations applicable to real data, discussing the effect of fine-tuning and what properties of disentanglement are preserved after the transfer. We provide an extensive empirical study to address these issues. In addition, we propose a new interpretable intervention-based metric, to measure the quality of factors encoding in the representation. Our results indicate that some level of disentanglement, transferring a representation from synthetic to real data, is possible and effective.

paragraphs: Disentangled representation learning aims to separate the underlying factors that generate data into meaningful parts of a learned representation. Demonstrating its usefulness on real images has been difficult because generative factors can be correlated, image resolution presents challenges, and ground-truth factor labels are limited. This paper focuses particularly on the shortage of those labels.

The authors investigate whether synthetic data can support learning general-purpose disentangled representations that subsequently transfer to real images. Their extensive empirical study examines the effect of fine-tuning and asks which disentanglement properties survive transfer. This makes preservation of the learned factor structure an explicit question, beyond whether a representation can simply be applied to another dataset.

The paper also introduces an interpretable intervention-based metric for assessing how well factors are encoded in the representation. The results indicate that some degree of disentanglement can transfer from synthetic to real data and be effective. The finding supports synthetic-data transfer as a promising route while retaining the paper's qualified conclusion: the evidence establishes partial preservation, rather than complete separation of every underlying real-image factor.
summary.tldr: An empirical study finds that some disentanglement can transfer from synthetic to real images and introduces an intervention-based metric for factor encoding.

title: Transferring disentangled representations: bridging the gap between synthetic and real images

abstract: Class-agnostic object detection (OD) can be a cornerstone or a bottleneck for many downstream vision tasks. Despite considerable advancements in bottom-up and multi-object discovery methods that leverage basic visual cues to identify salient objects, consistently achieving a high recall rate remains difficult due to the diversity of object types and their contextual complexity. In this work, we investigate using vision-language models (VLMs) to enhance object detection via a self-supervised prompt learning strategy. Our initial findings indicate that manually crafted text queries often result in undetected objects, primarily because detection confidence diminishes when the query words exhibit semantic overlap. To address this, we propose a Dispersing Prompt Expansion (DiPEx) approach. DiPEx progressively learns to expand a set of distinct, non-overlapping hyperspherical prompts to enhance recall rates, thereby improving performance in downstream tasks such as out-of-distribution OD. Specifically, DiPEx initiates the process by self-training generic parent prompts and selecting the one with the highest semantic uncertainty for further expansion. The resulting child prompts are expected to inherit semantics from their parent prompts while capturing more fine-grained semantics. We apply dispersion losses to ensure high inter-class discrepancy among child prompts while preserving semantic consistency between parent-child prompt pairs. To prevent excessive growth of the prompt sets, we utilize the maximum angular coverage (MAC) of the semantic space as a criterion for early termination. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DiPEx through extensive class-agnostic OD and OOD-OD experiments on MS-COCO and LVIS, surpassing other prompting methods by up to 20.1% in AR and achieving a 21.3% AP improvement over SAM.

title: DiPEx: Dispersing Prompt Expansion for Class-Agnostic Object Detection

abstract: Recent advances in microscopy have enabled the rapid generation of terabytes of image data in cell biology and biomedical research. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer a promising solution for large-scale biological image analysis, enhancing researchers’ efficiency, identifying new image biomarkers, and accelerating hypothesis generation and scientific discovery. However, there is a lack of standardized, diverse, and large-scale vision-language benchmarks to evaluate VLMs’ perception and cognition capabilities in biological image understanding. To address this gap, we introduce Micro-Bench, an expert-curated benchmark encompassing 24 biomedical tasks across various scientific disciplines (biology, pathology), microscopy modalities (electron, fluorescence, light), scales (subcellular, cellular, tissue), and organisms in both normal and abnormal states. We evaluate state-of-the-art biomedical, pathology, and general VLMs on Micro-Bench and find that: i) current models struggle on all categories, even for basic tasks such as distinguishing microscopy modalities; ii) current specialist models fine-tuned on biomedical data often perform worse than generalist models; iii) fine-tuning in specific microscopy domains can cause catastrophic forgetting, eroding prior biomedical knowledge encoded in their base model. iv) weight interpolation between fine-tuned and pre-trained models offers one solution to forgetting and improves general performance across biomedical tasks. We release Micro-Bench under a permissive license to accelerate the research and development of microscopy foundation models.

paragraphs: Microscopy produces enormous amounts of image data, creating demand for models that can interpret biological images and communicate about them. Micro-Bench supplies an expert-curated evaluation resource for this capability. It covers 24 biomedical tasks across biology and pathology, multiple microscopy modalities, and scales ranging from subcellular structures to tissue.

The benchmark includes different organisms in normal and abnormal states. Evaluations of biomedical, pathology, and general-purpose vision-language models find difficulties across every task category, including basic distinctions between microscopy modalities. Models specialized through biomedical fine-tuning often perform worse than generalist models, showing that specialization alone does not ensure broader microscopy competence.

The authors also find that fine-tuning within particular microscopy domains can cause catastrophic forgetting, eroding biomedical knowledge already present in the base model. Interpolating the weights of pretrained and fine-tuned models offers one remedy and improves general performance across biomedical tasks. Released under a permissive license, Micro-Bench provides a shared way to examine both domain understanding and the tradeoffs that arise when adapting models to specialized biological imagery.
summary.tldr: Micro-Bench exposes broad weaknesses in microscopy understanding and shows that specialized fine-tuning can erode existing biomedical knowledge.

title: Micro-Bench: A Microscopy Benchmark for Vision-Language Understanding

abstract: Non-autoregressive Transformers (NATs) are recently applied in direct speech-to-speech translation systems, which convert speech across different languages without intermediate text data. Although NATs generate high-quality outputs and offer faster inference than autoregressive models, they tend to produce incoherent and repetitive results due to complex data distribution (e.g., acoustic and linguistic variations in speech). In this work, we introduce DiffNorm, a diffusion-based normalization strategy that simplifies data distributions for training NAT models. After training with a self-supervised noise estimation objective, DiffNorm constructs normalized target data by denoising synthetically corrupted speech features. Additionally, we propose to regularize NATs with classifier-free guidance, improving model robustness and translation quality by randomly dropping out source information during training. Our strategies result in a notable improvement of about $+7$ ASR-BLEU for English-Spanish (En-Es) translation and $+2$ ASR-BLEU for English-French (En-Fr) on the CVSS benchmark, while attaining over $14\times$ speedup for En-Es and $5 \times$ speedup for En-Fr translations compared to autoregressive baselines.

paragraphs: Direct speech-to-speech translation converts spoken language without passing through intermediate text. Non-autoregressive transformers can generate translations faster than autoregressive models, but acoustic and linguistic variation makes their training distribution complicated. The resulting speech can contain repetition or lose coherence even when overall output quality is high.

DiffNorm simplifies the target data used to train these models. A diffusion model first learns a self-supervised noise-estimation task. It then denoises deliberately corrupted speech features to produce normalized training targets. The paper also introduces classifier-free-guidance regularization: randomly removing source information during training improves robustness and translation quality.

On CVSS, the combined strategies deliver approximately seven additional ASR-BLEU points for English-to-Spanish translation and two for English-to-French. They also achieve more than 14-fold and fivefold speedups, respectively, over autoregressive baselines. These findings show that simplifying the target distribution and changing how source conditioning is used can improve translation quality while retaining the speed advantages motivating non-autoregressive generation. The reported gains apply to the evaluated language pairs and benchmark.
summary.tldr: DiffNorm uses diffusion-based target normalization and source dropout to improve fast, direct speech-to-speech translation.

title: DiffNorm: Self-Supervised Normalization for Non-autoregressive Speech-to-speech Translation

abstract: Recently, the strong latent Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DPM) has been applied to high-quality Text-to-Image (T2I) generation (e.g., Stable Diffusion), by injecting the encoded target text prompt into the gradually denoised diffusion image generator. Despite the success of DPM in practice, the mechanism behind it remains to be explored. To fill this blank, we begin by examining the intermediate statuses during the gradual denoising generation process in DPM. The empirical observations indicate, the shape of image is reconstructed after the first few denoising steps, and then the image is filled with details (e.g., texture). The phenomenon is because the low-frequency signal (shape relevant) of the noisy image is not corrupted until the final stage in the forward process (initial stage of generation) of adding noise in DPM. Inspired by the observations, we proceed to explore the influence of each token in the text prompt during the two stages. After a series of experiments of T2I generations conditioned on a set of text prompts. We conclude that in the earlier generation stage, the image is mostly decided by the special token [\texttt{EOS}] in the text prompt, and the information in the text prompt is already conveyed in this stage. After that, the diffusion model completes the details of generated images by information from themselves. Finally, we propose to apply this observation to accelerate the process of T2I generation by properly removing text guidance, which finally accelerates the sampling up to 25\%+.
