Finally, we propose to apply this observation to accelerate the process of T2I generation by properly removing text guidance, which finally accelerates the sampling up to 25\%+.

paragraphs: The paper examines how text-to-image diffusion models construct images during gradual denoising. By inspecting intermediate generations, the authors observe that overall shape appears within the first few steps, followed by details such as texture. They connect this pattern to low-frequency information, which is associated with shape and survives until late in the forward noise-adding process.

The researchers then investigate how individual prompt tokens influence the early and late generation stages. In experiments with a set of text prompts, they find that the early image is mostly determined by the special end-of-sequence token. They conclude that prompt information is largely conveyed during this early stage, after which the model develops details using information from the evolving image itself.

These observations motivate removing text guidance at appropriate points during generation to reduce unnecessary computation. The resulting approach reports sampling acceleration reaching 25% or more. The work links an empirical account of when text and image information matter to a concrete acceleration strategy, grounding the proposed change in observed denoising behavior.
summary.tldr: Observed early shape formation and prompt influence motivate selectively removing text guidance, yielding reported sampling acceleration of 25% or more.

title: Towards Understanding the Working Mechanism of Text-to-Image Diffusion Model

abstract: Reward models trained on human preference data have been proven to effectively align Large Language Models (LLMs) with human intent within the framework of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). However, current reward models have limited generalization capabilities to unseen prompts and responses, which can lead to an unexpected phenomenon known as reward over-optimization, resulting in a decline in actual performance due to excessive optimization of rewards. While previous research has advocated for constraining policy optimization, our study introduces a novel approach to enhance the reward model's generalization ability against distribution shifts by regularizing the hidden states. Specifically, we retain the base model's language model head and incorporate a suite of text-generation losses to preserve the hidden states' text-generation capabilities, while concurrently learning a reward head behind the same hidden states. Our experimental results demonstrate that the introduced regularization technique markedly improves the accuracy of learned reward models across a variety of out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks and effectively alleviates the over-optimization issue in RLHF, offering a more reliable and robust preference learning paradigm.

paragraphs: Reward models learn from human preferences and guide language models during reinforcement learning from human feedback. When they generalize poorly to unfamiliar prompts or responses, optimizing their scores too aggressively can reduce actual performance. This paper addresses that reward over-optimization problem by improving the reward model’s internal representations.

The method retains the base model’s language-generation head while training a reward head on the same hidden states. Additional text-generation losses encourage those shared representations to preserve their ability to support language generation. Reward learning therefore takes place alongside an objective that maintains useful generative capabilities in the underlying representation.

The authors report markedly better reward-model accuracy across several out-of-distribution tasks and reduced over-optimization during reinforcement learning. This approach targets the quality of the learned reward signal, complementing the concern that policy optimization itself may need constraints. The results support hidden-state regularization as a way to make preference learning more robust when prompts and responses differ from those seen in reward-model training.
summary.tldr: Preserving text-generation capabilities while training a reward model improves its reported generalization and reduces reward over-optimization.

title: Regularizing Hidden States Enables Learning Generalizable Reward Model for LLMs

abstract: When fine-tuning zero-shot models like CLIP, our desideratum is for the fine-tuned model to excel in both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD). Recently, ensemble-based models (ESM) have been shown to offer significant robustness improvement, while preserving high ID accuracy. However, our study finds that ESMs do not solve the ID-OOD trade-offs: they achieve peak performance for ID and OOD accuracy at different mixing coefficients. When optimized for OOD accuracy, the ensemble model exhibits a noticeable decline in ID accuracy, and vice versa. In contrast, we propose a sample-wise ensembling technique that can simultaneously attain the best ID and OOD accuracy without the trade-offs. Specifically, we construct a Zero-Shot Failure (ZSF) set containing training samples incorrectly predicted by the zero-shot model. For each test sample, we calculate its distance to the ZSF set and assign a higher weight to the fine-tuned model in the ensemble if the distance is small. We term our method Variance Reduction Fine-tuning (VRF), as it effectively reduces the variance in ensemble predictions, thereby decreasing residual error. On ImageNet and five derived distribution shifts, our VRF further improves the OOD accuracy by 1.5 - 2.0 pp over the ensemble baselines while maintaining or increasing ID accuracy. VRF achieves similar large robustness gains on (0.9 - 3.1 pp) on other distribution shifts19 benchmarks. Codes are available in https://github.com/BeierZhu/VRF.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a zero-shot model aims to improve performance on the target data while preserving accuracy when the data distribution changes. Combining zero-shot and fine-tuned predictions can help, but the authors find that a single mixing coefficient reaches its best in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy at different values. Choosing one compromise can therefore sacrifice performance on the other.

Variance Reduction Fine-tuning, or VRF, changes the mixture for each test sample. It first collects training examples that the zero-shot model predicts incorrectly into a Zero-Shot Failure set. A test sample closer to that set receives more weight from the fine-tuned model. This uses the locations of known zero-shot failures to guide which model should contribute more to each prediction.

On ImageNet and five derived distribution shifts, VRF improves out-of-distribution accuracy by 1.5–2.0 percentage points over ensemble baselines while maintaining or increasing in-distribution accuracy. Other distribution-shift benchmarks show gains of 0.9–3.1 points. The authors explain the method through reduced prediction variance and residual error, supporting adaptive mixing as a way to improve both objectives in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: VRF adjusts zero-shot and fine-tuned prediction weights per sample using proximity to known zero-shot failures, improving robustness without sacrificing tested in-distribution accuracy.

title: Robust Fine-tuning of Zero-shot Models via Variance Reduction

abstract: While imitation learning requires access to high-quality data, offline reinforcement learning (RL) should, in principle, perform similarly or better with substantially lower data quality by using a value function. However, current results indicate that offline RL often performs worse than imitation learning, and it is often unclear what holds back the performance of offline RL. Motivated by this observation, we aim to understand the bottlenecks in current offline RL algorithms. While poor performance of offline RL is typically attributed to an imperfect value function, we ask: *is the main bottleneck of offline RL indeed in learning the value function, or something else?* To answer this question, we perform a systematic empirical study of (1) value learning, (2) policy extraction, and (3) policy generalization in offline RL problems, analyzing how these components affect performance. We make two surprising observations. First, we find that the choice of a policy extraction algorithm significantly affects the performance and scalability of offline RL, often more so than the value learning objective. For instance, we show that common value-weighted behavioral cloning objectives (e.g., AWR) do not fully leverage the learned value function, and switching to behavior-constrained policy gradient objectives (e.g., DDPG+BC) often leads to substantial improvements in performance and scalability. Second, we find that a big barrier to improving offline RL performance is often imperfect policy generalization on test-time states out of the support of the training data, rather than policy learning on in-distribution states. We then show that the use of suboptimal but high-coverage data or test-time policy training techniques can address this generalization issue in practice. Specifically, we propose two simple test-time policy improvement methods and show that these methods lead to better performance.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning should be able to use value estimates to learn from data that is less than expert quality. Yet it often underperforms imitation learning, raising a question about where the learning pipeline breaks down. This paper separately examines value learning, extracting a policy from learned values, and generalizing that policy to states encountered during testing.

The empirical study finds that policy extraction often affects performance and scalability more than the value-learning objective. Common value-weighted behavioral cloning methods do not fully use the learned value function. Switching to behavior-constrained policy gradient objectives often produces substantial improvements, showing that how values influence action choices can be a major bottleneck.

The study also identifies weak policy generalization to states outside the training data’s support as an important barrier. Data with broader coverage can help even when its behavior is suboptimal. The authors additionally propose two test-time policy improvement methods and report better performance. These findings shift attention toward extracting useful behavior and adapting it to unfamiliar states, alongside improving value estimates.
summary.tldr: An empirical study finds that policy extraction and generalization often constrain offline reinforcement learning more than value learning does.

title: Is Value Learning Really the Main Bottleneck in Offline RL?

abstract: Data heterogeneity is one of the key challenges in federated learning, and many efforts have been devoted to tackling this problem. However, distributed concept drift with data heterogeneity, where clients may additionally experience different concept drifts, is a largely unexplored area. In this work, we focus on real drift, where the conditional distribution $P(\mathcal{Y}|\mathcal{X})$ changes. We first study how distributed concept drift affects the model training and find that local classifier plays a critical role in drift adaptation. Moreover, to address data heterogeneity, we study the feature alignment under distributed concept drift, and find two factors that are crucial for feature alignment: the conditional distribution $P(\mathcal{Y}|\mathcal{X})$ and the degree of data heterogeneity. Motivated by the above findings, we propose FedCCFA, a federated learning framework with classifier clustering and feature alignment. To enhance collaboration under distributed concept drift, FedCCFA clusters local classifiers at class-level and generates clustered feature anchors according to the clustering results. Assisted by these anchors, FedCCFA adaptively aligns clients' feature spaces based on the entropy of label distribution $P(\mathcal{Y})$, alleviating the inconsistency in feature space. Our results demonstrate that FedCCFA significantly outperforms existing methods under various concept drift settings. Code is available at https://github.com/Chen-Junbao/FedCCFA.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes harder when clients have different data and also experience different changes over time. This paper studies real concept drift: changes in the relationship between an input and its label, expressed as P(Y|X). The authors find that local classifiers play a central role in adapting to these changes, making their treatment important for collaboration across clients.

The proposed FedCCFA framework clusters local classifiers separately at the class level. It then builds feature anchors from these clusters to guide the alignment of clients' feature representations. Alignment adapts according to the entropy of each client's label distribution. This design responds to the finding that useful alignment depends on both the input-label relationship and the degree of data heterogeneity.

The reported experiments show significant improvements over existing methods across various concept-drift settings. The approach matters because it connects collaboration to class-specific classifier groupings while adjusting feature alignment to client data. It addresses changing label relationships and inconsistent feature spaces within the same framework.
summary.tldr: FedCCFA combines class-level classifier clustering with adaptive feature alignment to improve federated learning when clients experience different concept drifts.

title: Classifier Clustering and Feature Alignment for Federated Learning under Distributed Concept Drift

abstract: Geometric deep learning (GDL) has gained significant attention in scientific fields, for its proficiency in modeling data with intricate geometric structures. Yet, very few works have delved into its capability of tackling the distribution shift problem, a prevalent challenge in many applications.To bridge this gap, we propose GeSS, a comprehensive benchmark designed for evaluating the performance of GDL models in scientific scenarios with distribution shifts.Our evaluation datasets cover diverse scientific domains from particle physics, materials science to biochemistry, and encapsulate a broad spectrum of distribution shifts including conditional, covariate, and concept shifts. Furthermore, we study three levels of information access from the out-of-distribution (OOD) test data, including no OOD information, only unlabeled OOD data, and OOD data with a few labels. Overall, our benchmark results in 30 different experiment settings, and evaluates 3 GDL backbones and 11 learning algorithms in each setting. A thorough analysis of the evaluation results is provided, poised to illuminate insights for GDL researchers and domain practitioners who are to use GDL in their applications.

paragraphs: GeSS provides a benchmark for evaluating geometric deep learning when scientific data change between training and testing. Models that handle geometric structure well still need to work under distribution shifts, and the paper identifies this as an underexplored part of their evaluation. Its contribution is a structured collection of settings for examining that problem.

The benchmark spans particle physics, materials science, and biochemistry. It includes conditional, covariate, and concept shifts, giving researchers several kinds of change to investigate. It also distinguishes three information conditions: no access to out-of-distribution data, access to unlabeled examples, and access to examples with a small number of labels.

Combining these dimensions produces 30 experimental settings, each evaluating three geometric model backbones and eleven learning algorithms. This design supports comparisons that account for both the scientific setting and the information available for adaptation. The paper analyzes the resulting evaluations to inform researchers and practitioners considering geometric learning for applications where training and deployment data may differ.
summary.tldr: GeSS benchmarks geometric deep learning across scientific domains, distribution shifts, and different levels of access to shifted data.

title: GeSS: Benchmarking Geometric Deep Learning under Scientific Applications with Distribution Shifts

abstract: Large language models have demonstrated impressive capabilities across various natural language processing tasks, especially in solving mathematical problems. However, large language models are not good at math theorem proving using formal languages like Lean. A significant challenge in this area is the scarcity of training data available in these formal languages. To address this issue, we propose a novel pipeline that iteratively generates and filters synthetic data to translate natural language mathematical problems into Lean 4 statements, and vice versa. Our results indicate that the synthetic data pipeline can provide useful training data and improve the performance of LLMs in translating and understanding complex mathematical problems and proofs. Our final dataset contains about 57K formal-informal question pairs along with searched proof from the math contest forum and 21 new IMO questions. We open-source our code at \url{https://github.com/InternLM/InternLM-Math} and our data at \url{https://huggingface.co/datasets/InternLM/Lean-Workbook}.

paragraphs: Lean Workbook addresses a training-data bottleneck in formal mathematical reasoning. Language models can perform well on mathematical problems written in ordinary language while struggling with theorem proving in formal languages such as Lean. The paper focuses on creating data that connects informal mathematical statements with their formal counterparts.

The authors build an iterative pipeline that generates and filters synthetic examples in both directions: from natural-language problems to Lean 4 statements and from formal statements back to natural language. Linking the two forms gives models material for learning how mathematical meaning is expressed under different representational requirements. Repeated generation and filtering are the central mechanisms used to construct this training resource.

The resulting dataset contains approximately 57,000 formal–informal question pairs, along with searched proofs from a mathematics contest forum and 21 new IMO questions. The authors report that the synthetic data improves models' translation and understanding of complex mathematical problems and proofs. The contribution is therefore both a dataset and a data-generation approach for strengthening the connection between informal mathematics and formal reasoning.
summary.tldr: Lean Workbook uses iterative synthetic-data generation and filtering to create about 57,000 paired informal and Lean mathematical questions.

title: Lean Workbook: A large-scale Lean problem set formalized from natural language math problems

abstract: Deploying deep neural networks for risk-sensitive tasks necessitates an uncertainty estimation mechanism. This paper introduces *hierarchical selective classification*, extending selective classification to a hierarchical setting. Our approach leverages the inherent structure of class relationships, enabling models to reduce the specificity of their predictions when faced with uncertainty. In this paper, we first formalize hierarchical risk and coverage, and introduce hierarchical risk-coverage curves. Next, we develop algorithms for hierarchical selective classification (which we refer to as "inference rules"), and propose an efficient algorithm that guarantees a target accuracy constraint with high probability. Lastly, we conduct extensive empirical studies on over a thousand ImageNet classifiers, revealing that training regimes such as CLIP, pretraining on ImageNet21k and knowledge distillation boost hierarchical selective performance.

paragraphs: When a classifier is uncertain, the structure connecting its possible labels can offer a useful response: make a broader prediction. This paper develops hierarchical selective classification, which lets a model reduce the specificity of its answer as uncertainty increases. The goal is to use class relationships when making predictions in settings sensitive to errors.

The authors formalize hierarchical versions of risk and coverage and introduce curves for examining their relationship. They then develop prediction procedures, called inference rules, that determine how to use the hierarchy. An efficient algorithm provides a high-probability guarantee that a target accuracy constraint is met, giving the approach a stated statistical assurance.

The empirical study examines more than a thousand ImageNet classifiers. It finds that CLIP training, pretraining on ImageNet21k, and knowledge distillation improve hierarchical selective performance. These findings connect training choices to how effectively a model can trade prediction specificity for reliability. The framework makes the breadth of an answer an explicit part of evaluating and controlling classifier behavior.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical selective classification lets uncertain models give broader answers and includes an algorithm with a high-probability target-accuracy guarantee.

title: Hierarchical Selective Classification

abstract: LLMs are increasingly fine-tuned using RLHF datasets to align them with human preferences and values. However, very limited research has investigated which specific human values are operationalized through these datasets. In this paper, we introduce Value Imprint, a framework for auditing and classifying the human values embedded within RLHF datasets. To investigate the viability of this framework, we conducted three case study experiments by auditing the Anthropic/hh-rlhf, OpenAI WebGPT Comparisons, and Alpaca GPT-4-LLM datasets to examine the human values embedded within them. Our analysis involved a two-phase process. During the first phase, we developed a taxonomy of human values through an integrated review of prior works from philosophy, axiology, and ethics. Then, we applied this taxonomy to annotate 6,501 RLHF preferences. During the second phase, we employed the labels generated from the annotation as ground truth data for training a transformer-based machine learning model to audit and classify the three RLHF datasets. Through this approach, we discovered that information-utility values, including Wisdom/Knowledge and Information Seeking, were the most dominant human values within all three RLHF datasets. In contrast, prosocial and democratic values, including Well-being, Justice, and Human/Animal Rights, were the least represented human values. These findings have significant implications for developing language models that align with societal values and norms. We contribute our datasets to support further research in this area. https://github.com/hv-rsrch/valueimprint

paragraphs: Preference datasets help align language models with human judgments, but the values expressed by those judgments are often left unspecified. Value Imprint provides a framework for auditing which values appear in such data. The study examines Anthropic/hh-rlhf, OpenAI WebGPT Comparisons, and Alpaca GPT-4-LLM as three case studies.

The researchers first build a taxonomy of human values through a review of philosophy, axiology, and ethics. They use it to annotate 6,501 preferences. Those annotations then serve as ground-truth labels for training a Transformer-based classifier that audits and categorizes values across the three datasets. This connects an explicit conceptual definition of values with a scalable classification process.

Across all three datasets, values concerned with information utility, including knowledge and information seeking, are most prominent. Well-being, justice, and human or animal rights are among the least represented. These findings describe the balance of values within the audited datasets and raise questions about what preference-based alignment emphasizes. The released datasets also support further research into how societal values are represented in training preferences.
summary.tldr: Value Imprint audits preference datasets and finds information-focused values more prominent than prosocial and democratic values across three case studies.

title: Value Imprint: A Technique for Auditing the Human Values Embedded in RLHF Datasets

abstract: Many causal discovery methods typically rely on the assumption of independent noise, yet real-life situations often involve deterministic relationships. In these cases, observed variables are represented as deterministic functions of their parental variables without noise.When determinism is present, constraint-based methods encounter challenges due to the violation of the faithfulness assumption. In this paper, we find, supported by both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence, that score-based methods with exact search can naturally address the issues of deterministic relations under rather mild assumptions. Nonetheless, exact score-based methods can be computationally expensive. To enhance the efficiency and scalability, we develop a novel framework for causal discovery that can detect and handle deterministic relations, called Determinism-aware Greedy Equivalent Search (DGES). DGES comprises three phases: (1) identify minimal deterministic clusters (i.e., a minimal set of variables with deterministic relationships), (2) run modified Greedy Equivalent Search (GES) to obtain an initial graph, and (3) perform exact search exclusively on the deterministic cluster and its neighbors. The proposed DGES accommodates both linear and nonlinear causal relationships, as well as both continuous and discrete data types. Furthermore, we investigate the identifiability conditions of DGES. We conducted extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets to show the efficacy of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Causal discovery becomes difficult when some observed variables are exact functions of their causes, with no added noise. Such deterministic relationships can violate the faithfulness assumption used by constraint-based methods. This paper investigates how score-based approaches behave in that setting and finds, theoretically and empirically, that exact search can handle determinism under relatively mild assumptions.

Because exact search can be computationally expensive, the authors introduce Determinism-aware Greedy Equivalent Search, or DGES. It first identifies minimal groups of variables linked by deterministic relationships. A modified greedy search then builds an initial causal graph, after which exact search is restricted to the deterministic groups and their neighboring variables.

This structure concentrates the expensive search on the portions of the graph where determinism needs special handling. DGES supports linear and nonlinear relationships as well as continuous and discrete data. The paper also investigates conditions for identifiability and evaluates the method on simulated and real datasets. The reported experiments support the effectiveness of combining broad greedy search with localized exact search.
summary.tldr: DGES handles deterministic relationships in causal discovery by combining greedy graph search with exact search around deterministic variable clusters.

title: On Causal Discovery in the Presence of Deterministic Relations

abstract: A comprehensive benchmark is yet to be established in the Image Manipulation Detection \& Localization (IMDL) field. The absence of such a benchmark leads to insufficient and misleading model evaluations, severely undermining the development of this field. However, the scarcity of open-sourced baseline models and inconsistent training and evaluation protocols make conducting rigorous experiments and faithful comparisons among IMDL models challenging. To address these challenges, we introduce IMDL-BenCo, the first comprehensive IMDL benchmark and modular codebase. paragraphs: Image manipulation detection and localization concern identifying edited images and locating their altered regions. Comparing methods is difficult when baseline implementations are unavailable and training or evaluation procedures differ. IMDL-BenCo addresses these obstacles with a shared benchmark and modular codebase intended to make experiments more consistent and model comparisons more informative.

The framework divides the workflow into reusable components and revises model construction to support customization. It also provides two sets of standard training and evaluation protocols, 15 GPU-accelerated metrics, and three forms of robustness evaluation.

Using this infrastructure, the authors analyze model architecture, dataset characteristics, and evaluation standards. Standard components reduce the effort required to construct experiments, while explicit protocols and multiple evaluation measures provide a common basis for assessing different manipulation-detection and localization systems.
summary.tldr: IMDL-BenCo standardizes implementations and evaluation for image-manipulation detection and localization.

title: IMDL-BenCo: A Comprehensive Benchmark and Codebase for Image Manipulation Detection & Localization

abstract: Graph classification is a challenging problem owing to the difficulty in quantifying the similarity between graphs or representing graphs as vectors, though there have been a few methods using graph kernels or graph neural networks (GNNs). Graph kernels often suffer from computational costs and manual feature engineering, while GNNs commonly utilize global pooling operations, risking the loss of structural or semantic information. This work introduces Graph Reference Distribution Learning (GRDL), an efficient and accurate graph classification method. GRDL treats each graph's latent node embeddings given by GNN layers as a discrete distribution, enabling direct classification without global pooling, based on maximum mean discrepancy to adaptively learned reference distributions. To fully understand this new model (the existing theories do not apply) and guide its configuration (e.g., network architecture, references' sizes, number, and regularization) for practical use, we derive generalization error bounds for GRDL and verify them numerically. More importantly, our theoretical and numerical results both show that GRDL has a stronger generalization ability than GNNs with global pooling operations. Experiments on moderate-scale and large-scale graph datasets show the superiority of GRDL over the state-of-the-art, emphasizing its remarkable efficiency, being at least 10 times faster than leading competitors in both training and inference stages.

paragraphs: Graph Reference Distribution Learning, or GRDL, classifies graphs by retaining their node representations as a distribution. This addresses a concern with global pooling in graph neural networks: compressing all nodes into one graph vector can discard structural or semantic information. GRDL uses the collection of learned node embeddings directly for classification.

The method treats those embeddings as a discrete distribution and compares it with adaptively learned reference distributions using maximum mean discrepancy. The authors derive generalization-error bounds tailored to this architecture and check them numerically. The analysis also informs practical choices such as network structure, reference sizes and counts, and regularization.

Both theoretical and numerical results indicate stronger generalization than the global-pooling graph networks considered in the paper. Experiments on moderate-scale and large-scale datasets report superior performance over state-of-the-art competitors. GRDL is also reported to be at least ten times faster than leading competitors in training and inference, combining distribution-based graph comparison with substantial measured efficiency.
summary.tldr: GRDL classifies graphs through learned reference distributions, with theoretical generalization results and strong reported accuracy and speed.

title: Graph Classification via Reference Distribution Learning: Theory and Practice

abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) demonstrate remarkable problem-solving capabilities through extended Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning but often produce excessively verbose and redundant reasoning traces. This inefficiency incurs high inference costs and limits practical deployment. While existing fine-tuning methods aim to improve reasoning efficiency, assessing their efficiency gains remains challenging due to inconsistent evaluations. In this work, we introduce the ***reasoning efficiency frontiers***, empirical upper bounds derived from fine-tuning a base LRM (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B) across diverse approaches and training configurations. Based on these frontiers, we propose the ***Reasoning Efficiency Gap (REG)***, a unified metric quantifying deviations of any fine-tuned LRMs from these frontiers. Systematic evaluation on challenging mathematical benchmarks, AMC23, AIME24, and AIME25, reveals significant gaps in current methods: they either sacrifice accuracy for short length or use excessive tokens to achieve sub-optimal accuracies despite high overall accuracy. To reduce the efficiency gap, we propose ***REO-RL***, a Reinforcement Learning algorithm that optimizes reasoning efficiency by targeting a sparse set of token budgets. Leveraging numerical integration over strategically selected budgets, REO-RL approximates the full efficiency objective with low error using a small set of token budgets. Experiments show that, compared to vanilla RL with outcome reward, REO-RL reduces the reasoning efficiency gap by 74.5\% and 64.2\% in the 1.5B and 7B settings. The 7B LRM fine-tuned with REO-RL achieves reasoning conciseness surpassing frontier LRMs like Qwen3 and Claude Sonnet 3.7. Ablation studies confirm the efficacy of our token budget strategy and highlight REO-RL’s flexibility across design choices. This work establishes a systematic framework for evaluating and optimizing reasoning efficiency in LRMs. We will release the related code, data, and models to support future research on efficient reasoning in LRMs.

paragraphs: Shorter reasoning is useful only if it preserves enough problem-solving accuracy. This paper evaluates that tradeoff through reasoning efficiency frontiers, constructed empirically by fine-tuning base reasoning models under varied methods and configurations. These frontiers describe observed performance boundaries rather than a proven universal optimum.

The proposed Reasoning Efficiency Gap measures how far a fine-tuned model falls from those boundaries. Evaluations on AMC23, AIME24, and AIME25 reveal methods that either lose accuracy when shortening answers or consume excessive tokens for the accuracy they achieve. The metric gives these different shortcomings a shared evaluation framework.

To improve the tradeoff, REO-RL optimizes across a strategically selected, sparse set of token budgets. Numerical integration approximates the broader efficiency objective without training over every budget. Compared with outcome-reward reinforcement learning, experiments report gap reductions of 74.5% for the 1.5B setting and 64.2% for 7B. The 7B model also produces more concise reasoning than the named frontier models in the reported comparison. The contribution combines an empirical measurement standard with a training method targeting that standard.
summary.tldr: The paper measures accuracy–length tradeoffs against empirical frontiers and introduces REO-RL to reduce the resulting reasoning efficiency gap.

title: How Far Are We from Optimal Reasoning Efficiency?

abstract: Existing benchmarks for evaluating the security risks and capabilities (e.g., vulnerability detection) of code-generating large language models (LLMs) face several key limitations:(1) limited coverage of risk and capabilities;(2) reliance on static evaluation metrics such as LLM judgments or rule-based detection, which lack the precision of dynamic analysis; and(3) a trade-off between data quality and benchmark scale.To address these challenges, we introduce a general and scalable benchmark construction framework that begins with manually validated, high-quality seed examples and expands them via targeted mutations.Each mutated sample retains the seed’s security semantics while providing diverse, unseen instances. The resulting benchmark bundles every artifact required for dynamic evaluation, including prompts, vulnerable and patched code, test cases, and ground-truth proofs of concept, enabling rigorous measurement of insecure coding, vulnerability detection, and patch generation. Applying this framework to Python, C/C++, and Java, we build SECODEPLT, a dataset of more than 5.9k samples spanning 44 CWE-based risk categories and three security capabilities. Compared with state-of-the-art benchmarks, SECODEPLT offers broader coverage, higher data fidelity, and substantially greater scale. We use SECODEPLT to evaluate leading code-generation LLMs and agents, revealing their strengths and weaknesses in both generating secure code and identifying or fixing vulnerabilities.We provide our code in \url{https://github.com/ucsb-mlsec/SeCodePLT}, data in \url{https://huggingface.co/datasets/UCSB-SURFI/SeCodePLT}

paragraphs: Evaluating code-generating models for security requires checking both whether they introduce vulnerabilities and whether they can identify or repair them. The paper argues that existing benchmarks have limited coverage, rely too heavily on static judgments, or struggle to combine data quality with scale. SECODEPLT addresses these issues through a reusable benchmark-construction framework.

The framework starts with manually validated examples and expands them using targeted mutations that preserve their security meaning. Each resulting sample includes the artifacts needed for dynamic evaluation: prompts, vulnerable and patched code, tests, and ground-truth proofs of concept. These materials enable evaluation through executable evidence, giving a more concrete basis for assessing security behavior.

The resulting dataset contains more than 5,900 samples across Python, C/C++, and Java, covering 44 CWE-based risk categories and three security capabilities. The authors report broader coverage, higher fidelity, and greater scale than compared benchmarks. Their evaluations reveal strengths and weaknesses of leading coding models and agents in secure generation, vulnerability detection, and patching.
summary.tldr: SECODEPLT scales validated security examples into a benchmark with executable artifacts for testing insecure coding, vulnerability detection, and patch generation.

title: SECODEPLT: A Unified Benchmark for Evaluating the Security Risks and Capabilities of Code GenAI

abstract: Designing models that can learn to reason in a systematic way is an important and long-standing challenge. In recent years, a wide range of solutions have been proposed for the specific case of systematic relational reasoning, including Neuro-Symbolic approaches, variants of the Transformer architecture, and specialized Graph Neural Networks. However, existing benchmarks for systematic relational reasoning focus on an overly simplified setting, based on the assumption that reasoning can be reduced to composing relational paths. In fact, this assumption is hard-baked into the architecture of several recent models, leading to approaches that can perform well on existing benchmarks but are difficult to generalize to other settings. To support further progress in the field of systematic relational reasoning with neural networks, we introduce a new benchmark that adds several levels of difficulty, requiring models to go beyond path-based reasoning.

paragraphs: This paper questions whether existing relational-reasoning benchmarks adequately test systematic reasoning. Many assume that solving a problem amounts to composing a path of relations. That simplifies the task and can favor models whose architectures already embody the same assumption, making strong benchmark performance difficult to interpret more broadly.

The concern applies across a field that includes neuro-symbolic methods, Transformer variants, and specialized graph neural networks. If both the benchmark and a model are organized around relational paths, success shows competence within that shared structure. It does not by itself establish that the approach transfers readily to reasoning settings requiring other forms of relational combination.

The authors introduce a benchmark with several difficulty levels that require models to go beyond path-based reasoning. Its contribution is to expand what evaluation asks a system to do, exposing a wider reasoning challenge than the existing simplified setting. This gives researchers a way to investigate whether proposed architectures support more general relational reasoning, rather than judging progress solely on tasks aligned with a restrictive architectural assumption.
summary.tldr: A new relational-reasoning benchmark adds difficulty levels that require reasoning beyond composing paths of relations.

title: When No Paths Lead to Rome: Benchmarking Systematic Neural Relational Reasoning

abstract: Recent advancements in large language models have demonstrated how chain-of-thought (CoT) and reinforcement learning (RL) can improve performance. However, applying such reasoning strategies to the visual generation domain remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we present **T2I-R1**, a novel reasoning-enhanced text-to-image generation model, powered by RL with a bi-level CoT reasoning process. Specifically, we identify two levels of CoT that can be utilized to enhance different stages of generation: (1) the semantic-level CoT for high-level planning of the prompt and (2) the token-level CoT for low-level pixel processing during patch-by-patch generation. To better coordinate these two levels of CoT, we introduce **BiCoT-GRPO** with an ensemble of generation rewards, which seamlessly optimizes both generated CoTs within the same training step. By applying our reasoning strategies to the baseline model, Janus-Pro, we achieve superior performance with 13% improvement on T2I-CompBench and 19% improvement on the WISE benchmark, even surpassing the state-of-the-art model FLUX.1. All the training code is in the supplementary material and will be made public.

paragraphs: T2I-R1 explores how reasoning and reinforcement learning can improve text-to-image generation. It divides the generation process into two reasoning levels: planning the prompt’s meaning at a high level and handling visual detail during patch-by-patch generation. This division connects decisions about what the image should depict with the lower-level process that produces it.

The model uses semantic-level chain-of-thought for planning and token-level chain-of-thought for pixel processing. The contribution is both a reasoning-enhanced generator and a reinforcement learning procedure for coordinating its two reasoning stages.
summary.tldr: T2I-R1 jointly reinforces semantic planning and token-level visual reasoning to improve text-to-image generation.

title: T2I-R1: Reinforcing Image Generation with Collaborative Semantic-level and Token-level CoT

abstract: We introduce a class of neural networks named PLEIADES (PoLynomial Expansion In Adaptive Distributed Event-based Systems), which contains temporal convolution kernels generated from orthogonal polynomial basis functions. We focus on interfacing these networks with event-based data to perform online spatiotemporal classification and detection with low latency. By virtue of using structured temporal kernels and event-based data, we have the freedom to vary the sample rate of the data along with the discretization step-size of the network without additional finetuning. We experimented with three event-based benchmarks and obtained state-of-the-art results on all three by large margins with significantly smaller memory and compute costs. We achieved: 1) 99.59% accuracy with 192K parameters on the DVS128 hand gesture recognition dataset and 100\% with a small additional output filter; 2) 99.58% test accuracy with 277K parameters on the AIS 2024 eye tracking challenge; and 3) 0.556 mAP with 576k parameters on the PROPHESEE 1 Megapixel Automotive Detection Dataset.

This matters when the rate at which data is processed needs to vary: the model’s temporal construction supports that adjustment without requiring another round of adaptation.

summary.tldr: PLEIADES uses polynomial temporal kernels for efficient event-based perception that tolerates sampling-rate changes without fine-tuning.

title: PLEIADES: Building Temporal Kernels with Orthogonal Polynomials

abstract: Class Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to continuously learn new categories while retaining the knowledge of old ones. Pre-trained models (PTMs) show promising capabilities in CIL. However, existing approaches that apply lightweight fine-tuning to backbones still induce parameter drift, thereby compromising the generalization capability of pre-trained models. Parameter drift can be conceptualized as a form of noise that obscures critical patterns learned for previous tasks. However, recent researches have shown that noise is not always harmful. For example, the large number of visual patterns learned from pre-training can be easily abused by a single task, and introducing appropriate noise can suppress some low-correlation features, thus leaving a margin for future tasks. To this end, we propose learning beneficial noise for CIL guided by information theory and propose Mixture of Noise (MiN), aiming to mitigate the degradation of backbone generalization from adapting new tasks. Specifically, task-specific noise is learned from high-dimension features of new tasks. Then, a set of weights is adjusted dynamically for optimal mixture of different task noise. Finally, MiN embeds the beneficial noise into the intermediate features to mask the response of inefficient patterns. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that MiN achieves state-of-the-art performance in most incremental settings, with particularly outstanding results in 50-steps incremental settings. This shows the significant potential for beneficial noise in continual learning. Code is available at https://github.com/ASCIIJK/MiN-NeurIPS2025.

paragraphs: Learning new classes can shift a pretrained model’s parameters and weaken knowledge useful for earlier tasks. This paper views that drift as harmful noise, while observing that carefully chosen noise can also help. Suppressing features weakly related to the current task may leave more room for future learning.

Mixture of Noise, or MiN, learns task-specific noise from high-dimensional features, guided by information theory. It then dynamically adjusts weights that combine noise learned for different tasks. The resulting mixture is inserted into intermediate features to mask responses from inefficient patterns. The aim is to reduce the loss of generalization that can accompany adaptation to new classes.

Experiments on six benchmark datasets report state-of-the-art performance in most incremental settings, with especially strong results in 50-step settings. These findings support treating noise as something that can be learned and combined for a useful purpose. The contribution is a mechanism for shaping feature use over successive tasks, using beneficial noise to help preserve the value of pretraining.
summary.tldr: MiN learns and mixes task-specific noise to suppress inefficient feature responses and improve class-incremental learning.

title: Mixture of Noise for Pre-Trained Model-Based Class-Incremental Learning

abstract: In cloud-scale systems, failures are the norm. A distributed computing cluster exhibits hundreds of machine failures and thousands of disk failures; software bugs and misconfigurations are reported to be more frequent. The demand for autonomous, AI-driven reliability engineering continues to grow, as existing human-in-the-loop practices can hardly keep up with the scale of modern clouds. This paper presents STRATUS, an LLM-based multi-agent system for realizing autonomous Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) of cloud services. STRATUS consists of multiple specialized agents (e.g., for failure detection, diagnosis, mitigation), organized in a state machine to assist system-level safety reasoning and enforcement. We formalize a key safety specification of agentic SRE systems like STRATUS, termed Transactional No-Regression (TNR), which enables safe exploration and iteration. We show that TNR can effectively improve autonomous failure mitigation. STRATUS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art SRE agents in terms of success rate of failure mitigation problems in AIOpsLab and ITBench (two SRE benchmark suites), by at least 1.5 times across various models. STRATUS shows a promising path toward practical deployment of agentic systems for cloud reliability.

summary.tldr: STRATUS coordinates specialized reliability agents with a formal safety specification, improving failure-mitigation success on two SRE benchmark suites.

title: STRATUS: A Multi-agent System for Autonomous Reliability Engineering of Modern Clouds

abstract: Differential privacy (DP) limits the impact of individual training data samples by bounding their gradient norms through clipping. Conventional clipping operations assign unequal scaling factors to sample gradients with different norms, leading to a direction mismatch between the true batch gradient and the aggregation of the clipped gradients. Applying a smaller but identical scaling factor to all sample gradients alleviates this direction mismatch; however, it intensifies the magnitude mismatch by excessively reducing the aggregation norm. This work proposes a novel clipping method, termed adaptive sigmoid (AdaSig), which uses a sigmoid function with an adjustable saturation slope to clip the sample gradients. The slope is adaptively adjusted during the training process to balance the trade-off between direction mismatch and magnitude mismatch, as the statistics of sample gradients evolve over the training iterations. Despite AdaSig’s adaptive nature, our convergence analysis demonstrates that differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) with AdaSig clipping retains the best-known convergence rate under non-convex loss functions. Evaluating AdaSig on sentence and image classification tasks across different datasets shows that it consistently improves learning performance compared with established clipping methods.
originalAbstract: Differential privacy (DP) limits the impact of individual training data samples by bounding their gradient norms through clipping. Conventional clipping operations assign unequal scaling factors to sample gradients with different norms, leading to a direction mismatch between the true batch gradient and the aggregation of the clipped gradients. Applying a smaller but identical scaling factor to all sample gradients alleviates this direction mismatch; however, it intensifies the magnitude mismatch by excessively reducing the aggregation norm. This work proposes a novel clipping method, termed adaptive sigmoid (AdaSig), which uses a sigmoid function with an adjustable saturation slope to clip the sample gradients. The slope is adaptively adjusted during the training process to balance the trade-off between direction mismatch and magnitude mismatch, as the statistics of sample gradients evolve over the training iterations. Despite AdaSig’s adaptive nature, our convergence analysis demonstrates that differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) with AdaSig clipping retains the best-known convergence rate under non-convex loss functions. Evaluating AdaSig on sentence and image classification tasks across different datasets shows that it consistently improves learning performance compared with established clipping methods.

paragraphs: Differentially private training bounds individual examples’ contributions by clipping their gradients, the directions used to update a model. Conventional clipping shrinks gradients by different amounts depending on their size. When these gradients are combined, that unequal shrinking can change the direction of the overall update relative to the original batch gradient.

Shrinking every gradient by the same small factor helps preserve direction, but it can make the combined update excessively weak. AdaSig addresses this direction–magnitude trade-off using a sigmoid function whose saturation slope can change during training. Adjusting the slope lets the clipping rule respond as the distribution of sample gradients evolves, rather than using the same balance throughout learning.

The authors show that DP-SGD with this adaptive clipping rule retains the best-known convergence rate for non-convex losses. On the sentence and image classification datasets evaluated, AdaSig consistently improves learning performance over established clipping methods. The contribution therefore combines an adaptive way to manage clipping distortion with a convergence result and empirical evidence of better classification performance.
summary.tldr: AdaSig adaptively balances changes to gradient direction and magnitude during private training, improving tested classification results while retaining the best-known convergence rate.

title: Adaptive Sigmoid Clipping for Balancing the Direction–Magnitude Mismatch Trade-off in Differentially Private Learning

abstract: Mixture-of-experts networks (MoEs) have demonstrated remarkable efficiency in modern deep learning. Despite their empirical success, the theoretical foundations underlying their ability to model complex tasks remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of the expressive power of MoEs in modeling complex tasks with two common structural priors: low-dimensionality and sparsity. For shallow MoEs, we prove that they can efficiently approximate functions supported on low-dimensional manifolds, overcoming the curse of dimensionality. For deep MoEs, we show that $\mathcal{O}(L)$-layer MoEs with $E$ experts per layer can approximate piecewise functions comprising $E^L$ pieces with compositional sparsity, i.e., they can exhibit an exponential number of structured tasks. Our analysis reveals the roles of critical architectural components and hyperparameters in MoEs, including the gating mechanism, expert networks, the number of experts, and the number of layers, and offers natural suggestions for MoE variants.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts networks divide computation among expert networks through a gating mechanism. Their empirical efficiency is well established, but this paper asks what kinds of complex functions they can represent efficiently. The analysis focuses on two structural properties: low-dimensionality and sparsity. These properties are assumptions that make the approximation results possible.

For shallow networks, the authors prove efficient approximation of functions supported on low-dimensional manifolds. Although the surrounding input space may have many dimensions, the relevant function is confined to a lower-dimensional structure. Under this setting, the result shows how mixture-of-experts models can overcome the curse of dimensionality.

For deep networks, the authors show that a number of layers proportional to L, with E experts per layer, can approximate piecewise functions containing E to the power L pieces when compositional sparsity holds. This establishes an exponential number of structured pieces under the stated structure, rather than arbitrary exponential capability. The analysis also explains the roles of gates, expert networks, expert counts, and depth, providing theoretical guidance for architectural variants.
summary.tldr: The paper proves efficient mixture-of-experts approximation results for functions with low-dimensional or compositionally sparse structure.

title: On the Expressive Power of Mixture-of-Experts for Structured Complex Tasks

abstract: Existing AutoML systems have advanced the automation of machine learning (ML); however, they still require substantial manual configuration and expert input, particularly when handling multimodal data. We introduce MLZero, a novel multi-agent framework powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) that enables end-to-end ML automation across diverse data modalities with minimal human intervention. A cognitive perception module is first employed, transforming raw multimodal inputs into perceptual context that effectively guides the subsequent workflow. To address key limitations of LLMs, such as hallucinated code generation and outdated API knowledge, we enhance the iterative code generation process with semantic and episodic memory. MLZero demonstrates superior performance on MLE-Bench Lite, outperforming all competitors in both success rate and solution quality, securing six gold medals. Furthermore, when evaluated on our Multimodal AutoML Agent Benchmark, which includes 25 more challenging tasks spanning diverse data modalities, MLZero outperforms the competing methods by a large margin with a success rate of 0.92 (+263.6\%) and an average rank of 2.28. Our approach maintains its robust effectiveness even with a compact 8B LLM, outperforming full-size systems from existing solutions.

paragraphs: Automated machine learning systems can still require substantial expert configuration, especially when inputs span different modalities. The system then generates and revises code iteratively. Semantic and episodic memory support this process, targeting problems such as fabricated code and outdated knowledge of software interfaces. The architecture therefore combines understanding the input data with memory-assisted code generation, addressing two obstacles to taking an automated workflow from raw data through an ML solution.

On the authors' 25-task Multimodal AutoML Agent Benchmark, it reports a success rate of 0.92 and an average rank of 2.28. The authors also find that a version using an 8B language model outperforms full-size competing systems. These results support the effectiveness of the overall workflow across the tested modalities and tasks.
summary.tldr: MLZero combines multimodal perception, multiple language-model agents, and memory-assisted coding to automate machine learning with strong benchmark results.

title: MLZero: A Multi-Agent System for End-to-end Machine Learning Automation

abstract: Learning from self-sampled data and sparse environmental feedback remains a fundamental challenge in training self-evolving agents. Temporal credit assignment mitigates this issue by transforming sparse feedback into dense supervision signals. However, previous approaches typically depend on domain-specific value functions for credit assignment, which suffer from poor sample efficiency and limited generalization. In this work, we propose to leverage pre-trained knowledge from large language models (LLMs) to transform sparse rewards into dense training signals (i.e., the advantage function) through retrospective in-context learning (RICL). We further propose an online learning framework, RICOL, which iteratively refines the policy based on the credit assignment results from RICL. We empirically demonstrate that RICL can accurately estimate the advantage function with limited samples and effectively identify critical states for temporal credit assignment. Extended evaluation on the BabyAI benchmark shows that RICOL significantly improves sample efficiency compared to traditional online RL algorithms while achieving performance comparable to imitation learning from expert demonstartions. Our findings highlight the potential of leveraging LLMs for temporal credit assignment, paving the way for more sample-efficient and generalizable RL paradigms.

paragraphs: An agent receiving only occasional rewards must determine which earlier decisions contributed to an outcome. This temporal credit-assignment problem makes learning from the agent's own experience difficult. Traditional approaches often rely on domain-specific value functions, which the paper identifies as having limited sample efficiency and generalization.

Retrospective in-context learning, or RICL, uses pretrained language-model knowledge to convert sparse rewards into denser advantage estimates. These estimates provide training signals about the usefulness of decisions along an experience. The accompanying RICOL framework repeatedly uses RICL's credit assignments to refine the policy during online learning.

Experiments show that RICL can estimate advantages accurately from limited samples and identify states that matter for assigning credit. On BabyAI, RICOL significantly improves sample efficiency over traditional online reinforcement-learning algorithms while reaching performance comparable to imitation learning from expert demonstrations. The findings support pretrained language models as a useful source of credit-assignment knowledge, with broader generalizability presented as a promising direction rather than an established result across domains.
summary.tldr: RICL uses language-model knowledge to turn sparse rewards into advantage estimates, improving online learning sample efficiency in BabyAI through RICOL.

title: Retrospective In-Context Learning for Temporal Credit Assignment with Large Language Models

abstract: Thompson sampling (TS) is a powerful and widely used strategy for sequential decision-making, with applications ranging from Bayesian optimization to reinforcement learning (RL). Despite its success, the theoretical foundations of TS remain limited, particularly in settings with complex temporal structure such as RL. We address this gap by establishing no-regret guarantees for TS using models with Gaussian marginal distributions. Specifically, we consider TS in episodic RL with joint Gaussian process (GP) priors over rewards and transitions. We prove a regret bound of $\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(\sqrt{KH\Gamma(KH)})$ over $K$ episodes of horizon $H$, where $\Gamma(\cdot)$ captures the complexity of the GP model. Our analysis addresses several challenges, including the non-Gaussian nature of value functions and the recursive structure of Bellman updates, and extends classical tools such as the elliptical potential lemma to multi-output settings. This work advances the understanding of TS in RL and highlights how structural assumptions and model uncertainty shape its performance in finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling is widely used for sequential decisions, but reinforcement learning creates additional theoretical difficulties because actions affect later outcomes. This paper establishes no-regret guarantees for an episodic setting with joint Gaussian process priors over rewards and transitions. These structural assumptions define the model class addressed by the analysis.

The regret bound is approximately the square root of K times H times Γ(KH), apart from logarithmic factors. Here K counts episodes, H is the episode horizon, and Γ measures the Gaussian process model’s complexity. The expression makes model complexity part of the guarantee, alongside the amount and temporal organization of experience.

The proof handles a key complication: Gaussian model components do not make the resulting value functions Gaussian. It also addresses recursive Bellman updates and extends the elliptical potential lemma to multiple outputs. The contribution is theoretical support for Thompson sampling in this structured reinforcement-learning setting, showing how uncertainty and model assumptions enter its performance guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper proves a complexity-dependent no-regret guarantee for episodic Thompson sampling with joint Gaussian process reward and transition priors.

title: No-Regret Thompson Sampling for Finite-Horizon Markov Decision Processes with Gaussian Processes

abstract: Federated Multi-Task Learning (FL-MTL) enables clients with heterogeneous data to collaboratively train models capable of handling multiple downstream tasks. However, FL-MTL faces key challenges, including statistical heterogeneity, task interference, and the need to balance local learning with global knowledge sharing. Traditional methods like FedAvg struggle in such settings due to the lack of explicit mechanisms to address these issues. In this paper, we propose FedRAM, a three-step framework that progressively updates two scalar hyperparameters: the task importance weight and the client aggregation coefficient. FedRAM introduces a reference-proxy-agent strategy, where the proxy model serves as an intermediate between the local reference model and the global agent model. This design reduces the need for repeated local training while preserving local performance. Extensive experiments on six real-world FL-MTL benchmarks show that FedRAM improves performance by at least 3$\%$ over the most baseline on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks, while reducing computational cost by 15$\times$. These results make FedRAM a robust and practical solution for large-scale FL-MTL applications. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/wwffvv/FedRAM}.

paragraphs: Federated multi-task learning lets clients with different data collaborate on models that serve several tasks. The challenge is balancing local needs with shared knowledge: clients may have different statistical patterns, and improving one task may interfere with another. FedRAM introduces explicit controls for both task importance and the way client contributions are combined.

Its three-step framework progressively updates two scalar hyperparameters: a task importance weight and a client aggregation coefficient. A reference-proxy-agent design connects a local reference model to a global agent model through an intermediate proxy. Its central idea is to coordinate task weighting and client aggregation while using the proxy to make that coordination less expensive.
summary.tldr: FedRAM coordinates task weights and client aggregation through a proxy model, improving federated multi-task results while reducing computation.

title: FedRAM: Federated Reweighting and Aggregation for Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Semi-Unbalanced Optimal Transport (SemiUOT) shows great promise in matching two probability measures by relaxing one of the marginal constraints. Previous solvers often incorporate an entropy regularization term, which can result in inaccurate matching solutions. To address this issue, we focus on determining the marginal probability distribution of SemiUOT with KL divergence using the proposed Equivalent Transformation Mechanism (ETM) approach. Furthermore, we extend the ETM-based method into exploiting the marginal probability distribution of Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) with KL divergence for validating its generalization. Once the marginal probabilities of UOT/SemiUOT are determined, they can be transformed into a classical Optimal Transport (OT) problem. Moreover, we propose a KKT-Multiplier regularization term combined with Multiplier Regularized Optimal Transport (MROT) to achieve more accurate matching results. We conduct several numerical experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods in addressing UOT/SemiUOT problems.

Furthermore, we extend the ETM-based method into exploiting the marginal probability distribution of Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) with KL divergence for validating its generalization. Once the marginal probabilities of UOT/SemiUOT are determined, they can be transformed into a classical Optimal Transport (OT) problem. paragraphs: Optimal transport finds a matching between distributions under constraints on their marginal probabilities. Semi-unbalanced transport relaxes one of those constraints, making matching more flexible. The paper focuses on formulations using KL divergence and addresses a concern with previous solvers: adding entropy regularization can lead to inaccurate matching solutions.

The proposed Equivalent Transformation Mechanism first determines the marginal probability distribution for the semi-unbalanced problem. The authors extend this approach to unbalanced optimal transport to examine its generality. Once the appropriate marginals are known, either problem can be transformed into a classical optimal transport problem, separating marginal determination from the subsequent matching step.

The paper also introduces a KKT-multiplier regularization term in combination with Multiplier Regularized Optimal Transport to improve matching accuracy. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods on the considered unbalanced and semi-unbalanced problems. The main contribution is a different computational route through these formulations: identify their marginals, recover a classical transport problem, and use the proposed regularization to obtain more accurate matches.
summary.tldr: The paper transforms KL-based unbalanced transport problems into classical transport after determining their marginals, then improves matching with multiplier regularization.

title: Solving Discrete (Semi) Unbalanced Optimal Transport with Equivalent Transformation Mechanism and KKT-Multiplier Regularization

abstract: Periodicity, as one of the most important basic characteristics, lays the foundation for facilitating structured knowledge acquisition and systematic cognitive processes within human learning paradigms. However, the potential flaws of periodicity modeling in Transformer affect the learning efficiency and establishment of underlying principles from data for large language models (LLMs) built upon it. In this paper, we demonstrate that integrating effective periodicity modeling can improve the learning efficiency and performance of LLMs. We introduce FANformer, which adapts Fourier Analysis Network (FAN) into attention mechanism to achieve efficient periodicity modeling, by modifying the feature projection process of attention mechanism. Extensive experimental results on language modeling show that FANformer consistently outperforms Transformer when scaling up model size and training tokens, underscoring its superior learning efficiency. Our pretrained FANformer-1B exhibits marked improvements on downstream tasks compared to open-source LLMs with similar model parameters or training tokens. Moreover, we reveal that FANformer exhibits superior ability to learn and apply rules for reasoning compared to Transformer. The results position FANformer as an effective and promising architecture for advancing LLMs.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether explicitly modeling periodic structure can improve how language models learn. Its starting point is that limitations in a Transformer’s handling of periodicity may hinder learning efficiency and the extraction of underlying rules. The proposed architecture, FANformer, brings Fourier Analysis Network components into the attention mechanism to address this issue.

The change occurs in attention’s feature-projection process, giving periodicity modeling a role within the architecture itself. Language-modeling experiments compare FANformer with Transformers as both model size and training-token counts increase. The authors report consistent improvements across these scaling experiments, supporting their claim that this architectural change can make learning more efficient.

The pretrained FANformer-1B also improves downstream performance over open-source models with similar parameter counts or training-token budgets. Further experiments report stronger ability to learn and apply rules for reasoning than a Transformer. These findings support periodicity modeling as a promising architectural direction; they establish empirical benefits for the proposed design rather than an identity between periodicity and all forms of reasoning.
summary.tldr: FANformer adds Fourier-based periodicity modeling to attention and reports improved language learning efficiency, downstream performance, and rule-based reasoning.

title: Reasoning is Periodicity? Improving Large Language Models Through Effective Periodicity Modeling

abstract: Recent works show that contrastive learning based on memory banks is an effective framework for unsupervised person Re-IDentification (ReID). In existing methods, memory banks are typically initialized with cluster centroids and rewritten with positive samples via the momentum mechanism along with the model training. However, this mechanism solely focuses on the intra-class compactness by pulling memory banks close to positive samples, neglecting the inter-class separability among different memory banks. Rewriting memory banks with partial constraint limits their discrimination capacities, and hence hinders learning discriminative features based on those memory banks. In this paper, we claim that memory banks should be rewritten with both intra-class and inter-class constraints, and therefore propose a unified memory bank rewriting mechanism, Bidirectionally Memory bank reWriting (BMW), to chase enhanced discrimination capacity. Specifically, BMW formulates the memory bank rewriting as the gradient descent update with two objectives, i.e., reducing intra-class diversity and enhancing inter-class separability. To effectively enhance the separability of memory banks with limited number of rewriting steps, we further design a novel objective formulation for the inter-class constraint, which is more effective for one step update. BMW enhances both representation and discrimination capacities of memory banks, thus leads to an effective ReID feature optimization. BMW is simple yet effective and can serve as a new paradigm for person ReID methods based on memory banks. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our BMW method in unsupervised ReID model training. Specially, BMW even outperforms previous methods that use stronger backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/liu-xb/BMW.

paragraphs: Unsupervised person re-identification learns to match images of people without identity labels. Memory-bank methods support this learning by maintaining representations initialized from clusters. Existing updates move these stored representations toward positive examples, encouraging members of a cluster to stay close together. The paper argues that this leaves a second requirement insufficiently addressed: different clusters also need distinct representations.

BMW updates the memory bank using two explicit objectives. One reduces variation within a class; the other increases separation between classes. The authors formulate these updates as gradient descent and design the separation objective to work effectively even when only a limited number of rewriting steps are available, particularly a single update.

The intended benefit is a better set of stored reference representations for training discriminative image features. Experiments on standard benchmarks support the approach's effectiveness in unsupervised re-identification, including results exceeding previous methods with stronger backbones. The contribution therefore concerns how the training memory is maintained, showing that its update rule can materially affect the features learned from it.
summary.tldr: BMW improves unsupervised person re-identification by updating memory banks to make each class more compact and different classes more distinct.

title: BMW: Bidirectionally Memory bank reWriting for Unsupervised Person Re-Identification

abstract: This paper presents a speech recognition system that directly transcribes audio data with text, without requiring an intermediate phonetic representation. The system is based on a combination of the deep bidirectional LSTM recurrent neural network architecture and the Connectionist Temporal Classification objective function. A modification to the objective function is introduced that trains the network to minimise the expectation of an arbitrary transcription loss function. This allows a direct optimisation of the word error rate, even in the absence of a lexicon or language model. The system achieves a word error rate of 27.3% on the Wall Street Journal corpus with no prior linguistic information, 21.9% with only a lexicon of allowed words, and 8.2% with a trigram language model. Combining the network with a baseline system further reduces the error rate to 6.7%.
