paragraphs: This paper presents a speech recognition system that maps audio directly to text without requiring an intermediate phonetic representation. It combines a deep bidirectional LSTM recurrent network with the Connectionist Temporal Classification objective. The approach places direct transcription at the center of the recognition system.

The authors modify the training objective to minimize the expected value of an arbitrary transcription loss. This allows training to target word error rate directly, including when no lexicon or language model is available. The change matters because it connects optimization to errors in the resulting transcription, rather than relying only on the original objective.

On the Wall Street Journal corpus, the system achieves 27.3% word error rate without prior linguistic information. Adding only a lexicon gives 21.9%, while using a trigram language model gives 8.2%. Combining the network with a baseline system reduces the rate further to 6.7%. These results demonstrate direct audio-to-text recognition while also showing the substantial benefits of linguistic resources and system combination in the reported setting.
summary.tldr: A deep bidirectional LSTM transcribes audio directly into text, with modified training that can optimize word error rate without a lexicon or language model.

title: Towards End-To-End Speech Recognition with Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: We introduce Mean-for-Mode estimation, a variant of an uncollapsed Gibbs sampler that we use to train LDA on a GPU. The algorithm combines benefits of both uncollapsed and collapsed Gibbs samplers. Like a collapsed Gibbs sampler — and unlike an uncollapsed Gibbs sampler — it has good statistical performance, and can use sampling complexity reduction techniques such as sparsity. Meanwhile, like an uncollapsed Gibbs sampler — and unlike a collapsed Gibbs sampler — it is embarrassingly parallel, and can use approximate counters.
originalAbstract: We introduce Mean-for-Mode estimation, a variant of an uncollapsed Gibbs sampler that we use to train LDA on a GPU. The algorithm combines benefits of both uncollapsed and collapsed Gibbs samplers. Like a collapsed Gibbs sampler — and unlike an uncollapsed Gibbs sampler — it has good statistical performance, and can use sampling complexity reduction techniques such as sparsity. Meanwhile, like an uncollapsed Gibbs sampler — and unlike a collapsed Gibbs sampler — it is embarrassingly parallel, and can use approximate counters.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Mean-for-Mode estimation to train latent Dirichlet allocation, or LDA, on a GPU. Its starting point is an uncollapsed Gibbs sampler. The motivation is to combine useful statistical behavior with a computation pattern that can take advantage of GPU parallelism, rather than treating the choice of sampler and hardware as separate concerns.

The proposed variant is described as sharing favorable properties with collapsed Gibbs sampling. In particular, it has good statistical performance and can use techniques such as sparsity to reduce sampling complexity. These properties address the amount and usefulness of the sampling work needed during training, both of which matter when scaling inference.

At the same time, Mean-for-Mode retains the highly parallel structure associated with uncollapsed Gibbs sampling and can use approximate counters. The stated contribution is this combination of properties that ordinarily favor different sampler designs. It brings statistical quality and sampling-cost reductions together with opportunities for extensive parallel execution, providing the basis for the paper's GPU training method.
summary.tldr: Mean-for-Mode estimation combines favorable sampling properties with extensive parallelism to train LDA on a GPU.

title: Efficient Training of LDA on a GPU by Mean-for-Mode Estimation

abstract: The choice of the approximate posterior distribution is one of the core problems in variational inference. Most applications of variational inference employ simple families of posterior approximations in order to allow for efficient inference, focusing on mean-field or other simple structured approximations. This restriction has a significant impact on the quality of inferences made using variational methods. We introduce a new approach for specifying flexible, arbitrarily complex and scalable approximate posterior distributions. Our approximations are distributions constructed through a normalizing flow, whereby a simple initial density is transformed into a more complex one by applying a sequence of invertible transformations until a desired level of complexity is attained. We use this view of normalizing flows to develop categories of finite and infinitesimal flows and provide a unified view of approaches for constructing rich posterior approximations. We demonstrate that the theoretical advantages of having posteriors that better match the true posterior, combined with the scalability of amortized variational approaches, provides a clear improvement in performance and applicability of variational inference.

paragraphs: Variational inference depends on choosing a family of distributions that can approximate a posterior. Simple families make inference efficient, but their restricted shapes can reduce the quality of the result. This paper introduces normalizing flows as a way to construct flexible approximate posteriors while retaining scalability.

A normalizing flow begins with a simple density and applies a sequence of invertible transformations. Each transformation changes the distribution, allowing the sequence to produce increasingly complex approximations. This makes the approximation family adjustable through the transformation process instead of restricting it from the outset to a simple fixed form.

The authors develop finite and infinitesimal flow categories and use them to give a unified view of approaches for constructing rich posterior approximations. They demonstrate improvements in the performance and applicability of variational inference by combining better posterior matching with scalable amortized inference. The central contribution is a construction that connects expressive distributions with practical inference, addressing the tradeoff between approximation flexibility and computational tractability.
summary.tldr: Normalizing flows build flexible approximate posteriors through invertible transformations, improving the expressiveness and applicability of scalable variational inference.

title: Variational Inference with Normalizing Flows

abstract: Anonymous messaging platforms like Whisper and Yik Yak allow users to spread messages over a network (e.g., a social network) without revealing message authorship to other users. The spread of messages on these platforms can be modeled by a diffusion process over a graph. Recent advances in network analysis have revealed that such diffusion processes are vulnerable to author deanonymization by adversaries with access to metadata, such as timing information. In this work, we ask the fundamental question of how to propagate anonymous messages over a graph to make it difficult for adversaries to infer the source. In particular, we study the performance of a message propagation protocol called adaptive diffusion introduced in (Fanti et al., 2015). We prove that when the adversary has access to metadata at a fraction of corrupted graph nodes, adaptive diffusion achieves asymptotically optimal source-hiding and significantly outperforms standard diffusion. We further demonstrate empirically that adaptive diffusion hides the source effectively on real social networks.

paragraphs: Removing an author’s name from a message does not necessarily hide where the message originated. As a message spreads through a network, timing and other metadata can expose clues about its source. This paper studies how the propagation process itself can make source inference difficult for an adversary observing part of the network.

The authors analyze adaptive diffusion, a message propagation protocol, under an adversary model in which a fraction of graph nodes is corrupted and exposes metadata. The graph represents the routes through which messages spread. The central question is whether a protocol can preserve anonymity even when an observer has information about that spread.

Under the studied observation setting, the authors prove asymptotically optimal source hiding and a substantial advantage over standard diffusion. They also report experiments showing effective source concealment on real social networks. The theoretical claim is tied to the specified adversary model and asymptotic setting, while the experiments provide evidence on network data. Together, the results make propagation design part of the anonymity mechanism.
summary.tldr: Adaptive diffusion achieves asymptotically optimal source hiding under the studied metadata adversary model and performs effectively on real social networks.

title: Metadata-conscious anonymous messaging

abstract: In the Object Recognition task, there exists a dichotomy between the categorization of objects and estimating object pose, where the former necessitates a view-invariant representation, while the latter requires a representation capable of capturing pose information over different categories of objects. With the rise of deep architectures, the prime focus has been on object category recognition. Deep learning methods have achieved wide success in this task. In contrast, object pose estimation using these approaches has received relatively less attention. In this work, we study how Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) architectures can be adapted to the task of simultaneous object recognition and pose estimation. We investigate and analyze the layers of various CNN models and extensively compare between them with the goal of discovering how the layers of distributed representations within CNNs represent object pose information and how this contradicts with object category representations. We extensively experiment on two recent large and challenging multi-view datasets and we achieve better than the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object and estimating its pose place different demands on an image representation. Category recognition should remain stable as the viewpoint changes, while pose estimation needs to preserve information about those changes. This paper studies how convolutional neural networks can support both tasks together, making that tension central to the analysis.

The authors adapt and compare several CNN architectures for simultaneous categorization and pose estimation. They examine the representations within different layers to understand how pose information is retained and how it interacts with category information. This makes the investigation about both model performance and the internal representations that support the two predictions.

Experiments on two large multiview datasets report performance beyond the previous state of the art. The contribution combines an empirical comparison with an investigation of where the two tasks impose competing requirements. Its practical significance is that designing a joint model requires attention to which variations its representations preserve, as well as which variations they suppress.
summary.tldr: The paper compares CNN architectures and their internal representations for jointly recognizing object categories and estimating pose.

title: A Comparative Analysis and Study of Multiview CNN Models for Joint Object Categorization and Pose Estimation

abstract: We propose a nonparametric statistical test for goodness-of-fit: given a set of samples, the test determines how likely it is that these were generated from a target density function. The measure of goodness-of-fit is a divergence constructed via Stein’s method using functions from a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space. Our test statistic is based on an empirical estimate of this divergence, taking the form of a V-statistic in terms of the log gradients of the target density and the kernel. We derive a statistical test, both for i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. samples, where we estimate the null distribution quantiles using a wild bootstrap procedure. We apply our test to quantifying convergence of approximate Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, statistical model criticism, and evaluating quality of fit vs model complexity in nonparametric density estimation.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether observed samples are consistent with a specified probability density. It proposes a nonparametric goodness-of-fit test, giving a statistical way to assess agreement between data and a target distribution. The task is to evaluate a proposed distribution, rather than simply fit another model to the observations.

The authors construct a measure of discrepancy using Stein’s method and functions from a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. They estimate this discrepancy from samples through a V-statistic involving the kernel and gradients of the target’s log density. This connects the statistical comparison to quantities computed from the observations and the target density.

The test accommodates both independent, identically distributed samples and samples with dependence. A wild bootstrap estimates the reference thresholds used for testing agreement with the target. The paper applies the method to checking approximate Markov chain Monte Carlo convergence, criticizing statistical models, and examining fit against model complexity in nonparametric density estimation. These applications make distribution checking a common tool across several modeling tasks.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based statistical test checks whether independent or dependent samples agree with a target probability density.

title: A Kernel Test of Goodness of Fit

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms involve the deep nesting of highly irregular computation patterns, each of which typically exhibits opportunities for distributed computation. We argue for distributing RL components in a composable way by adapting algorithms for top-down hierarchical control, thereby encapsulating parallelism and resource requirements within short-running compute tasks. We demonstrate the benefits of this principle through RLlib: a library that provides scalable software primitives for RL. These primitives enable a broad range of algorithms to be implemented with high performance, scalability, and substantial code reuse. RLlib is available as part of the open source Ray project at http://rllib.io/.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning algorithms contain nested computations whose structure can be irregular. Opportunities to distribute work appear at several levels, so building a scalable implementation involves more than parallelizing one isolated operation. This paper argues for software components that can be combined while keeping their distributed execution manageable.

The proposed organizing principle is top-down hierarchical control. Parallelism and resource requirements are packaged inside short-running compute tasks, allowing larger algorithms to coordinate components without exposing every internal execution detail. This composability is the central design idea: distributed pieces should remain reusable when assembled into different reinforcement learning algorithms.

RLlib implements this principle as scalable software primitives within the open-source Ray project. The paper demonstrates that these primitives support a broad range of algorithms with high performance, scalability, and substantial code reuse. Its contribution is therefore an architecture for implementing distributed reinforcement learning, connecting the structure of computation to the organization of reusable software rather than introducing a single new learning rule.
summary.tldr: RLlib uses composable distributed tasks and hierarchical control to support scalable reinforcement learning with substantial code reuse.

title: RLlib: Abstractions for Distributed Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In many areas of neuroscience and biological data analysis, it is desired to reveal common patterns among a group of subjects. Such analyses play important roles e.g., in detecting functional brain networks from fMRI scans and in identifying brain regions which show increased activity in response to certain stimuli. Group level techniques usually assume that all subjects in the group behave according to a single statistical model, or that deviations from the common model have simple parametric forms. Therefore, complex subject-specific deviations from the common model severely impair the performance of such methods. In this paper, we propose nonparametric algorithms for estimating the common covariance matrix and the common density function of several variables in a heterogeneous group of subjects. Our estimates converge to the true model as the number of subjects tends to infinity, under very mild conditions. We illustrate the effectiveness of our methods through extensive simulations as well as on real-data from fMRI scans and from arterial blood pressure and photoplethysmogram measurements.

paragraphs: Group analyses often seek patterns shared across people, such as common brain networks or responses to stimuli. Many techniques assume that all subjects follow one statistical model, or differ from it in a simple prescribed way. Complex individual differences can substantially impair those methods and obscure the shared pattern of interest.

The paper proposes nonparametric algorithms for estimating a common covariance matrix and a common density function across a heterogeneous group. These targets describe shared relationships among variables and their joint statistical behavior. The approach addresses subject variation without requiring the simple parametric deviations assumed by the group methods discussed in the paper.

The authors prove that their estimates converge to the true model as the number of subjects grows without bound, under conditions described as very mild. Simulations and applications to fMRI, arterial blood pressure, and photoplethysmogram measurements illustrate effectiveness. The result supports recovering common population behavior despite complex individual variation, with the convergence claim specifically tied to increasing the number of subjects.
summary.tldr: Nonparametric estimators recover shared covariance and density patterns across heterogeneous subjects, with convergence guarantees as subject numbers grow.

title: Revealing Common Statistical Behaviors in Heterogeneous Populations

abstract: We study the control of linear dynamical systems with adversarial disturbances, as opposed to statistical noise. We present an efficient algorithm that achieves nearly-tight regret bounds in this setting. Our result generalizes upon previous work in two main aspects: the algorithm can accommodate adversarial noise in the dynamics, and can handle general convex costs.
originalAbstract: We study the control of linear dynamical systems with adversarial disturbances, as opposed to statistical noise. We present an efficient algorithm that achieves nearly-tight regret bounds in this setting. Our result generalizes upon previous work in two main aspects: the algorithm can accommodate adversarial noise in the dynamics, and can handle general convex costs.

paragraphs: This paper studies control of linear dynamical systems when disturbances can be adversarial. A controller must choose actions as the system evolves, while external disturbances affect that evolution. Treating these disturbances as adversarial asks for performance guarantees that do not depend on modeling them as ordinary statistical noise.

The authors present an efficient algorithm with nearly tight regret bounds. Regret measures accumulated performance relative to a comparison standard, so the result addresses the cost of making control decisions online. A nearly tight bound indicates that the guarantee is close to the relevant achievable limit, rather than merely showing that some bound exists.

The contribution broadens earlier work in two directions at once: it permits adversarial disturbances in the dynamics and supports general convex costs. The latter allows the control objective to take a wider range of convex forms. Together, these features give a theoretical approach to online control under difficult disturbances while retaining computational efficiency. The stated setting remains linear dynamics with convex costs, which defines the scope of the result.
summary.tldr: An efficient online controller achieves nearly tight regret bounds for linear systems with adversarial disturbances and general convex costs.

title: Online Control with Adversarial Disturbances

abstract: This manuscript presents some new impossibility results on adversarial robustness in machine learning, a very important yet largely open problem. We show that if conditioned on a class label the data distribution satisfies the $W_2$ Talagrand transportation-cost inequality (for example, this condition is satisfied if the conditional distribution has density which is log-concave; is the uniform measure on a compact Riemannian manifold with positive Ricci curvature, any classifier can be adversarially fooled with high probability once the perturbations are slightly greater than the natural noise level in the problem. We call this result The Strong "No Free Lunch" Theorem as some recent results (Tsipras et al. 2018, Fawzi et al. 2018, etc.) on the subject can be immediately recovered as very particular cases. Our theoretical bounds are demonstrated on both simulated and real data (MNIST). We conclude the manuscript with some speculation on possible future research directions.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether properties of a data distribution can make adversarial vulnerability unavoidable for any classifier. Its main result is conditional: the distribution within each class must satisfy a mathematical property called the W2 Talagrand transportation-cost inequality. The theorem therefore concerns a specified family of distributions rather than every possible classification problem.

Under that condition, the authors show that a classifier can be fooled with high probability when perturbations become slightly larger than the problem’s natural noise level. The scale of the permitted disturbance is central to the statement. The result ties an impossibility of robustness to the distribution’s structure and noise, rather than to a particular architecture or training procedure.

The authors present this as a strong no-free-lunch theorem because several earlier results follow as special cases. They also demonstrate their theoretical bounds using simulated data and MNIST. The contribution broadens the conditions under which adversarial vulnerability can be established mathematically, while retaining an explicit distributional assumption and perturbation threshold.
summary.tldr: Under a stated class-conditional distribution assumption, perturbations slightly above the natural noise level can fool any classifier with high probability.

title: Generalized No Free Lunch Theorem for Adversarial Robustness

abstract: The field of reinforcement learning (RL) is facing increasingly challenging domains with combinatorial complexity. For an RL agent to address these challenges, it is essential that it can plan effectively. Prior work has typically utilized an explicit model of the environment, combined with a specific planning algorithm (such as tree search). More recently, a new family of methods have been proposed that learn how to plan, by providing the structure for planning via an inductive bias in the function approximator (such as a tree structured neural network), trained end-to-end by a model-free RL algorithm. In this paper, we go even further, and demonstrate empirically that an entirely model-free approach, without special structure beyond standard neural network components such as convolutional networks and LSTMs, can learn to exhibit many of the characteristics typically associated with a model-based planner. We measure our agent’s effectiveness at planning in terms of its ability to generalize across a combinatorial and irreversible state space, its data efficiency, and its ability to utilize additional thinking time. We find that our agent has many of the characteristics that one might expect to find in a planning algorithm. Furthermore, it exceeds the state-of-the-art in challenging combinatorial domains such as Sokoban and outperforms other model-free approaches that utilize strong inductive biases toward planning.

Other approaches build planning-oriented structures directly into a neural network. This paper asks whether an agent trained entirely through model-free reinforcement learning can show planning-like behavior using standard components such as convolutional networks and LSTMs.

The authors evaluate planning through several observable capabilities: generalization across a combinatorial state space with irreversible actions, efficient use of training data, and the ability to benefit from additional thinking time. These criteria examine how the agent behaves when solving difficult problems, rather than identifying planning solely by the presence of a particular architecture.

Their experiments find many characteristics associated with planning algorithms. The agent exceeds the reported state of the art in challenging combinatorial domains including Sokoban, and beats other model-free approaches with strong planning-oriented inductive biases. These are empirical demonstrations that ordinary neural components can learn substantial planning-like capabilities; they do not establish that every model-free agent will develop them.
summary.tldr: A model-free agent built from standard neural components empirically exhibits several planning-like capabilities and strong performance on combinatorial tasks.

title: An Investigation of Model-Free Planning

abstract: Measuring the similarity between data points often requires domain knowledge, which can in parts be compensated by relying on unsupervised methods such as latent-variable models, where similarity/distance is estimated in a more compact latent space. Prevalent is the use of the Euclidean metric, which has the drawback of ignoring information about similarity of data stored in the decoder, as captured by the framework of Riemannian geometry. We propose an extension to the framework of variational auto-encoders allows learning flat latent manifolds, where the Euclidean metric is a proxy for the similarity between data points. This is achieved by defining the latent space as a Riemannian manifold and by regularising the metric tensor to be a scaled identity matrix. Additionally, we replace the compact prior typically used in variational auto-encoders with a recently presented, more expressive hierarchical one—and formulate the learning problem as a constrained optimisation problem. We evaluate our method on a range of data-sets, including a video-tracking benchmark, where the performance of our unsupervised approach nears that of state-of-the-art supervised approaches, while retaining the computational efficiency of straight-line-based approaches.

paragraphs: Latent-variable models can help measure similarity by representing data in a smaller space. However, ordinary Euclidean distance in that space ignores similarity information contained in the decoder. This paper modifies variational autoencoders so that simple distances in the learned latent space better reflect the geometry associated with decoded data.

The authors describe latent space as a Riemannian manifold and regularize its metric tensor toward a scaled identity matrix. In plain terms, they encourage a geometry in which distance behaves uniformly enough for Euclidean measurements to serve as a useful proxy. They also introduce a more expressive hierarchical prior and formulate training as constrained optimization.

The method is evaluated on multiple datasets, including a video-tracking benchmark. On that benchmark, the unsupervised approach approaches the performance of leading supervised methods while keeping the computational efficiency of approaches based on straight lines. The result illustrates the motivation for learning a flatter geometry: incorporating decoder-informed similarity can remain compatible with inexpensive distance calculations.
summary.tldr: A modified variational autoencoder learns flatter latent geometry so efficient Euclidean distances can better represent data similarity.

title: Learning Flat Latent Manifolds with VAEs

abstract: We propose a novel stochastic network model, called Fractal Gaussian Network (FGN), that embodies well-defined and analytically tractable fractal structures. Such fractal structures have been empirically observed in diverse applications. FGNs interpolate continuously between the popular purely random geometric graphs (a.k.a. the Poisson Boolean network), and random graphs with increasingly fractal behavior. In fact, they form a parametric family of sparse random geometric graphs that are parametrised by a fractality parameter $\nu$ which governs the strength of the fractal structure. FGNs are driven by the latent spatial geometry of Gaussian Multiplicative Chaos (GMC), a canonical model of fractality in its own right. We explore the natural question of detecting the presence of fractality and the problem of parameter estimation based on observed network data. Finally, we explore fractality in community structures by unveiling a natural stochastic block model in the setting of FGNs.

paragraphs: Fractal patterns have been observed in networks across diverse applications, motivating models that express this structure explicitly. This paper introduces Fractal Gaussian Networks, a family of sparse random geometric graphs with mathematically defined and analytically tractable fractal behavior. The aim is to make fractality something that can be modeled and investigated systematically.

A parameter controls the strength of the fractal structure. Varying it continuously connects familiar purely random geometric graphs with networks exhibiting increasingly fractal behavior. The underlying spatial geometry comes from Gaussian Multiplicative Chaos, which supplies the model’s source of fractality. This construction places different degrees of fractal organization within a single parameterized family.

The authors explore whether observed network data can reveal the presence of fractality and how the model’s parameters can be estimated. They also introduce a natural stochastic block model within the same setting to examine fractal community structure. These directions connect the graph construction to questions about detecting, measuring, and organizing fractality in observed networks.
summary.tldr: Fractal Gaussian Networks provide a tractable sparse graph family with adjustable fractality and extensions for studying community structure.

title: Fractal Gaussian Networks: A sparse random graph model based on Gaussian Multiplicative Chaos

abstract: Drug discovery aims to find novel compounds with specified chemical property profiles. In terms of generative modeling, the goal is to learn to sample molecules in the intersection of multiple property constraints. This task becomes increasingly challenging when there are many property constraints. We propose to offset this complexity by composing molecules from a vocabulary of substructures that we call molecular rationales. These rationales are identified from molecules as substructures that are likely responsible for each property of interest. We then learn to expand rationales into a full molecule using graph generative models. Our final generative model composes molecules as mixtures of multiple rationale completions, and this mixture is fine-tuned to preserve the properties of interest. We evaluate our model on various drug design tasks and demonstrate significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy, diversity, and novelty of generated compounds.

We then learn to expand rationales into a full molecule using graph generative models. paragraphs: Molecule generation for drug discovery often requires satisfying several chemical-property constraints at once. As more constraints are added, sampling compounds in their intersection becomes increasingly difficult. This paper approaches that challenge by building around interpretable molecular substructures associated with the individual properties of interest.

The authors call these substructures molecular rationales. They identify them within molecules as pieces likely to account for a desired property, then train graph generative models to expand them into complete molecules. The final generator combines multiple rationale completions through a mixture model and fine-tunes that mixture to preserve the target properties.

This design gives property-related substructures an explicit role in generation, rather than leaving the entire multi-property problem to an undifferentiated molecular representation. Evaluations on several drug-design tasks show significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in accuracy, diversity, and novelty of generated compounds. The rationales are described as likely contributors to properties, so their interpretability should not be read as proof that each substructure causally guarantees its associated property.
summary.tldr: The model expands property-associated molecular substructures into compounds, improving multi-objective generation in accuracy, diversity, and novelty.

title: Multi-Objective Molecule Generation using Interpretable Substructures

abstract: We propose a latent space energy-based prior model for text generation and classification. The model stands on a generator network that generates the text sequence based on a continuous latent vector. The energy term of the prior model couples a continuous latent vector and a symbolic one-hot vector, so that discrete category can be inferred from the observed example based on the continuous latent vector. Such a latent space coupling naturally enables incorporation of information bottleneck regularization to encourage the continuous latent vector to extract information from the observed example that is informative of the underlying category. In our learning method, the symbol-vector coupling, the generator network and the inference network are learned jointly. Our model can be learned in an unsupervised setting where no category labels are provided. It can also be learned in semi-supervised setting where category labels are provided for a subset of training examples. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed model learns well-structured and meaningful latent space, which (1) guides the generator to generate text with high quality, diversity, and interpretability, and (2) effectively classifies text.

The model stands on a generator network that generates the text sequence based on a continuous latent vector. The energy term of the prior model couples a continuous latent vector and a symbolic one-hot vector, so that discrete category can be inferred from the observed example based on the continuous latent vector. Such a latent space coupling naturally enables incorporation of information bottleneck regularization to encourage the continuous latent vector to extract information from the observed example that is informative of the underlying category. In our learning method, the symbol-vector coupling, the generator network and the inference network are learned jointly. Our model can be learned in an unsupervised setting where no category labels are provided. It can also be learned in semi-supervised setting where category labels are provided for a subset of training examples. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed model learns well-structured and meaningful latent space, which (1) guides the generator to generate text with high quality, diversity, and interpretability, and (2) effectively classifies text.

The category-vector relationship, generator, and inference network are learned jointly, so the representation’s organization develops alongside the mechanisms that interpret and generate text.

Training can proceed without category labels or in a semi-supervised setting where only some examples have labels. Experiments show a meaningful, well-structured latent space that supports both effective classification and generation with high quality, diversity, and interpretability. The stated findings suggest that coupling symbolic categories with continuous representations can serve both tasks within one learned model, including settings with limited or absent category supervision.
summary.tldr: An energy-based prior couples continuous text representations with discrete categories to support generation and classification with limited or no labels.

title: Latent Space Energy-Based Model of Symbol-Vector Coupling for Text Generation and Classification

abstract: Learning to classify time series with limited data is a practical yet challenging problem. Current methods are primarily based on hand-designed feature extraction rules or domain-specific data augmentation. Motivated by the advances in deep speech processing models and the fact that voice data are univariate temporal signals, in this paper we propose Voice2Serie (V2S), a novel end-to-end approach that reprograms acoustic models for time series classification, through input transformation learning and output label mapping. Leveraging the representation learning power of a large-scale pre-trained speech processing model, on 31 different time series tasks we show that V2S outperforms or is on part with state-of-the-art methods on 22 tasks, and improves their average accuracy by 1.72%. We further provide theoretical justification of V2S by proving its population risk is upper bounded by the source risk and a Wasserstein distance accounting for feature alignment via reprogramming. Our results offer new and effective means to time series classification.

Voice2Series learns an input transformation and an output-label mapping to reprogram the acoustic model for the target classification task. These components connect the new inputs and desired outputs to the pretrained model in an end-to-end approach. The method draws on the speech model’s representation-learning capability instead of relying solely on hand-designed features or domain-specific augmentation.

The authors also prove a population-risk upper bound involving source risk and a Wasserstein distance measuring feature alignment through reprogramming. This connects the theoretical justification to how well the transformed target data align with the source model’s features.
summary.tldr: Voice2Series reprograms pretrained speech models through learned input transformations and label mappings for time-series classification.

title: Voice2Series: Reprogramming Acoustic Models for Time Series Classification

abstract: Reliable evaluation benchmarks designed for replicability and comprehensiveness have driven progress in machine learning. Due to the lack of a multilingual benchmark, however, vision-and-language research has mostly focused on English language tasks. To fill this gap, we introduce the Image-Grounded Language Understanding Evaluation benchmark. IGLUE brings together{—}by both aggregating pre-existing datasets and creating new ones{—}visual question answering, cross-modal retrieval, grounded reasoning, and grounded entailment tasks across 20 diverse languages. Our benchmark enables the evaluation of multilingual multimodal models for transfer learning, not only in a zero-shot setting, but also in newly defined few-shot learning setups. Based on the evaluation of the available state-of-the-art models, we find that translate-test transfer is superior to zero-shot transfer and that few-shot learning is hard to harness for many tasks. Moreover, downstream performance is partially explained by the amount of available unlabelled textual data for pretraining, and only weakly by the typological distance of target{–}source languages. We hope to encourage future research efforts in this area by releasing the benchmark to the community.

paragraphs: IGLUE addresses an evaluation gap that has kept much vision-and-language research centered on English. It combines existing datasets with newly created ones to evaluate models across 20 languages. Its tasks cover answering questions about images, retrieving across text and images, reasoning grounded in images, and judging grounded entailment.

The benchmark evaluates transfer both without target-task examples and through newly defined few-shot setups. This makes it possible to examine whether multilingual multimodal models transfer directly and whether a small amount of additional supervision helps. Its breadth also allows performance to be compared across different kinds of image-grounded language understanding.

In evaluations of available leading models, translating test inputs performs better than direct zero-shot transfer, while few-shot learning is difficult to exploit for many tasks. The amount of unlabeled pretraining text partly explains downstream performance; linguistic distance between source and target languages explains it only weakly. These findings identify practical weaknesses in the evaluated models and provide a shared benchmark for studying them.
summary.tldr: IGLUE evaluates multilingual vision-and-language transfer across 20 languages, revealing difficulties with direct zero-shot and few-shot transfer.

title: IGLUE: A Benchmark for Transfer Learning across Modalities, Tasks, and Languages

abstract: Private inference (PI) enables inferences directly on cryptographically secure data. While promising to address many privacy issues, it has seen limited use due to extreme runtimes. Unlike plaintext inference, where latency is dominated by FLOPs, in PI non-linear functions (namely ReLU) are the bottleneck. Thus, practical PI demands novel ReLU-aware optimizations. To reduce PI latency we propose a gradient-based algorithm that selectively linearizes ReLUs while maintaining prediction accuracy. We evaluate our algorithm on several standard PI benchmarks. The results demonstrate up to $4.25%$ more accuracy (iso-ReLU count at 50K) or $2.2\times$ less latency (iso-accuracy at 70%) than the current state of the art and advance the Pareto frontier across the latency-accuracy space. To complement empirical results, we present a “no free lunch" theorem that sheds light on how and when network linearization is possible while maintaining prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: Private inference runs predictions directly on cryptographically protected data, but its runtime can be extremely high. The relevant computational bottleneck differs from ordinary inference: nonlinear functions such as ReLU dominate latency. This paper therefore targets the number and placement of nonlinear activations as a route to faster private prediction.

The authors propose a gradient-based method that selectively turns ReLUs into linear operations while maintaining prediction accuracy. This adjusts the network around the costs of private execution. The optimization seeks useful accuracy-latency tradeoffs by deciding which nonlinearities the model can give up.

On standard private-inference benchmarks, the method reports up to 4.25% higher accuracy at a fixed count of 50,000 ReLUs, or 2.2 times lower latency at a fixed accuracy of 70%, compared with the current state of the art. These are separate comparison settings. A complementary no-free-lunch theorem examines how and when linearization can preserve accuracy, connecting the empirical improvements to theoretical constraints on removing network nonlinearity.
summary.tldr: Selective ReLU linearization improves the accuracy-latency tradeoff of neural inference on cryptographically protected data.

title: Selective Network Linearization for Efficient Private Inference

abstract: Continual learning—learning new tasks in sequence while maintaining performance on old tasks—remains particularly challenging for artificial neural networks. Surprisingly, the amount of forgetting does not increase with the dissimilarity between the learned tasks, but appears to be worst in an intermediate similarity regime. In this paper we theoretically analyse both a synthetic teacher-student framework and a real data setup to provide an explanation of this phenomenon that we name Maslow’s Hammer hypothesis. Our analysis reveals the presence of a trade-off between node activation and node re-use that results in worst forgetting in the intermediate regime. Using this understanding we reinterpret popular algorithmic interventions for catastrophic interference in terms of this trade-off, and identify the regimes in which they are most effective.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a neural network to acquire new tasks while retaining earlier ones. A puzzling observation is that forgetting does not simply grow as tasks become more different. Instead, it appears most severe when tasks have an intermediate degree of similarity. This paper seeks a theoretical explanation for that pattern.

The authors analyze both a synthetic teacher-student framework and a real-data setup. Their explanation, called the Maslow’s Hammer hypothesis, centers on a trade-off between activating nodes and reusing nodes. The analysis connects this trade-off to the intermediate-similarity regime where forgetting is worst, giving task similarity a more nuanced role in interference.

The paper then uses this account to reinterpret popular interventions against catastrophic forgetting. It identifies the regimes in which those interventions are most effective through their relationship to activation and reuse. The contribution is an explanation that helps organize existing methods: understanding how tasks engage network nodes provides a basis for assessing when a particular intervention is likely to help.
summary.tldr: A trade-off between node activation and reuse explains why forgetting can peak at intermediate task similarity.

title: Maslow’s Hammer in Catastrophic Forgetting: Node Re-Use vs. Node Activation

abstract: This paper studies the accelerated gradient descent for general nonconvex problems under the gradient Lipschitz and Hessian Lipschitz assumptions. We establish that a simple restarted accelerated gradient descent (AGD) finds an $\epsilon$-approximate first-order stationary point in $O(\epsilon^{-7/4})$ gradient computations with simple proofs. Our complexity does not hide any polylogarithmic factors, and thus it improves over the state-of-the-art one by the $O(\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ factor. Our simple algorithm only consists of Nesterov’s classical AGD and a restart mechanism, and it does not need the negative curvature exploitation or the optimization of regularized surrogate functions. Technically, our simple proof does not invoke the analysis for the strongly convex AGD, which is crucial to remove the $O(\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ factor.

paragraphs: The paper studies how quickly accelerated gradient descent can reach an approximately stationary point of a nonconvex objective. Such a point has a sufficiently small gradient, so the target is a first-order stationarity guarantee. The analysis assumes both Lipschitz gradients and Lipschitz Hessians, controlling how rapidly derivatives change.

The proposed algorithm combines Nesterov’s classical accelerated gradient descent with a restart mechanism. It reaches an ε-approximate first-order stationary point using O(ε^−7/4) gradient computations. The bound contains no hidden polylogarithmic factors, improving the stated previous complexity by a factor of O(log(1/ε)). This makes the dependence on the requested accuracy sharper.

The method does not require explicit negative-curvature exploitation or optimization of regularized surrogate objectives. The proof is also simplified: it avoids relying on the analysis of strongly convex accelerated gradient descent, which the authors identify as crucial for removing the logarithmic factor. The contribution couples a simpler algorithmic structure with a tighter computation bound under the stated smoothness assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under Lipschitz gradient and Hessian assumptions, restarted accelerated gradient descent reaches approximate first-order stationarity in O(ε^−7/4) gradient computations without hidden logarithmic factors.

title: Restarted Nonconvex Accelerated Gradient Descent: No More Polylogarithmic Factor in the $O(ε^-7/4)$ Complexity

abstract: The ubiquity of distributed machine learning (ML) in sensitive public domain applications calls for algorithms that protect data privacy, while being robust to faults and adversarial behaviors. Although privacy and robustness have been extensively studied independently in distributed ML, their synthesis remains poorly understood. We present the first tight analysis of the error incurred by any algorithm ensuring robustness against a fraction of adversarial machines, as well as differential privacy (DP) for honest machines’ data against any other curious entity. Our analysis exhibits a fundamental trade-off between privacy, robustness, and utility. To prove our lower bound, we consider the case of mean estimation, subject to distributed DP and robustness constraints, and devise reductions to centralized estimation of one-way marginals. We prove our matching upper bound by presenting a new distributed ML algorithm using a high-dimensional robust aggregation rule. The latter amortizes the dependence on the dimension in the error (caused by adversarial workers and DP), while being agnostic to the statistical properties of the data.

paragraphs: Distributed learning may need to protect honest participants' data while tolerating machines that behave adversarially. These goals have often been studied separately. This paper analyzes their combined effect on utility, expressed through the error incurred by algorithms that provide both differential privacy and robustness against a fraction of adversarial machines.

The authors establish a tight trade-off by proving both a lower bound and a matching upper bound. The lower-bound argument studies mean estimation under distributed privacy and robustness requirements, reducing it to centralized estimation of one-way marginals. It identifies an error cost that any algorithm meeting the stated requirements must incur, rather than a weakness of one particular implementation.

To match that lower bound, the paper introduces a distributed learning algorithm with a high-dimensional robust aggregation rule. The rule amortizes the dimension dependence in the error caused jointly by adversarial workers and privacy, without relying on the data's statistical properties. Together, the bounds characterize both an unavoidable cost and an attainable performance level, clarifying why privacy, robustness, and utility cannot be optimized independently in this setting.
summary.tldr: Matching error bounds characterize a fundamental trade-off between privacy, adversarial robustness, and utility in distributed learning.

title: On the Privacy-Robustness-Utility Trilemma in Distributed Learning

abstract: Reward machines (RMs) are a recent formalism for representing the reward function of a reinforcement learning task through a finite-state machine whose edges encode subgoals of the task using high-level events. The structure of RMs enables the decomposition of a task into simpler and independently solvable subtasks that help tackle long-horizon and/or sparse reward tasks. We propose a formalism for further abstracting the subtask structure by endowing an RM with the ability to call other RMs, thus composing a hierarchy of RMs (HRM). We exploit HRMs by treating each call to an RM as an independently solvable subtask using the options framework, and describe a curriculum-based method to learn HRMs from traces observed by the agent. Our experiments reveal that exploiting a handcrafted HRM leads to faster convergence than with a flat HRM, and that learning an HRM is feasible in cases where its equivalent flat representation is not.

paragraphs: Reward machines describe a reinforcement learning task using a finite-state machine whose transitions encode subgoals through high-level events. This structure exposes smaller tasks that can be solved independently, helping with long horizons and sparse rewards. The paper extends that idea by allowing a reward machine to call another reward machine.

These calls create a hierarchy in which task structure can be expressed at multiple levels. The authors use the options framework to treat each call as an independently solvable subtask. They also describe a curriculum-based method for learning a hierarchy from traces observed by the agent, connecting the representation to experience rather than relying only on manual construction.

Experiments show that exploiting a handcrafted hierarchy produces faster convergence than using a flat representation. They also show that learning a hierarchy is feasible in cases where learning its equivalent flat form is not. These findings demonstrate that hierarchical structure can benefit both the agent's task learning and the process of acquiring the task representation itself.
summary.tldr: Reward machines that call other reward machines enable faster task learning and make some otherwise infeasible reward representations learnable.

title: Hierarchies of Reward Machines

abstract: We propose a tuning-free dynamic SGD step size formula, which we call Distance over Gradients (DoG). The DoG step sizes depend on simple empirical quantities (distance from the initial point and norms of gradients) and have no “learning rate” parameter. Theoretically, we show that, for stochastic convex optimization, a slight variation of the DoG formula enjoys strong, high-probability parameter-free convergence guarantees and iterate movement bounds. Empirically, we consider a broad range of vision and language transfer learning tasks, and show that DoG’s performance is close to that of SGD with tuned learning rate. We also propose a per-layer variant of DoG that generally outperforms tuned SGD, approaching the performance of tuned Adam. A PyTorch implementation of our algorithms is available at https://github.com/formll/dog.

Theoretically, we show that, for stochastic convex optimization, a slight variation of the DoG formula enjoys strong, high-probability parameter-free convergence guarantees and iterate movement bounds. Empirically, we consider a broad range of vision and language transfer learning tasks, and show that DoG’s performance is close to that of SGD with tuned learning rate. We also propose a per-layer variant of DoG that generally outperforms tuned SGD, approaching the performance of tuned Adam. paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent requires step sizes that determine how far each update moves the model. Choosing their scale usually involves tuning a learning rate. Distance over Gradients, or DoG, replaces that choice with a dynamic formula based on quantities observed during optimization: distance from the starting point and the sizes of gradients.

The formula has no learning-rate parameter, making the update scale responsive to the optimization trajectory itself. For stochastic convex optimization, the authors analyze a slight variation of DoG and establish strong convergence guarantees that hold with high probability, together with bounds on how far the iterates move. These theoretical claims apply to the analyzed variation and setting.

Empirically, DoG performs close to learning-rate-tuned SGD across a broad collection of vision and language transfer tasks. A layer-specific version generally surpasses tuned SGD and approaches tuned Adam in those evaluations. The results suggest that simple measurements gathered during training can replace substantial learning-rate tuning while preserving much of the performance of carefully tuned optimizers.
summary.tldr: DoG sets SGD step sizes from observed distances and gradient norms, achieving performance close to tuned SGD without a learning-rate parameter.

title: DoG is SGD’s Best Friend: A Parameter-Free Dynamic Step Size Schedule

abstract: The fairness of machine learning-based decisions has become an increasingly important focus in the design of supervised machine learning methods. Most fairness approaches optimize a specified trade-off between performance measure(s) (e.g., accuracy, log loss, or AUC) and fairness metric(s) (e.g., demographic parity, equalized odds). This begs the question: are the right performance-fairness trade-offs being specified? We instead re-cast fair machine learning as an imitation learning task by introducing superhuman fairness, which seeks to simultaneously outperform human decisions on multiple predictive performance and fairness measures. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach given suboptimal decisions.
originalAbstract: The fairness of machine learning-based decisions has become an increasingly important focus in the design of supervised machine learning methods. Most fairness approaches optimize a specified trade-off between performance measure(s) (e.g., accuracy, log loss, or AUC) and fairness metric(s) (e.g., demographic parity, equalized odds). This begs the question: are the right performance-fairness trade-offs being specified? We instead re-cast fair machine learning as an imitation learning task by introducing superhuman fairness, which seeks to simultaneously outperform human decisions on multiple predictive performance and fairness measures. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach given suboptimal decisions.

paragraphs: Fair machine learning often starts by specifying how predictive performance should trade off against fairness. A method then optimizes that chosen compromise. This paper asks whether the trade-off itself is the right one, since selecting it determines which combinations of performance and fairness the method will pursue.

The authors introduce superhuman fairness as an imitation-learning formulation. Human decisions provide the reference point, and the objective is to surpass them simultaneously on multiple measures of predictive performance and fairness. This shifts attention toward whether a learned decision system can improve several aspects of the decisions already being made.

The paper demonstrates benefits when the reference decisions are suboptimal. That condition matters: the proposed goal is to exploit opportunities for joint improvement, and the abstract does not establish that such opportunities always exist. The contribution is a different formulation of fair learning, grounded in improving observed decisions across multiple measures rather than beginning with a specified performance-fairness compromise.
summary.tldr: Superhuman fairness frames fair learning as surpassing human decisions on multiple predictive and fairness measures, with benefits demonstrated for suboptimal decisions.

title: Superhuman Fairness

abstract: Neural Differential Equations have become an important modeling framework due to their ability to adapt to new problems automatically. Training a neural differential equation is effectively a search over a space of plausible dynamical systems. Controlling the computational cost for these models is difficult since it relies on the number of steps the adaptive solver takes. Most prior works have used higher-order methods to reduce prediction timings while greatly increasing training time or reducing both training and prediction timings by relying on specific training algorithms, which are harder to use as a drop-in replacement. In this manuscript, we use internal cost heuristics of adaptive differential equation solvers at stochastic time-points to guide the training towards learning a dynamical system that is easier to integrate . We “close the blackbox” and allow the use of our method with any sensitivity method. We perform experimental studies to compare our method to global regularization to show that we attain similar performance numbers without compromising on the flexibility of implementation. We develop two sampling strategies to trade-off between performance and training time . Our method reduces the number of function evaluations to 0.556x - 0.733x and accelerates predictions by 1.3x - 2x.

paragraphs: A neural differential equation learns a dynamical system, but its computational cost depends on how many steps an adaptive numerical solver needs to follow that system. Earlier approaches to reducing this cost can increase training time or depend on particular training algorithms. This paper seeks dynamics that are easier to integrate while retaining flexibility in how gradients are computed.

The method uses cost heuristics already available inside adaptive solvers and evaluates them at randomly sampled times during training. These local signals guide the learned system toward behavior that the solver can handle more efficiently. The construction supports any sensitivity method, and the authors develop two sampling strategies that offer different tradeoffs between performance and training time.

Experiments report performance comparable to global regularization while preserving implementation flexibility. The number of function evaluations falls to between 0.556 and 0.733 times the comparison level, and predictions become 1.3 to 2 times faster. The results show that solver-aware training signals can reduce prediction cost without requiring the method to be tied to a particular gradient-computation approach.
summary.tldr: Local solver-cost regularization learns neural differential equations that are easier to integrate, accelerating predictions while supporting any sensitivity method.

title: Locally Regularized Neural Differential Equations: Some Black Boxes were meant to remain closed!

abstract: In this paper, we propose sample complexity bounds for learning a simplex from noisy samples. A dataset of size $n$ is given which includes i.i.d. samples drawn from a uniform distribution over an unknown arbitrary simplex in $\mathbb{R}^K$, where samples are assumed to be corrupted by a multi-variate additive Gaussian noise of an arbitrary magnitude. We prove the existence of an algorithm that with high probability outputs a simplex having a $\ell_2$ distance of at most $\varepsilon$ from the true simplex (for any $\varepsilon>0$). Also, we theoretically show that in order to achieve this bound, it is sufficient to have $n\ge\tilde{\Omega}\left(K^2/\varepsilon^2\right)e^{\Omega\left(K/\mathrm{SNR}^2\right)}$ samples, where $\mathrm{SNR}$ stands for the signal-to-noise ratio and is defined as the ratio of the maximum component-wise standard deviation of the simplex (signal) to that of the noise vector. This result solves an important open problem in this area of research, and shows as long as $\mathrm{SNR}\ge\Omega\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ the sample complexity of the noisy regime has the same order to that of the noiseless case. Our proofs are a combination of the so-called sample compression technique in (Ashtiani et al., 2018), mathematical tools from high-dimensional geometry, and Fourier analysis. In particular, we have proposed a general Fourier-based technique for recovery of a more general class of distribution families from additive Gaussian noise, which can be further used in a variety of other related problems.

Our proofs are a combination of the so-called sample compression technique in (Ashtiani et al., 2018), mathematical tools from high-dimensional geometry, and Fourier analysis. In particular, we have proposed a general Fourier-based technique for recovery of a more general class of distribution families from additive Gaussian noise, which can be further used in a variety of other related problems.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many observations suffice to recover an unknown high-dimensional simplex when the observations are noisy. Samples are assumed to be independent draws from the uniform distribution over the simplex, corrupted by additive multivariate Gaussian noise. The noise can have arbitrary magnitude, with its effect reflected in the sample requirement.

The authors prove that an algorithm exists which recovers a simplex within any specified positive L2 error tolerance with high probability. Their sufficient sample bound combines dimension and inverse-accuracy factors with an exponential dependence involving dimension divided by squared signal-to-noise ratio. This is a sufficiency result, not a claim that the displayed sample count is necessary.

When signal-to-noise ratio is at least on the order of the square root of dimension, the resulting sample complexity matches the noiseless order. The proofs combine sample compression, high-dimensional geometry, and Fourier analysis. They also introduce a Fourier-based recovery technique for a broader class of distributions under additive Gaussian noise, which may be useful in related recovery problems.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds sufficient samples for recovering a simplex under Gaussian noise and identifies a signal regime matching noiseless sample complexity.

title: Sample Complexity Bounds for Learning High-dimensional Simplices in Noisy Regimes

abstract: The question-answering (QA) capabilities of foundation models are highly sensitive to prompt variations, rendering their performance susceptible to superficial, non-meaning-altering changes. This vulnerability often stems from the model’s preference or bias towards specific input characteristics, such as option position or superficial image features in multi-modal settings. We propose to rectify this bias directly in the model’s internal representation. Our approach, SteerFair, finds the bias direction in the model’s representation space and steers activation values away from it during inference. Specifically, we exploit the observation that bias often adheres to simple association rules, such as the spurious association between the first option and correctness likelihood. Next, we construct demonstrations of these rules from unlabeled samples and use them to identify the bias directions. We empirically show that SteerFair significantly reduces instruction-tuned model performance variance across prompt modifications on three benchmark tasks. Remarkably, our approach surpasses a supervised baseline with 100 labels by an average of 10.86% accuracy points and 12.95 score points and matches the performance with 500 labels.

summary.tldr: SteerFair uses unlabeled examples to identify internal bias directions and reduce sensitivity to superficial prompt changes.

title: Discovering Bias in Latent Space: An Unsupervised Debiasing Approach

abstract: The emergence of accurate open large language models (LLMs) has led to a race towards performant quantization techniques which can enable their execution on end-user devices. In this paper, we revisit the problem of “extreme” LLM compression—defined as targeting extremely low bit counts, such as 2 to 3 bits per parameter—from the point of view of classic methods in Multi-Codebook Quantization (MCQ). Our algorithm, called AQLM, generalizes the classic Additive Quantization (AQ) approach for information retrieval to advance the state-of-the-art in LLM compression, via two innovations: 1) learned additive quantization of weight matrices in input-adaptive fashion, and 2) joint optimization of codebook parameters across each transformer blocks. Broadly, AQLM is the first scheme that is Pareto optimal in terms of accuracy-vs-model-size when compressing to less than 3 bits per parameter, and significantly improves upon all known schemes in the extreme compression (2bit) regime. In addition, AQLM is practical: we provide fast GPU and CPU implementations of AQLM for token generation, which enable us to match or outperform optimized FP16 implementations for speed, while executing in a much smaller memory footprint.

paragraphs: Running large language models on end-user devices motivates compression to very small storage budgets. This paper targets extreme quantization, including representations using only two to three bits per parameter. Its method, AQLM, adapts additive quantization from information retrieval to compress language-model weights while retaining useful predictive accuracy.

It learns additive representations of weight matrices in a way that adapts to their inputs, and it jointly optimizes codebook parameters within each transformer block. The method therefore coordinates the compressed representation across a block instead of treating its codebook parameters as entirely independent choices.

These results connect compression quality with practical execution, showing that the representation can support efficient inference as well as smaller storage.
summary.tldr: AQLM uses learned additive quantization to improve extreme LLM compression while supporting fast CPU and GPU token generation.

title: Extreme Compression of Large Language Models via Additive Quantization

abstract: Recent work provides promising evidence that Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN) can efficiently solve partial differential equations (PDE). However, previous works have failed to provide guarantees on the worst-case residual error of a PINN across the spatio-temporal domain - a measure akin to the tolerance of numerical solvers - focusing instead on point-wise comparisons between their solution and the ones obtained by a solver on a set of inputs. In real-world applications, one cannot consider tests on a finite set of points to be sufficient grounds for deployment, as the performance could be substantially worse on a different set. To alleviate this issue, we establish guaranteed error-based conditions for PINNs over their continuous applicability domain. To verify the extent to which they hold, we introduce $\partial$-CROWN: a general, efficient and scalable post-training framework to bound PINN residual errors. We demonstrate its effectiveness in obtaining tight certificates by applying it to two classically studied PINNs – Burgers’ and Schrödinger’s equations –, and two more challenging ones with real-world applications – the Allan-Cahn and Diffusion-Sorption equations.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks approximate solutions to partial differential equations, but checking their outputs at selected points leaves gaps between those checks. A model could behave substantially worse elsewhere in its space-and-time domain. This paper addresses that gap by seeking guarantees on worst-case residual error throughout the continuous domain where the model is intended to apply.

The authors establish error-based conditions and introduce partial-CROWN, a framework that bounds residual errors after a network has been trained. Residual error measures how closely the network satisfies the governing equation. Certifying that quantity across a domain gives a different form of evidence from comparing predictions with a numerical solver at a finite collection of inputs.

The framework is presented as general, efficient, and scalable. The authors demonstrate tight certificates for networks associated with Burgers', Schrödinger's, Allan-Cahn, and Diffusion-Sorption equations. These results show how post-training certification can strengthen the evidence available for a physics-informed network by bounding equation violations beyond individually tested locations.
summary.tldr: Partial-CROWN certifies bounds on physics-informed neural networks' residual errors across continuous domains after training.

title: Efficient Error Certification for Physics-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: Masked face recognition is important for social good but challenged by diverse occlusions that cause insufficient or inaccurate representations. In this work, we propose a unified deep network to learn generative-to-discriminative representations for facilitating masked face recognition. To this end, we split the network into three modules and learn them on synthetic masked faces in a greedy module-wise pretraining manner. First, we leverage a generative encoder pretrained for face inpainting and finetune it to represent masked faces into category-aware descriptors. Attribute to the generative encoder’s ability in recovering context information, the resulting descriptors can provide occlusion-robust representations for masked faces, mitigating the effect of diverse masks. Then, we incorporate a multi-layer convolutional network as a discriminative reformer and learn it to convert the category-aware descriptors into identity-aware vectors, where the learning is effectively supervised by distilling relation knowledge from off-the-shelf face recognition model. In this way, the discriminative reformer together with the generative encoder serves as the pretrained backbone, providing general and discriminative representations towards masked faces. Finally, we cascade one fully-connected layer following by one softmax layer into a feature classifier and finetune it to identify the reformed identity-aware vectors. Extensive experiments on synthetic and realistic datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in recognizing masked faces.

paragraphs: Masks obscure facial information and can make face representations incomplete or inaccurate. This paper proposes a unified network that transfers information from a generative task into identity recognition. It trains three modules in sequence using synthetic masked faces, giving each stage a distinct role in handling occlusion and distinguishing identities.

First, an encoder pretrained for face inpainting is fine-tuned to produce category-aware descriptors of masked faces. Its ability to recover contextual information supports representations that are robust to different masks. A multilayer convolutional module then converts those descriptors into identity-aware vectors. This conversion is supervised by distilling relational knowledge from an existing face recognition model.

The encoder and conversion module together form the pretrained backbone. A final classifier, consisting of a fully connected layer followed by a softmax layer, is fine-tuned to identify the resulting vectors. Experiments on synthetic and realistic datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The central idea is to connect contextual recovery with identity discrimination through an explicitly staged representation-learning process.
summary.tldr: The method turns representations learned for face inpainting into identity-aware features to improve masked face recognition.

title: Masked Face Recognition with Generative-to-Discriminative Representations

abstract: The $k$-Weisfeiler-Leman ($k$-WL) graph isomorphism test hierarchy is a common method for assessing the expressive power of graph neural networks (GNNs). Recently, GNNs whose expressive power is equivalent to the $2$-WL test were proven to be universal on weighted graphs which encode $3\mathrm{D}$ point cloud data, yet this result is limited to invariant continuous functions on point clouds. In this paper, we extend this result in three ways: Firstly, we show that PPGN can simulate $2$-WL uniformly on all point clouds with low complexity. Secondly, we show that $2$-WL tests can be extended to point clouds which include both positions and velocities, a scenario often encountered in applications. Finally, we provide a general framework for proving equivariant universality and leverage it to prove that a simple modification of this invariant PPGN architecture can be used to obtain a universal equivariant architecture that can approximate all continuous equivariant functions uniformly. Building on our results, we develop our WeLNet architecture, which sets new state-of-the-art results on the N-Body dynamics task and the GEOM-QM9 molecular conformation generation task.

paragraphs: The Weisfeiler–Leman hierarchy provides a way to reason about what graph neural networks can distinguish and represent. Earlier results connected the 2-WL test to universal approximation of continuous invariant functions on weighted graphs encoding three-dimensional point clouds. This paper extends that connection toward richer inputs and outputs that transform with the geometry.

The authors first show that PPGN can simulate 2-WL uniformly across point clouds with low complexity. They then extend the tests to point clouds containing both positions and velocities. A further theoretical framework establishes equivariant universality: a simple modification of invariant PPGN can uniformly approximate all continuous equivariant functions within the stated framework.

Building on these results, the authors introduce WeLNet and report state-of-the-art results on N-Body dynamics and GEOM-QM9 molecular conformation generation. The paper thus connects expressiveness theory to a working architecture. Its approximation result concerns what the architecture can represent, while the task results provide separate empirical evidence that the construction is effective in the evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: Extensions of 2-WL establish equivariant approximation results and motivate WeLNet, which achieves leading results on two geometric learning tasks.

title: Weisfeiler Leman for Euclidean Equivariant Machine Learning

abstract: Learning to assemble geometric shapes into a larger target structure is a pivotal task in various practical applications. In this work, we tackle this problem by establishing local correspondences between point clouds of part shapes in both coarse- and fine-levels. To this end, we introduce Proxy Match Transform (PMT), an approximate high-order feature transform layer that enables reliable matching between mating surfaces of parts while incurring low costs in memory and compute. Building upon PMT, we introduce a new framework, dubbed Proxy Match TransformeR (PMTR), for the geometric assembly task. We evaluate the proposed PMTR on the large-scale 3D geometric shape assembly benchmark dataset of Breaking Bad and demonstrate its superior performance and efficiency compared to state-of-the-art methods. Project page: https://nahyuklee.github.io/pmtr
